Why does the Firebase integration guide require enabling `output: 'server'` in astro.config.mjs before initializing Firebase in an Astro project?

Because the Firebase setup is server-side: `src/firebase/server.ts` initializes `firebase-admin` with service account credentials, and the guide's Firestore and auth steps rely on server endpoints (`APIRoute` handlers such as `POST /api/friends`) that must execute when a request arrives. The guide lists "An Astro project with `output: 'server'` for on-demand rendering enabled" as a prerequisite of initializing Firebase — that output mode is what provides the runtime for the Admin SDK initialization and those API routes. The browser-side `firebase` package in `client.ts` alone would not require it.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/backend/firebase/

In production the Firebase server initialization calls `initializeApp()` with no arguments, but locally it passes `cert(serviceAccount)`. Why does the no-argument call work when deployed to Firebase Functions but not on your local machine?

Because on Firebase Functions the default configuration is already injected into the server by Firebase — the code comment in `initApp()` states "Use default config in firebase functions. Should be already injected in the server by Firebase" — so `initializeApp()` with no arguments picks up that ambient service account when `import.meta.env.PROD` is set. Your local machine has no such injected default config, so the no-argument call has nothing to authenticate with; locally you must pass credentials explicitly with `initializeApp({ credential: cert(serviceAccount as ServiceAccount) })`, built from the `FIREBASE_*` variables in `.env`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/backend/firebase/
Which two npm packages do you install to connect an Astro project to Firebase, and which one is used in the browser versus on the server?

Install `firebase` and `firebase-admin` (e.g. `npm install firebase firebase-admin`). The `firebase` package is the Firebase SDK used on the client/browser side — initialized in `src/firebase/client.ts` with your web app credentials via `initializeApp` from `firebase/app`. The `firebase-admin` package is the Firebase Admin SDK used on the server side — initialized in `src/firebase/server.ts` with project/service-account credentials from `.env`, then consumed by server endpoints such as `getFirestore(app)` in `src/pages/api/friends/`.
In src/firebase/server.ts, the code checks `getApps()` before calling `initApp()`. What problem does this guard prevent, and what happens if you remove it and always call `initializeApp()` directly?

`getApps()` returns the apps already initialized in this server process, and the guard makes initialization idempotent: `export const app = activeApps.length === 0 ? initApp() : activeApps[0]` reuses the existing default app and only creates one when none exists. If you removed the guard and always called `initializeApp()`, every evaluation of `server.ts` in the same runtime would create an additional app instance instead of returning the single shared `app` that the API endpoints (`getFirestore(app)`, etc.) import — so each endpoint could end up talking to a different instance rather than one common initialized app.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/backend/firebase/
Why should the `PUBLIC_` prefix not be used when adding Turso database URL and auth token to Astro environment variables, and what symptom would appear on the client if it were incorrectly prefixed?

The `PUBLIC_` prefix should not be used for Turso database URL and auth token because it would expose these private values on the client. If incorrectly prefixed, the credentials would be available in client-side code.
How do I set up environment variables for Supabase in Astro so I can access them with import.meta.env?

Add the two credentials to `.env` (unprefixed, so they stay server-side only) and declare them for IntelliSense in `src/env.d.ts`:

```
SUPABASE_URL=YOUR_SUPABASE_URL
SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=YOUR_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY
```

```ts
interface ImportMetaEnv {
  readonly SUPABASE_URL: string
  readonly SUPABASE_ANON_KEY: string
}
interface ImportMeta {
  readonly env: ImportMetaEnv
}
```

Then read them with `import.meta.env.SUPABASE_URL` and `import.meta.env.SUPABASE_ANON_KEY`. Astro checks the server environment first and falls back to `.env` files, and only `PUBLIC_`-prefixed variables are exposed to client-side code.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/backend/supabase/
In an Astro 7 project that connects to Neon, where do I define the NEON_DATABASE_URL connection string so pages can read it through import.meta.env?

Define it in the `.env` file in your project root, which Astro loads so pages can read it via `import.meta.env.NEON_DATABASE_URL`:

```
NEON_DATABASE_URL="postgresql://<user>:<password>@<endpoint_hostname>.neon.tech:<port>/<dbname>?sslmode=require"
```

Then consume it in a client module such as `src/lib/neon.ts`:

```
import { neon } from '@neondatabase/serverless';
export const sql = neon(import.meta.env.NEON_DATABASE_URL);
```

Requires an Astro project with on-demand rendering (SSR) enabled. For branch-specific values, use `.env.development` and `.env.production`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/backend/neon/
What is the distinction between the dsn option and the authToken inside sourceMapsUploadOptions when configuring the Sentry integration in astro.config.mjs?

The `dsn` (Data Source Name) is the client key that identifies your Sentry project for runtime error reporting, found in Project Settings → Client Keys. The `authToken` inside `sourceMapsUploadOptions` is a separate organization-level token used exclusively for authenticating source map uploads during build, created in Organization Settings → Auth Tokens. They serve different purposes: `dsn` for runtime event ingestion, `authToken` for build-time source map upload authorization.
After configuring the Sentry integration with a valid DSN and sourceMapsUploadOptions, what happens automatically when errors or performance events occur in the Astro application?
The Sentry SDK automatically captures and sends errors and performance events to Sentry once the integration is configured with `dsn` and `sourceMapsUploadOptions`.

You added TURSO_DATABASE_URL and TURSO_AUTH_TOKEN to your .env file with the PUBLIC_ prefix so they'd be available in your client-side components. Now your Turso credentials are exposed in the browser. Why did this happen, and how should you fix it?

In Astro 7, when calling GET /api/auth/signin, the endpoint returns 401 'No token found' even though the Authorization header contains a JWT token. What format does the endpoint expect for the Authorization header?

It expects `Authorization: Bearer <token>`; the endpoint extracts the token via `request.headers.get("Authorization")?.split("Bearer ")[1]`, so a bare JWT without the `Bearer ` prefix yields `undefined` and the 401 "No token found" response.
After running the Xata CLI setup, what role does .xatarc play in an Astro project and how does it relate to the databaseURL needed by the SDK?

`.xatarc` is the Xata CLI config file created during setup, and it defines the `databaseUrl` the SDK needs:

```json
{ "databaseUrl": "https://your-database-url" }
```

Along with `.env` (which supplies `XATA_API_KEY` and optionally `XATA_BRANCH`), it provides the configuration the generated SDK instance automatically pulls — environment variables plus database URL — so the client is ready to query with no further setup.
How do you install the Sentry integration in an Astro 7 project using the Astro CLI with npm?
Run `npx astro add @sentry/astro` in your terminal. The Astro CLI installs the SDK package and automatically adds the Sentry integration to your `astro.config.mjs` file.

I'm structuring an SSR Astro app that queries Prisma Postgres from many pages and API routes. Where should the PrismaClient with its PrismaPg adapter be instantiated and exported so the whole project shares one client, and what does that file look like?
In my `tsconfig.json`, I have TypeScript configured with `strict: true`. What additional validation does `npm run build` perform that it would skip if strict mode were disabled?

With TypeScript configured as `strict` (or `strictest`), `npm run build` also type-checks your project for type errors; if strict mode is disabled, the build skips that check and only produces your site output. The `strict`/`strictest` presets also supply the compiler settings content collections rely on (e.g. `strictNullChecks`, `allowJs`) for Zod validation, IntelliSense, and editor type checking — whereas `base` requires adding those manually.
After running `npm run build`, I made more edits to my components but `npm run preview` still shows the old output. Why doesn't preview reflect my latest changes, and what should I do instead?

Because `npm run preview` serves the static output in `dist/` exactly as it existed when `npm run build` last ran — it never recompiles your source. Either run `npm run build` again to regenerate `dist/`, or use `npm run dev`, whose dev server listens for changes in `src/` and updates the live preview as you edit.

I'm setting up routes by hand in a new Astro project. Which file extensions can I put inside src/pages/ to have them become routes, and what do I have to install before .mdx files there are actually treated as pages? Does an .html file there behave like a normal Astro page?

Supported extensions in `src/pages/` are `.astro`, `.md`, and `.mdx` (the latter requires installing the MDX integration via `astro add mdx`). An `.html` file in `src/pages/` is not listed as a supported page type and will not behave like an Astro page.
What occurs if you attempt to share state directly between a React island and a Vue island on the same Astro page, given that each framework runs in isolation?

State does not transfer between them: each island runs in isolation in its own component context, so a framework-specific sharing mechanism (e.g. React context providers) cannot cross island boundaries and won't affect the other island. Sharing still works if you use a framework-agnostic client-side store such as Nano Stores, which both the React and Vue island import and subscribe to. Nano Stores are framework-agnostic, lightweight (<1 KB, zero dependencies), so sharing state between frameworks is seamless.
Why might Astro 7 not apply view transitions when navigating between pages despite the guide 'Enhance navigation with view transitions' being available?

Because view transitions only occur once you render the `<ClientRouter />` component from `astro:transitions` in your page `<head>`; without it, every navigation is a normal full-page browser refresh. Two related gotchas can also make transitions appear broken: `navigate()` from `astro:transitions/client` has no effect if called during server-side rendering of a component, and bundled module scripts execute only once, so logic that previously re-ran on each full reload will not re-run after a transition — wrap it in a lifecycle event such as `astro:page-load` instead.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/view-transitions/
In an Astro project, where do layout components conventionally live, and is putting them in `src/layouts` a hard requirement? Can they be placed elsewhere?

Layout components conventionally live in a `src/layouts` directory, but this is not a requirement — you can place them anywhere in your project. They are ordinary Astro components with nothing special about them, and they can even be colocated alongside your pages in `src/pages` by prefixing the layout filename with `_` so it isn't treated as a route.

My Markdown layout throws `TypeError: Astro.props.getHeadings is not a function` even though `getHeadings()` works fine in my `.md` frontmatter. Why does this happen, and how do I get the heading data inside a layout?

`getHeadings()` is not available in Markdown layouts—it only exists on imported Markdown modules and content-collection `render()` results. In a layout, heading data is provided as the `headings` array on `Astro.props` (type `{ depth: number; slug: string; text: string }[]`). Access it via `Astro.props.headings` instead.

In `src/pages/index.astro`, how do you give two interactive components on the same page different loading behavior — a header nav that should become interactive immediately and a comments widget that can wait?

To give two interactive components different loading behavior in `src/pages/index.astro`, use the `client:load` directive for the header nav to make it interactive immediately, and `client:idle` for the comments widget to delay hydration until after the initial page load.

Example:
```astro
---
import HeaderNav from '../components/HeaderNav.jsx';
import CommentsWidget from '../components/CommentsWidget.jsx';
---

<HeaderNav client:load />
<CommentsWidget client:idle />
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/directives-reference/#client-directives

I'm building a Markdown layout that must show each heading's nesting level and link to its anchor in the rendered page. Given only `headings` with `depth`, `slug`, and `text`, plus `compiledContent()` returning the document as an HTML string, how should I structure the layout so the anchor ids in the table of contents actually match the ids in the emitted HTML?

The `headings` array already provides `slug` values that match the `id` attributes Astro injects into headings (generated via `github-slugger`). Build your table of contents by mapping `headings` to links like `{h.text}`. The `compiledContent()` HTML will have matching `id` attributes on each heading because Astro injects IDs after plugins run, and the `slug` in `headings` reflects those final IDs. No additional coordination is needed.

I have a layout chain where `BaseLayout.astro` defines `<slot name="head" />` and `<slot />`, and `HomeLayout.astro` transfers both to BaseLayout using `<slot name="head" slot="head" />` and `<slot />`. If I add a new `<slot name="footer" />` to BaseLayout, what exact changes do I need to make in HomeLayout so that pages using HomeLayout can pass footer content through to BaseLayout?

To pass a `footer` slot from `HomeLayout.astro` to `BaseLayout.astro`, you must add `<slot name="footer" slot="footer" />` inside `HomeLayout.astro`.

Example:

```astro
---import BaseLayout from './BaseLayout.astro';---
<BaseLayout>
  <slot name="head" slot="head" />
  <slot name="footer" slot="footer" />
  <slot />
</BaseLayout>
```

This transfers the `footer` slot to `BaseLayout`, where it can be used like any other named slot.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/astro-components/#transferring-slots

My Astro project's `package.json` has both `dependencies` and `devDependencies` sections. Does Astro treat them differently at build time, and where should I put a package like `astro-icon` that I only import in my components during the build?

Astro treats `dependencies` and `devDependencies` the same at build time—both are installed and available. The docs recommend putting all dependencies in `dependencies` to start, only using `devDependencies` if you have a specific need. For `astro-icon` (imported in components during build), place it in `dependencies`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/project-structure/

I serve HTML fragments to htmx with hx-post="/partials/clicked/" and src/pages/partials/clicked.astro exports const partial = true. Can I keep a <style> block and an inline <script> in that partial so my component styling and behavior survive, and can I mark a .md file in src/pages/ as a partial the same way?

No. Page partials strip `<style>` and `<script>` blocks because they do not include `<head>` content. Also, `.md` files cannot be marked as partials — only `.astro` and `.mdx` files can export `const partial = true`.

`eslint-plugin-astro` is installed and `npx eslint .` runs clean, but an invalid selector inside my component's `<style>` block is never reported. Why is ESLint silent about that code, and what tool should I use to lint it?

ESLint does not analyze CSS or style blocks within Astro components by default, as its focus is on JavaScript/TypeScript code. Invalid selectors in `<style>` tags are not reported because `eslint-plugin-astro` doesn't include rules for CSS linting.

To catch invalid CSS selectors, use a dedicated CSS linter like Stylelint with the appropriate configuration for Astro projects.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/invalid-component-args/
What is the purpose of `tsconfig.json` in an Astro project, and why might npm package imports not work fully in the editor without it?

`tsconfig.json` holds the TypeScript configuration options for your Astro project, and it is generated in every starter template. Without it, some features—specifically npm package imports—are not fully supported in the editor, so autocompletion and resolution for those imports degrade or fail. Create the file (or keep the one your starter provides) to restore full editor support; adjust compiler options via the TypeScript Guide.

I created src/pages/index.astro with just an <h1> and no <html>, <head>, or <!DOCTYPE html>. What does Astro output for that file, and what's the recommended way to share a single <head> and <body> shell across every page instead of repeating the markup?

If a page contains only `<h1>` and no `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<!DOCTYPE html>`, Astro still outputs that markup as the page content. To share a single `<head>` and `<body>` shell across every page, use a shared layout component (`.astro`) that provides the common structure and renders page content via `<slot />`.

In `CustomTable.astro` I have `<slot name="header" />` inside `<thead>` and `<slot name="body" />` inside `<tbody>`. From a parent component I need to pass a header row with two `<th>` cells and three separate `<tr>` rows to the body slot — but wrapping them in a `<div>` would break table semantics. What exact markup do I write in the parent to target each named slot with multiple sibling elements and no wrapper?

Use Astro's `` component with the `slot` attribute to pass multiple sibling elements into named slots without a wrapper div. src/components/StockTable.astro ``` ---import CustomTable from './CustomTable.astro';--- Product nameStock units Flip-flops64 Boots32 Sneakers0 ``` This passes the header row and body rows directly to their respective named slots, preserving table semantics.
When migrating an existing website to Astro, what is the recommended approach to incrementally replace a React section with a Svelte component without downtime?

Astro supports running multiple frameworks simultaneously, so you can keep existing React components while adding new Svelte components on the same page. Import both frameworks' components into an `.astro` page and hydrate only the parts that need interactivity with `client:*` directives. This allows incremental replacement with no downtime — the rest of the page stays static HTML.

I'm building a `GreetingHeadline.astro` component that should render "Hello, Astronaut!" when no props are passed, but "Howdy, Partner!" when I use `<GreetingHeadline greeting="Howdy" name="Partner" />`. How do I define those props, and how do I also pass a value from a variable in the parent component's frontmatter instead of a hardcoded string?

Define props with defaults in `GreetingHeadline.astro` frontmatter: ```astro --- const { greeting = "Hello", name = "Astronaut" } = Astro.props; ---

{greeting}, {name}!

``` Pass a parent variable in `GreetingCard.astro`: ```astro --- import GreetingHeadline from './GreetingHeadline.astro'; const name = 'Astro'; --- ``` Props are destructured from `Astro.props`; default values apply when omitted. Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/astro-components/

I have src/pages/guides/setup.md and a layout component at src/layouts/DocsLayout.astro. What frontmatter do I add to the Markdown file so its rendered content is wrapped in a full <html>...</html> document from that layout, and how is the relative path to the layout resolved?

Add this frontmatter to `src/pages/guides/setup.md`:

```
---
layout: ../../layouts/DocsLayout.astro
---
```

The path is resolved relative to the Markdown file itself: from `src/pages/guides/`, go up two levels to `src/`, then into `layouts/DocsLayout.astro`. The layout supplies the full `<html>...</html>` page shell, and the rendered Markdown content is injected into its default `<slot />`.

I added export const partial = true to src/pages/partials/clicked.astro so htmx can fetch it via hx-post, but the returned HTML fragment has none of the component's scoped <style> or <script> tags. Why are they stripped, and what's the recommended approach if I need scoped styles on dynamically loaded content?

Partials (added in `astro@3.4.0`) intentionally omit the `<!DOCTYPE html>` declaration and all `<head>` content — including your component's scoped `<style>` and `<script>` tags — which is why they are stripped from the HTML output. Astro's guidance is to avoid partials when the component contains scoped styles or scripts; instead use a regular, non-partial page together with a frontend library (e.g. htmx) that knows how to merge the returned head contents into the document.
What is the difference between `rawContent()` and `compiledContent()` in an Astro Markdown layout, and what happens if I interpolate `compiledContent()` into my layout template without `await`ing it?

`rawContent()` is a synchronous function returning the raw Markdown source as a string; `compiledContent()` returns that same document compiled to an HTML string — and since Astro 5.0 it is an async function (top-level await was removed from Markdown modules), so it must be awaited. Interpolating `compiledContent()` without `await` yields a pending Promise, not HTML, so you'd render `[object Promise]` (or nothing useful) instead of your content. Await it first:

```astro
---
const content = await compiledContent();
---
<Fragment set:html={content} />
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/upgrade-to/v5/
What does Astro mean by the design principle 'opt in to complexity', and how does this relate to its goal of being accessible to every web developer?

"Opt in to complexity" means Astro removes required complexity by default: you can build a "Hello World" site with just HTML and CSS, then incrementally reach for new features and APIs as your needs grow. This directly serves the goal of being accessible to every web developer, since Astro was designed to feel familiar and approachable regardless of skill level—you don't need to be an expert to build something with Astro, and advanced capabilities are only adopted when you choose them.
What's the difference between placing an image in `src/images/` versus `public/images/` in terms of how Astro handles it during the build?

Images in `src/images/` are processed, optimized, and transformed by Astro — usable with `<Image />`, `<Picture />`, and Markdown `![]()` syntax. Images in `public/images/` are copied untouched, never optimized, and must be referenced via URL path (e.g., `/images/file.jpg`); they cannot use Astro's optimized image components.

A page needs a personalized dashboard panel that hits a private database, plus an interactive React counter. One part should stream in after page load without delaying the whole page, the other should hydrate immediately on the client. Which Astro feature do I use for each, and what is the key behavioral difference between them at render time?

Use a server island (`server:defer`) for the dashboard panel and `client:load` for the React counter:

```astro
<DashboardPanel server:defer />
<Counter client:load />
```

The key difference at render time: a `server:defer` component defers its *server* rendering — it renders on the server when its data is available, streaming in without delaying the rest of the page (the panel hits your private database on the server). A framework component with `client:load` first renders on the server to static HTML, then its JavaScript is sent to the browser as the page loads, where it hydrates and becomes interactive. In short: `server:defer` delays server output; `client:load` delays nothing server-side but hydrates immediately on the client.

Trace a change from my editor to a deployed site: which command reflects my edits to files in `src/` live, which one produces the deploy-ready output folder, and which one only serves the result of the most recent build?

- **Live edits:** `npm run dev` (`astro dev`) — the dev server shows a live preview that updates as you edit files in `src/`.
- **Deploy-ready output:** `npm run build` (`astro build`) — writes the production site to `dist/` by default, with built assets like JS/CSS placed in an `_astro/` directory under hashed filenames.
- **Most recent build only:** `npm run preview` (`astro preview`) — serves the built site exactly as it existed when `build` last ran; changes made after building are not reflected until you rebuild.

After a rebuild, commit and push so your host can deploy the updated output.
How does Astro 7's server-first rendering approach differ from the single-page app model used by frameworks like Next.js, and what default rendering strategy does it employ for content-driven sites?

Astro uses a server-first Multi-Page App (MPA) approach, rendering HTML on the server by default, while Next.js uses a Single-Page App (SPA) model built for client-side rendering with SSR added for performance. Astro's default rendering strategy for content-driven sites is full prerendering to static HTML.

I have a directory of ~50 Markdown blog posts that all share the same structure (title, publishDate, tags, body). Should I put them in src/pages/blog/ as .md files with a `layout:` frontmatter property pointing at my layout component, or should I model them as a content collection? When is the Markdown-page approach the wrong choice?

For ~50 Markdown posts with the same structure, use Markdown pages in `src/pages/blog/*.md` with a `layout:` frontmatter pointing to your layout if you just need file-based routing. Use content collections when you need to programmatically query, filter, sort, validate entries (schema), or generate routes dynamically. The Markdown-page approach is the wrong choice when you need structured querying/sorting, a catalog (lists, tags, pagination), or enforced schema across entries.

The 'Using streaming to improve page performance' recipe demonstrates streaming HTML responses. In what scenario would streaming NOT improve perceived performance for a page that fetches data from a slow third-party API?

Streaming gives no perceived gain when nothing can be sent to the browser before the slow third-party fetch resolves. If the fetch is `await`ed in the page's frontmatter, Astro waits for all `fetch` calls to resolve before sending any HTML, so the entire response is delayed by the slow API and streaming never helps. Likewise, if all meaningful markup sits behind the awaited value, the user sees only empty or fallback content regardless of streaming. Benefit comes from moving fetches into separate components or passing promises directly in the template so earlier HTML renders while the slow request is still in flight.
How do I manually upgrade specific versions of Astro and its integrations?

Install exact versions by naming them with your package manager:
```
npm install astro@4.5.3 @astrojs/react@3.0.10
pnpm add astro@4.5.3 @astrojs/react@3.0.10
yarn add astro@4.5.3 @astrojs/react@3.0.10
```
To move to the current latest instead, append `@latest` (e.g. `npm install astro@latest @astrojs/react@latest @astrojs/partytown@latest`), or run `npx @astrojs/upgrade` (`pnpm dlx @astrojs/upgrade` / `yarn dlx @astrojs/upgrade`) to update Astro and all official integrations together.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/upgrade-astro/

After the official tutorial I want more guided practice. How do the two partner courses differ in format and depth — one is a premium course with 150+ video lessons about Astro's built-in tooling, the other a 35-lesson Scrimba build where video and IDE are merged. Which one suits someone who wants a long, structured curriculum versus someone who wants to type along in a live IDE?

**Learn Astro with Coding in Public** is the premium 150+ lesson course covering Astro's built-in tooling in depth — suited for a long, structured curriculum. **Learn Astro with James Q Quick** is the 35-lesson Scrimba course where video and a live IDE are merged — suited for typing along interactively. The former emphasizes comprehensive tooling mastery; the latter emphasizes hands-on building in a browser IDE.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/astro-courses/
What happens if I define a content collection schema in Astro but my frontmatter doesn't match the expected types during build?

Astro validates every entry against the collection's Zod schema, and a mismatch fails the build with a helpful error naming the file and the violations, e.g. **blog** → **post** data does not match collection schema, “title” is required, “date” must be a valid date. Fix the frontmatter (or relax the schema) in `src/content.config.*` and rebuild. Note that `InvalidContentEntryFrontmatterError` applies only to legacy content collections, removed in Astro 6; current collections report `InvalidContentEntryDataError`. After editing a schema, restart the dev server or sync the content layer (`s + enter`) so the `astro:content` types regenerate.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/invalid-content-entry-data-error/
What directive do you add to an Astro component to make it a server island that renders in parallel with fallback content?

Use the `server:defer` directive on an Astro component: `<Avatar server:defer />`. This makes it a server island that renders in parallel with fallback content provided via `slot="fallback"` on a child element.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/server-islands/
My product catalog lives in a CMS with thousands of entries — do I need one real file per product in src/pages/, or can a single file there produce many routes? How does that work in Astro?

No, you don't need one real file per product. Astro supports dynamic routes using `[slug].astro` or `[[slug]].astro` syntax in the `src/pages/` directory to generate multiple routes from a single file. For example, a file named `src/pages/products/[id].astro` will match any URL like `/products/123`, where `id` becomes a route parameter. You can also use optional catch-all patterns with `[[slug]].astro` for more flexible routing. You can generate these dynamic routes at build time by using the `getStaticPaths()` function in your page component, or dynamically render them during SSR if needed. Example: ```astro --- // src/pages/products/[id].astro const { id } = Astro.params; // Fetch product data based on ID... ---

Product: {id}

``` Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/routing/#dynamic-routes
What is the key difference between adding `server:defer` to a component versus adding `client:load` to a component in terms of where the rendering work happens?

`server:defer` renders the component on the server (deferred, fetched via separate request) while `client:load` hydrates a UI framework component in the browser immediately on page load. Server islands keep rendering server-side; client directives enable client-side interactivity for framework components.

Reviewing a component whose frontmatter does `await fetch('SOME_SECRET_API_URL/users')` and imports a React `.jsx` component plus a JSON file. Why is it safe for that private endpoint and token to live in the code fence, and under what conditions does the JSX component's client-side code actually reach the user's browser?

The frontmatter code fence is guaranteed to keep JavaScript "fenced in": Astro components don't render on the client, they render to HTML at build-time or on-demand, and all frontmatter code is stripped from the final page. The fetch to your private endpoint, the token, and the JSON import therefore run only on the server and never reach users' browsers — you can safely write sensitive or expensive code there.

The JSX component's client-side code reaches the browser only when you render it with a `client:*` directive (`client:load`, `client:idle`, `client:visible`, `client:media`, or `client:only`); the directive determines when that JavaScript is sent. Without one, the component contributes no client JavaScript.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/astro-components/
I'm organizing content in my Astro site and I want each entry's frontmatter validated with automatic type-safety. Which Astro feature should I use?

Use **content collections**: define your collection and its schema in `src/content.config.*`, and Astro validates every entry's frontmatter against that schema, giving you automatic type-safety. This is exactly Astro's "frontmatter validation and automatic type-safety" feature. A mismatch (e.g. a missing required `title` or an invalid `date`) is reported as a schema error rather than slipping through. Note the distinction: the `InvalidContentEntryFrontmatterError` applies only to legacy content collections, which were removed in Astro 6 — current collections check entries against the schema you define in `src/content.config.*`.
What is extended maintenance and how long does it last?

Extended maintenance provides security fixes only for one previous major version. For example, if the current major is `v4.*`, the Core team will backport security fixes and issue new `v3.*` releases. This lasts until the next major version is released.

I've finished a round of edits and want to inspect in my browser exactly the version of my site that will be deployed. Starting from a running dev server, which terminal commands do I run and in what order, and why does the preview command have to come after the build command?

First, stop the development server with `Ctrl` + `C`. Then run `npm run build`, `pnpm build`, or `yarn run build` depending on your package manager. Finally, run `npm run preview`, `pnpm preview`, or `yarn run preview` to start a local server that serves the built files from the `dist/` directory.

The `preview` command must come after `build` because it serves the static output generated by `astro build`. The `build` command compiles your site into deployable assets in the `dist/` folder, and `preview` serves those specific files locally to simulate how your site will appear when deployed. Running `preview` before `build` would result in an empty or missing server since no built output exists yet.

Example:
```bash
# After stopping dev server
npm run build
npm run preview
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/develop-and-build/
I'm new to open source and want to start contributing to Astro. How do I find beginner-friendly issues in the Astro project?

Start with Astro's contribute page, which links to a GitHub search of all open issues across every `withastro` repository labeled `good first issue` and `help wanted` — covering the core codebase, docs, Starlight, the compiler, language tools, websites, GitHub Actions, and bots. Every repository's README links to a `CONTRIBUTING.md`. If code feels daunting, reviewing PRs (including translation PRs), fixing docs typos, or tackling "Pinned" maintenance issues are friendly entry points, and the Discord `#docs` channel and Docs repo welcome new contributors.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/contribute/
I want Astro to generate optimized, resized versions of my site logo from a single source image. Should I put that logo in `public/`, and why or why not?

You should place your site logo in the `src/` directory and use Astro's `` component for optimization, rather than the `public/` folder. The `public/` directory is intended for static assets that are served as-is without processing. For image optimization, resizing, and format conversion (e.g., WebP or AVIF), you should use Astro’s built-in image optimization features via the `` component or `getImage()` function. These tools require the source images to be in your project's source directory (`src/`) so they can process them using Sharp or another configured service. Placing an image in `public/` and referencing it directly (e.g., ``) will bypass Astro’s optimization pipeline, meaning no resizing or format conversion occurs. If you want to generate optimized versions of your logo with specific dimensions or formats, use the `` component from `astro:assets`. Example: ```astro --- import { Image } from 'astro:assets'; --- ``` Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/configuration-reference/
How do I upgrade Astro and all of my official @astrojs integrations to their latest versions together in a single command when using npm?

To upgrade Astro and all official `@astrojs` integrations to their latest versions together using npm, run:

```
npx @astrojs/upgrade
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/upgrade-astro/

Inside an Astro Markdown layout, how do I build a table of contents from a document's headings? I know `Astro.props` exposes heading data, but I can't figure out whether I should call a function or read an array, and what fields each entry contains.

Read the `headings` array from `Astro.props` — it is an array, not a function call (the `getHeadings()` function exists only on imported Markdown modules, not in layouts). Each entry is `{ depth: number; slug: string; text: string }`, where `slug` matches the auto-generated heading `id` (via github-slugger), so you can link directly: ```astro --- const { headings } = Astro.props; ---
    {headings.filter(h => h.depth === 2).map(h => (
  • {h.text}
    • ))}
``` Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/layouts/
My Astro site feels sluggish during page-to-page navigation. Which Astro 7 guide addresses enhancing that navigation experience, and what is the feature called?

The View Transitions guide (`/guides/view-transitions/`) — the feature is **view transitions**, enabled with the `<ClientRouter />` component, which turns page-to-page links into client-side navigation: it fetches the next page, runs `document.startViewTransition`, swaps the head and body (persisting `transition:persist` elements and stylesheets), then fires `astro:page-load`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/view-transitions/

Which Markdown layout props can I rely on to render the post body into a `<Content />`-style slot, which to use for feeding a syntax highlighter or a full-text search index, and which one gives me the document's own frontmatter verbatim?

- Render the post body into a `<slot />` (the default slot receives the compiled HTML automatically).
- Use `rawContent()` for a syntax highlighter or full-text search index—it returns the raw Markdown source as a string synchronously.
- Use `frontmatter` (the object) for the document's own frontmatter verbatim; it contains all frontmatter properties from the Markdown/MDX file.
Is adding `server:defer` the right call for a feature-comparison table whose HTML is identical for every visitor and is already cheap to render?

No, adding `server:defer` is not necessary for a feature-comparison table that is identical for every visitor and already cheap to render. Server islands are intended for on-demand rendering of dynamic or personalized content that benefits from being fetched separately to improve initial page load performance.

If the table's HTML is static and inexpensive to generate, rendering it directly in the page without `server:defer` is more efficient than deferring its rendering. The overhead of managing a server island would not provide benefit for such a case.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/server-islands/
What is the purpose of the Astro 7 guide 'Create type safe content collections'?

It teaches you to organize related content into collections with a schema that validates each entry's shape (ensuring data is correct and complete and avoiding production errors), and to query that content with content-focused APIs such as `getCollection()` instead of `import.meta.glob()`. The guide covers both build-time collections (prerendered and cached, supporting MDX and image optimization via loaders like `glob()` and the low-level Content Loader API) and live collections fetched at runtime for frequently changing data, plus when *not* to create a collection. Both types expose similar APIs, so querying feels familiar while you always know which type you're working with.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/content-collections/
In an Astro Markdown layout I need both the original Markdown source and the rendered HTML string. Which two `Astro.props` members do I use, and is either of them asynchronous?

Use `rawContent()` for the original Markdown source (synchronous function returning a string) and `compiledContent()` for the rendered HTML string (async function returning a Promise<string>). `compiledContent()` is asynchronous; `rawContent()` is not.
What is the key behavioral difference between running `astro dev` and running `astro preview` after a build when I modify a component file in `src/`?

`astro dev` listens for live file changes in your `src/` directory and updates the site in the browser as you edit, no restart needed. `astro preview` only serves the static output in `dist/` (by default) produced by the last `astro build`, so it shows your code exactly as it existed at build time; edits made afterward are not reflected until you build again.
How does using server islands for personalized elements like a user avatar allow the main product page content to be more aggressively cached in an e-commerce site?

Server islands extract dynamic personalized elements (avatar, deals, reviews) into separate on-demand requests, allowing the static product page shell to be fully cached at the edge/CDN. The main content serves instantly from cache while personalized islands load in parallel.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/concepts/islands/#benefits-of-server-islands
How do I add the React integration to an Astro 7 project?

Run the `astro add` command for your package manager: `npx astro add react` (or `pnpm astro add react`, `yarn astro add react`). This installs `@astrojs/react` and registers it in the `integrations` array of `astro.config.mjs` automatically; manual installation is also possible. Note that `@astrojs/react` v7.0.0 replaces Babel with Oxc for JSX compilation and Fast Refresh and upgrades to `@vitejs/plugin-react` v6, and its former `babel` option is removed — custom Babel transforms now go through `@rolldown/plugin-babel` in `vite.plugins`. Once installed, render React components with a client directive such as `client:load`, or `client:only="react"` to skip server rendering.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/integrations-guide/react/

During local dev my Astro error page looked fine, but after `astro build` and serving the output, a visitor hitting a failing route sees a block of internal file paths and method names. What in my component most likely caused that, and what is the fix inside the code that handles the `error` prop?

The component likely renders `error.stack` (or the whole error object), which includes internal file paths and method names. Fix: guard with `error instanceof Error` and only display `error.message`; for unknown errors, show a generic message like `"Unknown error"`.
In Astro 7, under what circumstances would you opt into client-side rendering for a component, and how does this differ from making the entire page client-only?

You opt into client-side rendering for a component when it needs interactivity, using `client:*` directives (`client:load`, `client:visible`, `client:idle`, etc.) — this creates an interactive "island" while the rest of the page stays static HTML. `client:only` differs by skipping server rendering entirely for that component (requiring a framework hint), whereas regular `client:*` directives render on the server first, then hydrate on the client.
During a manual build, if you reference an image as /logo.png in your component template versus importing it in the frontmatter, what different build-time behaviors occur for each approach?

A hardcoded URL like `/logo.png` gets no build-time image processing: images in `public/` are never optimized, and responsive images are not supported for them, so the raw file is used as-is. Importing the asset in frontmatter instead — `import myImage from '../assets/my_image.png'` rendered with `<Image src={myImage} alt="A description of my image." layout="constrained" width={800} height={600} />` from `astro:assets` — makes Astro process it, emitting a hashed optimized output such as `/_astro/my_image.hash3.webp` and, with `layout` set, generating `srcset`/`sizes`. On prerendered pages those variants are created during the build (increasing build time); with on-demand rendering they're generated when a page is visited.

My Astro dev server is running but the browser shows a different URL than http://localhost:4321. The terminal output mentions an error. What should I check first to understand why the expected URL isn't working?

Check the terminal where you ran the `dev` command first — the message displayed there will tell you whether an error occurred, or whether your project is being served at a different URL than http://localhost:4321/. Use the URL it reports, or fix the error it names, before troubleshooting the browser.
I want to organize my Astro project with pages in `app/routes/` instead of `src/pages/`. Is this possible, and what is the only directory name that Astro strictly requires?

No — pages must live in `src/pages/`; it is the only directory reserved (and required) by Astro, and without it your site has no routes. `app/routes/` cannot serve as the pages directory. Every other directory is merely convention: you are free to rename and reorganize `components`, `layouts`, `styles`, and similar folders however you like (though they typically live under `src/`, whose contents are processed and optimized by Astro).
How can you dynamically import images in an Astro project using Vite's built-in functionality without configuring additional plugins?

Use Vite's built-in `import.meta.glob` function. The recipe shows `const images = import.meta.glob<{ default: ImageMetadata }>('/src/assets/*.{jpeg,jpg,png,gif}')` to create an object of dynamic import functions, then invoking the matched path: `<Image src={images[imagePath]()} alt={altText} />`. No additional plugins are required.

I added `layout: ../layouts/BaseLayout.astro` to the frontmatter of an entry in my content collection, but the rendered entry ignores it and my layout never wraps the content. Why doesn't the `layout` frontmatter property work in this case?

The `layout` frontmatter property only works for Markdown files or MDX files, not for Astro components (`.astro` files) in content collections.

In Astro 7, when you define a layout in the frontmatter of a `.md` or `.mdx` file, it will be used to wrap that page's content. However, if your content collection entry is an `.astro` component file instead of Markdown, then the `layout` property has no effect because Astro components are rendered directly and do not support layout wrapping via frontmatter.

To apply a layout to an Astro component in a content collection, you must manually wrap it with the desired layout inside the component itself or use a custom integration that handles this behavior. The layout system is designed for Markdown/MDX files where the `layout` property allows dynamic selection of how content should be rendered.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/layouts/#markdown-layouts
A visitor to my Astro error page can see my server file paths and internal function names in the output. What am I most likely rendering from the `error` prop, and what should I render instead?

You're most likely rendering the error's `stack` (or the raw error object), which contains information about how your code is structured on the server — file paths, internal function names, and similar details. Evaluate the error first and render only an appropriate message instead, e.g. `error instanceof Error ? error.message : "Unknown error"` with a generic fallback, never the stack. Note this `error` prop only exists on `src/pages/500.astro` for on-demand rendered pages; prerendered pages don't have this custom error page.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/astro-pages/

All about Fred

- `` renders at ``, i.e. after `

` and bare `
