`. Using `slot="default"` changes nothing: children without a `slot` attribute and children with `slot="default"` both go to the default (unnamed) ``.
I need to add a PDF resume to my Astro site that should be downloadable as-is without any processing. Where should I place this file?

Place it in the `public/` directory. Files in `public/` are not processed during Astro's build; they are copied into the build folder untouched, which makes that directory ideal for assets that must be served as-is, such as a downloadable PDF resume.

I want full type safety in a Markdown layout, so that missing frontmatter keys like `title` or `author` are caught at build time and the layout's special props are typed. How do I type the props, and how do I then safely build a canonical link from the `url` layout prop?
Why does the manual installation guide explicitly warn against installing Astro globally with npm install -g astro or equivalent pnpm/yarn commands?

Astro must be installed locally as a project dependency, not globally. The manual setup explicitly warns against `npm install -g astro`, `pnpm add -g astro`, or `yarn global add astro` because Astro must be part of your project's dependencies so that the `astro dev`, `astro build`, and `astro preview` CLI commands resolve the correct project-local version and run within the project context.
What should I do if my project needs to continue using features from a previous version of Astro?

Removed features cannot be kept — projects containing them are unable to build — so migrate to the supported replacements: return `Response` from endpoints, use `Astro.params`, `getHeadings()`, `@astrojs/rss`, adapter configuration options instead of `build.split`/`build.excludeMiddleware`, and content collections with `draft: true` filtering instead of `markdown.drafts`. For content collections specifically, you can temporarily enable the `legacy.collections` flag, which lets you keep collections in their current state until the legacy flag is no longer supported; convert to the Content Layer API as soon as you can.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/upgrade-to/v5/
Why don't Astro components need to worry about React hooks, stale closures, Vue refs, or Svelte observables? What property of Astro's rendering model makes this complexity unnecessary?

Because Astro components render only on the server (at build time or on-demand) to static HTML with no client-side runtime and no reactivity—Astro was designed to render on the server, not in the browser, so "there is no reactivity on the server" and hooks, stale closures, refs, observables, atoms and reactions have nothing to act on. That complexity only reappears if you explicitly opt into a hydrated UI-framework island or a client `<script>`.

I added src/pages/500.astro with a friendly error message, but visitors hitting a broken blog post still get my host's generic 500 page. That post is statically generated at build time, not rendered on demand. Why is my 500.astro ignored, and what filename should I use instead if I also want a custom not-found page?

The `500.astro` page only works for on-demand rendered pages, not for prerendered (statically generated) pages. Your blog post is prerendered at build time, so the custom 500 page is ignored. For a custom not-found page, use `src/pages/404.astro`.
Why does Astro strip all client-side JavaScript from UI components by default?

Because Astro components never render on the client: they render to HTML at build-time or on-demand, and the component script (the `---` frontmatter) is fenced so its JavaScript never escapes into the page sent to the browser. The result is a faster site with zero JavaScript footprint by default; interactivity is added only where needed via standard `<script>` tags or hydrated framework components as "client islands." This "fast by default" principle underlies Astro's server-first architecture.
How can you render components from two different UI frameworks, such as React and Vue, on the same Astro page?

Import components from both frameworks into a single `.astro` file and render them together; Astro picks the renderer by file extension: ```astro --- import MyReactComponent from '../components/MyReactComponent.jsx'; import MyVueComponent from '../components/MyVueComponent.vue'; ---
``` Only Astro components can mix frameworks—framework files themselves (`.jsx`, `.vue`) cannot. Multiple JSX frameworks (e.g. React and Preact) need extra configuration to be distinguished.
I want to reorganize my Astro project and rename `src/components` to `src/ui` and `src/layouts` to `src/wrappers`. Will the build still work, or are these directory names enforced by Astro?

Only `src/pages/` is required and reserved by Astro. You can freely rename `src/components` to `src/ui` and `src/layouts` to `src/wrappers`—the build will still work. These are conventions, not enforced directories.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/project-structure/

We need `.astro` formatting to come out identical whether a teammate formats from the terminal (e.g. in CI), edits inside VS Code, or works in an editor that doesn't support Astro's editor tooling. What setup makes that consistent across all three?

To ensure consistent `.astro` file formatting across editors and CLI tools like CI, use Prettier with the `prettier-plugin-astro` plugin.

1. Install dependencies:
```bash
npm install --save-dev --save-exact prettier prettier-plugin-astro
```

2. Create a `.prettierrc` config:
```json
{
  "plugins": ["prettier-plugin-astro"],
  "overrides": [
    {
      "files": "*.astro",
      "options": { "parser": "astro" }
    }
  ]
}
```

3. Format files via CLI:
```bash
npx prettier . --write
```

This setup ensures consistent formatting regardless of editor or environment, as long as all team members use the same Prettier version and plugin.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/editor-setup/

I want to learn Astro from the docs, but when I get stuck or want bleeding-edge techniques I need a plan. How should I layer the official tutorial, curated community collections, and the community chat so each covers what the others don't?

Layer them by depth: start with the official tutorial, which assumes only basic HTML/CSS/JS, walks you through setup → pages → components with per-page checklists and a Tutorial Tracker (skip Unit 1 if you're already set up). When you need advanced, experimental, or unusual techniques, use curated community collections — Astro Tips, and community video/stream roundups like Starlight's community content page. When you get stuck or want interactive help, go to the Astro Discord: the support forum channel for questions, `#general`/`#off-topic` for chat, and `#docs` (or a GitHub issue) for tutorial feedback. Use upgrade guides when your project's behavior diverges from current docs.
When creating a Markdown page in src/pages/post.md, what frontmatter property tells Astro which layout component to use, and what prop does that layout automatically receive?

Use the special frontmatter `layout` property, set to a relative path to the Astro layout component (e.g. `layout: ../../layouts/BlogPostLayout.astro`). The layout automatically receives all of the Markdown file's frontmatter YAML values through `Astro.props.frontmatter` (e.g. `const { frontmatter } = Astro.props;`), plus a default `<slot />` for the rendered Markdown. Note `layout` is only special for individual `.md` files in `src/pages/`, not for content collections, and your layout must include `<meta charset="utf-8">` itself.

I want visitors to get a polished document when they navigate directly to a URL in their browser — is marking that route's file in src/pages/ with `export const partial = true` the right choice, and what would they actually receive?

No, marking a route’s file in `src/pages/` with `export const partial = true` is not the right choice if you want visitors to get a polished document when they navigate directly to that URL.

A partial page does not include the full HTML document structure (`<!DOCTYPE html>`, `<head>`, etc.), nor any scoped styles or scripts. It only outputs the component’s content as raw HTML, intended for dynamic updates by frontend libraries like htmx or Stimulus.

Visitors navigating directly to a partial URL would receive an incomplete and likely broken page — just the inner HTML of the partial component without proper document structure or styling.

For fully rendered pages with complete HTML documents, use regular `.astro` files in `src/pages/` without setting `partial = true`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/astro-pages/
If you import a React component in an Astro page without any `client:*` directive, what exactly gets sent to the browser for that component?

Only the component's static HTML output is sent to the browser—no JavaScript for that component. Without a `client:*` directive, UI framework components render to HTML on the server and are not hydrated on the client.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/directives-reference/#client-directives

My Markdown layout throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'then')` when I write `
{Astro.props.compiledContent()}
` without `await`. Why does this happen, and what is the correct way to interpolate the compiled HTML?

In Astro 5+, `compiledContent()` is an async function that must be awaited. Calling it without `await` returns a Promise, which causes the error when trying to render it directly.

To fix this, await the result of `compiledContent()` and use it in a slot or with `set:html`.

Example:

```astro
---
const content = await import('/src/content/post.md').then(m => m.default.compiledContent());
---

<div set:html={content} />
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/upgrade-to/v5/
My terminal stopped with an error when I ran `npm run build` instead of producing a deploy-ready `dist/` folder. What did Astro just tell me, and why does catching this here matter?

Astro stopped the build and reported the underlying error instead of writing `dist/` — commonly an *unknown filesystem error* (reading/writing files, e.g. missing permissions or a nonexistent file), an *unknown Markdown error* (usually a syntax error, with details in the message), or an *unknown Vite error* while rendering your project. Catching it here matters because the build alerts you to errors **before you deploy to production**, and with TypeScript configured to `strict` or `strictest` the `build` script also checks your project for type errors — so a broken build never reaches your host.
I just created a new Astro project and want to start the dev server. What command do I run, and what URL should I expect the site to be served on?

Run `npm run dev` (or `pnpm run dev` / `yarn run dev`) to start Astro's built-in development server. The site is served at `http://localhost:4321` by default if port `4321` is available — click the `localhost` link printed in the terminal to open it. Stop the server anytime with `Ctrl + C`.
How can I check if my Node.js version is supported by Astro?

Your Node.js version is supported if it is the latest *Maintenance* LTS or current *Active* LTS release; Astro can also support odd versions, though they may be dropped once the next even version ships. The upgrade policy defines exactly when support changes: minimum Maintenance LTS bumps can occur in a minor release (or a patch, for security fixes affecting Astro), while non-Maintenance-LTS version bumps happen only in major releases. On Vercel with `@astrojs/vercel`, open your project's settings tab and scroll to the "Node.js Version" section to see the versions available.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/upgrade-astro/

I'm setting up a new Astro 7 project in VS Code. What do I need to install to get syntax highlighting for `.astro` files plus TypeScript type information and IntelliSense inside those files, and where do I get it?

Install the official **Astro VS Code Extension** from the VS Code Marketplace. It provides syntax highlighting for `.astro` files, TypeScript type information for `.astro` files, and VS Code IntelliSense (code completion, hints, errors). Astro always treats component code as TypeScript and the extension infers as much as it can; also keep a `tsconfig.json` in your project (e.g. extending `astro/tsconfigs/strict`) so the type system is fully configured.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/editor-setup/
After switching my MDX posts to use a shared layout, my pages lost their `<meta charset="utf-8">` tag and text renders with mojibake. What changed and what do I have to add?

Astro 5.0 stopped sending `charset=utf-8` in the Content-Type header for Markdown/MDX pages and instead injects a `<meta charset="utf-8">` tag — but only when the page has no layout. Once your MDX content imports a wrapping `Layout` component (or uses the `layout` frontmatter property), Astro treats encoding as the layout's responsibility and no longer adds the tag. Add it to your layout's `<head>`:

```astro
<html>
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8" />
  </head>
  <body>
    <slot />
  </body>
</html>
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/upgrade-to/v5/
The 'Dynamically import images' recipe uses `import.meta.glob`. What is a realistic edge case where this pattern would fail to include images added at runtime after the dev server starts?

`import.meta.glob()` is evaluated statically at build time (or when the dev server starts). The returned `images` object is a fixed map of matching files present at that moment. If you add new image files to `src/assets/` after the dev server has started, they will not appear in the `images` object — the glob result is not re-evaluated for newly added files. You would need to restart the dev server for new images to be included.

I've already built a couple of small Astro sites and now I want unusual, advanced, and experimental Astro techniques — community-written recipes rather than the official basics tutorial. Which resource is the curated home for that, and how does it differ from the official docs' contribution and community channels?

The curated home for advanced, unusual, and experimental community-written Astro recipes is **Astro Tips** (astro-tips.dev), listed under "Community learning resources" on the Astro Courses page. It differs from the official docs' contribution channels (GitHub issues/PRs, docs translations, Discord support) and community channels (Discord chat) by focusing specifically on curated, practical recipes and quick tips rather than core framework development or general discussion. The Starlight community-content page is narrower — only Starlight-specific guides.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/astro-courses/
What files and directories does the `create astro` CLI wizard generate by default in a new Astro project?

The `create astro` wizard generates a project root containing `src/` (your pages, components, layouts, styles, images, and content), `public/` (unprocessed assets like `robots.txt` and `favicon.svg`), `package.json`, `astro.config.mjs`, and `tsconfig.json`. Only `src/pages/` is strictly reserved; the example tree also shows conventions like `src/components/`, `src/layouts/`, `src/styles/`, and `content.config.ts`, which you may rename or reorganize. The wizard additionally adds `dev`, `build`, and `preview` scripts to `package.json` (`astro dev`, `astro build`, `astro preview`) and can initialize a git repository and install dependencies when you accept those prompts.
Why is it not recommended to use odd versions of Node.js with Astro?

Odd (non-LTS) versions are outside Astro's core support: Astro supports only the latest *Maintenance* LTS and current *Active* LTS releases. Odd versions may be supported, but they can be deprecated and dropped in a **minor** release of Astro as soon as the next even version is published (after a period of extended support decided by the Core team) — so your toolchain can break without a major Astro upgrade. Even LTS releases follow the stable policy: minor bumps only within the same major range, or a patch bump for a security flaw affecting Astro.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/upgrade-astro/

In a Markdown layout, my `.md` file declares `author: Jane` and `tags: [astro]` in its frontmatter. Where do those values show up in `Astro.props` — only nested under `frontmatter`, only as top-level props, or both?

In a Markdown layout, the `author: Jane` and `tags: [astro]` values from the `.md` file’s frontmatter are available **only nested under `frontmatter`** in `Astro.props`.

For example:

```ts
// In your Markdown layout component:
const { frontmatter } = Astro.props;
console.log(frontmatter.author); // "Jane"
console.log(frontmatter.tags);   // ["astro"]
```

The top-level `file` and `url` properties are also available, but not the nested `frontmatter.file` or `frontmatter.url`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/layouts/#markdown-layout-props
Why does `npm run preview` show a static snapshot of my site that doesn't update when I edit files, whereas `npm run dev` reflects changes instantly?

`astro preview` serves the static files in `dist/` created by your last `astro build` — a snapshot of your code as it existed at build time — so edits are never reflected until you rebuild. `astro dev` runs a development server that listens for live file changes in your `src/` directory and updates your site as you edit, giving you an always up-to-date preview.
In an Astro page component, how do you wrap page content with a layout component from src/layouts/MySiteLayout.astro that expects a title prop?

Import the layout in the page's frontmatter and wrap the page content in it, passing `title` as a prop; content between the tags is injected into the layout's ``: ```astro --- import MySiteLayout from '../layouts/MySiteLayout.astro'; ---

My page content, wrapped in a layout!

 ``` Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/layouts/

I'm linking from src/pages/index.astro to a page at src/pages/authors/sonali.astro. The docs say to use a URL path relative to the root domain — what exact href should I write, and why does a relative file path like ../authors/sonali.astro not work?

Write `href="/authors/sonali/"` — a URL path relative to your root domain: ```astro Read more about Sonali. ``` Astro uses file-based routing: each file in `src/pages/` becomes a site endpoint based on its file path, so `src/pages/authors/sonali.astro` is served at `/authors/sonali/`. A relative file path like `../authors/sonali.astro` references the source-file system, not the deployed URL space — the browser has no knowledge of your `src/` directory, so the link would resolve to a nonexistent path.

You added `server:defer` to a personalized dashboard widget but notice a layout shift when the deferred content arrives. What mechanism in server islands is designed to prevent this, and why might it fail in this case?

The mechanism is fallback content: children marked with `slot="fallback"` are rendered along with the rest of the page on initial load and are replaced by the island's real content when it arrives. Correctly sized fallback content is intended to prevent layout shift. It fails when the real content occupies a different amount of space than the fallback (for example, a longer name, a taller reviews list, or a different-sized image), or when no fallback is provided at all—so the reserved placeholder is the wrong size and the layout shifts once the island replaces it.
How do you provide custom fallback content for a server island while its dynamic content is loading, instead of showing a generic placeholder?

Pass your custom content to the named `"fallback"` slot on the `server:defer`-marked component:

```astro
---
import Avatar from '../components/Avatar.astro';
import GenericAvatar from '../components/GenericAvatar.astro';
---
<Avatar server:defer>
  <GenericAvatar slot="fallback" />
</Avatar>
```

The fallback content is rendered along with the rest of the page on initial load, then replaced with the island's real content once it arrives from its own route. Fallbacks can be generic avatars, custom messages, or loading indicators, and server islands require an installed adapter for the delayed rendering.

In `src/components/PokemonCard.astro` I have a `pokemon` prop with a `types` array and want the wrapper `<article>` to have classes `['card', 'pokemon']` plus a dynamic `{ [pokemon.types[0]]: true }` object. How do I apply all three using the `class:list` directive in the template?

Use `class:list` with an array combining static strings, the dynamic class object, and the types array:

```astro
<article class:list={["card", "pokemon", { [pokemon.types[0]]: true }]} />
```

This applies classes `card`, `pokemon`, and the first type from `pokemon.types` if truthy. The directive uses `clsx` under the hood, so it handles object keys and arrays correctly.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/directives-reference/#classlist

Which file extensions in src/pages/ can I mark as page partials with `export const partial = true`, and what URL does a partial at src/pages/partials/clicked.astro get served from so an htmx `hx-post` attribute can target it? Does a .md file work for this?

Only `.astro` and `.mdx` files in `src/pages/` can be marked as page partials with `export const partial = true` (`.md` files do not work). A partial at `src/pages/partials/clicked.astro` is served at the URL corresponding to its file path: `/partials/clicked/`, which is what an htmx `hx-post` attribute should target.
Which `client:*` directive would you use on a heavy image carousel component to ensure its JavaScript only loads after the browser finishes higher-priority work and becomes idle?

Use `client:idle` — it loads and hydrates the component once the browser finishes initial page load and fires `requestIdleCallback`, ensuring higher-priority work completes first.

```astro
<HeavyImageCarousel client:idle />
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/directives-reference/#clientidle
In an Astro project with TypeScript strict mode enabled, what additional type-checking does npm run build perform compared to a project without strict mode?

None. In Astro, `astro build` (and `astro start`) transpile code with esbuild but never run type checking — this holds whether your `tsconfig.json` extends `astro/tsconfigs/strict`, `strictest`, or `base`. Strict mode only changes the diagnostics reported by `astro check` and your editor. To make the build fail on TypeScript errors, change the `build` script to `"astro check && astro build"`; `astro check` then checks all files in your TypeScript project.
How do I correctly update my project to Astro v7 from v6?

Run `npx @astrojs/upgrade` (or `pnpm dlx @astrojs/upgrade` / `yarn dlx @astrojs/upgrade`) to upgrade Astro and all official integrations together, and upgrade other dependencies as needed. You may not need any code changes at all; if you see errors or unexpected behavior, check the guide's breaking-changes and deprecated sections — e.g. `getContainerRenderer()` imported from an integration package root (like `@astrojs/react`) is deprecated in 7.0 in favor of the dedicated entrypoint:
```
import { getContainerRenderer } from '@astrojs/react/container-renderer';
```
Available for `@astrojs/react`, `@astrojs/preact`, `@astrojs/solid-js`, `@astrojs/svelte`, `@astrojs/vue`, and `@astrojs/mdx`. Coming from an older version? Upgrade to v6 first.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/upgrade-to/v7/
In an MDX file, what is the difference between using the frontmatter layout property versus importing and using a Layout component directly in the MDX body?

Using the frontmatter `layout` property automatically passes `frontmatter` and `headings` props to the layout and injects content via `<slot />`. Importing a Layout component directly works like any Astro component — it receives no automatic props, so you must pass them explicitly, but allows passing data not in frontmatter (e.g., exported functions). Both require `<meta charset="utf-8">` in the layout.

How is Astro's learning content split across the official docs, education partner courses, and community resources — and if I find a gap in the documentation, what is the intended path for getting that knowledge into Astro or sharing it with other users?

Learning is layered: the official docs' Build a Blog tutorial covers fundamentals, the Astro Courses page adds recommended education-partner video courses ( Coding in Public, James Q Quick on Scrimba) plus curated community collections like Astro Tips, and individual guide pages curate community articles (e.g. the migration guides' "Community Resources" lists). To fill a gap, contribute directly: community guides are added by editing the docs pages on GitHub (each curated list invites you to add your resource via a GitHub edit link), and the site-wide Contribute entry point covers other ways to help. Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/astro-courses/

I want to show an estimated reading time in my `src/layouts/PostLayout.astro` without installing a plugin — I just need the post's text so I can count words. Which member of `Astro.props` gives me the Markdown source, and do I read it as a property or call it as a function?

The `rawContent()` method on `Astro.props` returns the Markdown source as a string, which you can use to calculate word count and estimate reading time. ```astro ---const { rawContent } = Astro.props;const text = rawContent();const words = text.split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean).length;const minutes = Math.ceil(words / 200); // avg 200 wpm---

Estimated reading time: {minutes} min

``` Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/layouts/#markdown-layout-props

On a product page I need a logged-in visitor's avatar (server-side data, nothing to click) and an "Add to cart" button that must respond to clicks in the browser. Which island approach fits each component, and what makes the difference?

For the logged-in visitor’s avatar, use a **server island** because it requires server-side data fetching (e.g., from a database or auth service) and renders dynamic content that should not be client-rendered.

For the "Add to cart" button, use a **client island** since it needs to respond to browser events like clicks and update the UI dynamically without a page reload.

The key difference is that server islands run in an isolated server context and are ideal for rendering personalized or dynamic content on the server, while client islands execute in the browser and provide interactivity. Server islands cannot access `Astro.url` directly; instead, they must use the Referer header to determine the originating page URL.

Example:
```astro
<!-- Server island for avatar -->
<ServerIsland>
  <Avatar />
</ServerIsland>

<!-- Client island for add-to-cart button -->
<ClientIsland>
  <AddToCartButton />
</ClientIsland>
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/concepts/islands/

I'm migrating an existing Create React App single-page application to Astro. Does the SPA have to be broken apart into islands before it can live inside an Astro site, and what is the trade-off of leaving it whole?

No, you do not need to break apart your CRA SPA into islands before integrating it into Astro. You can embed your entire React app directly using the `client:load` directive in an `.astro` page.

Example:
```astro
---
import App from '../cra-project/App.jsx';
---

<App client:load />
```

This approach preserves your app's full interactivity and structure, making migration easier. However, leaving it whole means all JavaScript is sent to the browser upfront, which may increase initial load time and bundle size.

Astro’s islands architecture allows for more granular control over when and where interactive components are hydrated, potentially improving performance. For a straightforward migration, keeping your SPA intact works well, but consider converting parts into islands later for better optimization.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/migrate-to-astro/from-create-react-app/
What is the difference between `astro dev` and `astro build` in terms of what each produces and when you would use each one during development?

`astro dev` (usually `npm run dev`) starts the local development server: it serves your project at `http://localhost:4321/`, watches `src/` and refreshes the preview live as you edit, and provides the dev toolbar — use it while building your site. `astro build` (usually `npm run build`) instead compiles a deploy-ready version into a separate folder (`dist/` by default), surfacing build errors and type errors when TypeScript is `strict`/`strictest`; use it to verify your production output, which you can then inspect locally with `astro preview`.
When should I avoid putting a JavaScript utility file in `public/` and instead place it in `src/`, even if the file doesn't import any Astro-specific APIs?

Place it in `src/` whenever you want it processed by the build. Files in `public/` are copied into the build folder untouched — CSS or JavaScript there is not bundled or optimized in your final build, and is referenced only by absolute URL path. Files under `src/` can be imported (e.g. from a `<script>`), in which case Astro builds, optimizes, and bundles them with your client-side JavaScript. As a general rule, any CSS or JavaScript you write yourself should live in `src/`.
How do you create a new Astro project using npm without manually creating an empty directory first?

Run `npm create astro@latest` in your terminal. The create-astro wizard will automatically create a new, empty project directory for you (prompting you for its name) without requiring you to create one manually.
I want to colocate a layout component alongside my pages in `src/pages` so it doesn't get treated as a route. What naming convention do I use, and what does the underscore prefix accomplish?

Prefix the layout filename with an underscore (e.g. `src/pages/_Layout.astro`); the `_` prefix excludes that file from routing so it won't be generated as a page, letting you colocate the layout with your pages while still importing and using it like any other component.

I copied my blog's Markdown posts into public/blog/ so they'd be served directly, but none of them produced routes at /blog/... — what actually happens to those files at build time, and where do page routes come from?

Files placed in the `public/` directory are copied as-is to the final build output and served directly by the web server, but they do not generate Astro pages or routes. Page routes in Astro come exclusively from files in the `src/pages/` directory.

To create dynamic blog post routes like `/blog/post-1`, you must place Markdown files inside `src/pages/posts/`. These are processed by Astro’s content collections system to generate pages at build time or on-demand, depending on your adapter and configuration. Files in `public/` bypass this entirely; they’re not parsed as Astro pages or content collections.

You can verify that a file is being served directly from `public/` if you access it via the root URL (e.g., `/blog/post-1.md`) — but such files will not render with Astro’s layout, frontmatter handling, or content collection features.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/project-structure/#public

In an Astro Markdown layout I can read both `Astro.props.url` and `Astro.props.frontmatter.url` (same for `file`). Why are both exposed, are they guaranteed identical, and when would I care about the nested `frontmatter` form?

Both forms exist because a Markdown layout receives the page's data through `Astro.props`: the top-level `file` and `url` are provided for convenience, while `frontmatter` holds the file's complete frontmatter object, which also contains them. They are guaranteed identical — `frontmatter.file` is documented as "the same as the top-level `file` property," and likewise for `frontmatter.url`. Use the nested `frontmatter` form when you already read other frontmatter fields (`title`, `author`, …) or pass the whole `frontmatter` object to a child component; use the top-level `url` when you only need the page URL, e.g. `const { frontmatter, url } = Astro.props;` to build a canonical link in a `MarkdownLayoutProps`-typed layout. These props apply only to Markdown/MDX pages using the `layout` property, not to content collections.

I want each item of `myRows` to land in its own named slot so a table component can place them in different spots, so I'm trying `<div slot={row.id}>` inside a `myRows.map()` callback. Can Astro actually do that? What happens at build time, and if the slot consumer is a React component instead of an Astro component, where should those per-item slots be created?

Astro cannot dynamically generate slot names; it is not possible to use an expression like `<div slot={row.id}>` inside a `map()` callback at build time. If the slot consumer is a React component instead of an Astro component, generate those per-item slots within the framework itself rather than trying to create dynamic Astro slot names in the Astro template.

Astro describes itself as a content-driven framework. What types of websites is it specifically designed for, and how does this differ from the types of applications that SPA frameworks like Next.js or SvelteKit are better suited for?

Astro is a content-driven, multi-page framework designed to showcase content with interactivity opt-in only where needed: pages render on the server, framework components render as static HTML by default, and you hydrate individual islands with `client:*` directives for interactivity. SPA frameworks like SvelteKit (which defaults to an SPA with server-side rendering, but can also build MPAs or traditional SPAs) suit applications built for high client-side interactivity — Astro's built-in content capabilities cover page generation, while highly interactive items such as dashboards are more challenging to replicate with `.astro` components.

Our Astro deployment leaks implementation details only on server-rendered failure paths — the error is evaluated and displayed after the error is thrown. What class of information disclosure is this, and what is the correct remediation inside the `error` prop handling code?

This is disclosure of server-side implementation details (code structure) via stack traces on failure paths. Remediation inside `error` prop handling: evaluate the error first and branch to return appropriate safe content based on what was thrown (e.g. `error instanceof Error ? error.message : "Unknown error"`); do not display the error's stack, which contains information about how your code is structured on the server.

My layout iterates `Astro.props.headings` and casts each item to my own interface with only `slug` and `text`. TypeScript still errors about a missing property — what is the complete per-item type of the `headings` array in a Markdown layout, and how should the interface be written?

Each item in `Astro.props.headings` has the type `{ depth: number; slug: string; text: string }`. Your interface must include all three properties — `depth`, `slug`, and `text` — to satisfy TypeScript.

I moved a reusable block of markup into `src/components/legacy-banner.html` and imported it into an `.astro` page, but inside that file an imported value is undefined, a `<script>` tag isn't being bundled or processed, and an image path I wrote relative to the component doesn't resolve. What's going on with `.html` components, and what are the three restrictions I have to work within?

`.html` components are plain, valid-HTML-only files, so Astro gives them no component machinery. The three restrictions: (1) no frontmatter, server-side imports, or dynamic expressions — hence your imported value is undefined; (2) any `<script>` tags are left unbundled, treated as if they had an `is:inline` directive — hence no bundling or processing; (3) they can only reference assets in the `public/` folder — hence your relative image path fails. A `<slot />` inside them still works as it does in an Astro component.

I'm building a blog in Astro 7 and want structured, validated content with full TypeScript support. Which guide covers setting this up, and what keyword in the guide title indicates the type safety aspect?

The Content Collections guide, titled "Create type safe content collections" — the keyword is **type safe** (the title phrase "type safe"). It covers defining a collection schema that validates your entries, giving you structured content checked by TypeScript plus content-focused querying APIs such as `getCollection()`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/content-collections/

When an Astro page fails, who should decide what the response body says about the failure — the route/page that owns the error handling, or the presentational components deeper in the tree that receive the error? What's the advantage of evaluating the error at that boundary?

The route/page that owns the error handling — e.g. `src/pages/500.astro` — should decide what the response body says, not presentational components deeper in the tree. The 500 page is automatically passed an `error` prop (typed `unknown`) for any error thrown during rendering, so that boundary can evaluate the value once and choose appropriate content. Evaluating the error at the boundary prevents disclosure: you can return a safe, generic message instead of leaking details such as the stack, which reveals how your server code is structured. Layout and child components then stay purely presentational.
How do I get the absolute filesystem path of the current Markdown file from an Astro layout — and is the value reachable at more than one place in `Astro.props`?

Read the `file` Markdown layout prop: a layout applied through the frontmatter `layout` property has access via `Astro.props` to `file`, documented as "The absolute path of this file (e.g. `/home/user/projects/.../file.md`)." The same value is reachable in a second place — the nested `frontmatter.file`, described as "the same as the top-level `file` property" — so both locations exist and always hold the identical path.

```
---
const { file, frontmatter } = Astro.props;
// frontmatter.file is the same absolute path as file
---
```

These are Markdown layout props (`file`, `url`, `frontmatter`, `headings`, `rawContent()`, `compiledContent()`), available to a layout used by an individual `.md`/`.mdx` page in `src/pages/` via the special `layout` frontmatter property, which is not recognized when querying content collections.

My `src/components/MyLayout.astro` pulls `title`, `description`, `publishDate` and `viewCount` out of `Astro.props` and renders `<meta name="description" content={description}>` plus a "Published on" and "Viewed by" block. Right now nothing catches a page that forgets to pass `viewCount`. How do I add type safety and autocompletion for those props, and does declaring the type change anything about how the consuming page must pass them?
Can multiple client islands on the same page share state and communicate with each other despite running in isolation?

Yes. Client islands run in isolation, but they can still share state and communicate across component contexts. Astro's recommended solution is Nano Stores: framework-agnostic stores under 1 KB with zero dependencies, so they work across React, Preact, Vue, Svelte, and Solid islands on the same page. Alternatives include Svelte built-in stores, Solid signals exported from a shared file, Vue's reactivity API, or custom browser events. Note that writing to a store from `.astro` frontmatter does not affect hydrated client components, and stores can't be passed as props to them.
Which scripts should exist in my Astro project's package.json to cover the standard local workflow, and what does each one run?

Three scripts cover the standard local workflow:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "astro dev",
    "build": "astro build",
    "preview": "astro preview"
  }
}
```

- `dev` runs `astro dev`, the development server with a live preview that updates as you edit.
- `build` runs `astro build`, producing a deploy-ready site in `dist/` (default) and surfacing build errors; with TypeScript set to `strict` or `strictest`, it also checks the project for type errors.
- `preview` runs `astro preview`, serving the built site locally.

The `create astro` wizard adds these automatically; add them yourself during manual setup, plus any extra commands you use often.
When viewing my Astro site in the browser during development, what specific features does the dev toolbar provide access to for inspecting and debugging?

The dev toolbar appears at the bottom of every page while the dev server runs (hover to reveal; dev-only, never on your published site) and exposes four built-in apps: **Astro Menu** (project info, links to docs/GitHub/Discord, and a "Copy debug info" button that runs `astro info`), **Inspect** (shows each island's props and its client directive), **Audit** (runs performance and accessibility audits, flags issues with a red dot, and highlights the affected elements on the page), and **Settings** (verbose logging, notifications, toolbar placement). Integrations can add further toolbar apps.

I put an Astro component with frontmatter and Astro-specific behavior into src/pages/landing.html, and key Astro features silently don't work. What's the limitation with .html files in src/pages/, and which page file type should I use instead?

HTML components placed in `src/pages/` do not support Astro-specific features like frontmatter, server-side imports, dynamic expressions, or `<script>` tags with bundling. These limitations apply to all `.html` files in the `src/pages/` directory.

Use `.astro` files instead for full Astro functionality, including frontmatter and component features.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/astro-pages/#html-pages

I have a legacy snippet in `src/components/LegacyBanner.html` that uses `<script>` tags and template expressions like `{title}`. The script runs against globals but isn't processed by Vite, and the expression outputs as literal text. Why does this happen, and what is the one Astro component feature that HTML components *do* support despite their limitations?

Because `.html` components must contain only valid HTML, they lack frontmatter, server-side imports, and dynamic expressions — so `{title}` is emitted literally instead of being evaluated — and their `<script>` tags are left unbundled, treated as if they had an `is:inline` directive, so Vite never processes them. The one Astro component feature they do support is `<slot />`: a slot inside an HTML component works as it would in an Astro component (add `is:inline` to use the native HTML Web Component slot instead).

My Markdown layout crashes with `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')` on the line `Astro.props.frontmatter.headings.map(...)`. Where is heading data actually exposed in an Astro Markdown layout?

In Astro Markdown layouts, heading data is available via the `headings` property directly on `Astro.props`, not nested inside `frontmatter`. The correct access pattern is: ```astro ---const { headings } = Astro.props;--- {headings.map((heading) => ( {heading.text} ))} ``` The error occurs because `frontmatter.headings` does not exist in Markdown layouts. Instead, `headings` is a top-level property of `Astro.props`, containing an array of objects with `depth`, `slug`, and `text` keys. Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/layouts/#markdown-layouts
I put a custom CSS file in `public/styles/custom.css` and imported it in my layout. Why isn't Astro bundling or optimizing this stylesheet in the production build?

Files in `public/` skip Astro's CSS processing, bundling, and optimizations. The stylesheet is served as-is. To get bundling/optimization, move the file to `src/` (e.g., `src/styles/custom.css`) and import it via ESM in your layout.

I serve an HTML fragment to htmx with hx-post="/partials/clicked/" and hx-swap="innerHTML" targeting #parent-div, and src/pages/partials/clicked.astro starts with export const partial = true. Why doesn't Astro inject <!DOCTYPE html> and <head> into that response the way it does for other files in src/pages/, and what exactly has to match between the hx-post URL and my file on disk for the swap to work?

Because `export const partial = true` marks the file as a page partial, Astro intentionally omits `<!DOCTYPE html>`, `<head>`, and scoped styles/scripts. The `hx-post` URL path must exactly match the file's path under `src/pages/` (e.g., `/partials/clicked/` ↔ `src/pages/partials/clicked.astro`).
What is the difference between the 'Add integrations' guide and the 'Create type safe content collections' guide in terms of what each helps you accomplish in an Astro project?

The "Add integrations" guide covers extending your project with integrations — its title names React and Partytown — i.e. adding framework and third-party tooling. The "Create type safe content collections" guide instead covers content collections: defining a schema so each entry is validated as correct and complete, querying with content-focused APIs like `getCollection()` instead of `import.meta.glob()`, and choosing between build-time collections (cached, prerendered, MDX and image optimization) and live collections (fetched at request time).

During a phased rewrite, one section of my Astro site still uses Vue components while its replacement is built with SolidJS, and both must ship in the same deployment. Can one Astro project render both frameworks (even on the same page), and what do I need to install and configure?

Yes, a single Astro project can render both Vue and SolidJS components on the same page during a phased rewrite. You need to install the official integrations for both frameworks: ```bash npm install @astrojs/vue @astrojs/solid-js ``` Then configure them in your `astro.config.mjs`: ```js import { defineConfig } from 'astro/config'; import vue from '@astrojs/vue'; import solid from '@astrojs/solid-js'; export default defineConfig({ integrations: [vue(), solid()] }); ``` Import and use components directly in your Astro files: ```astro --- import VueComponent from '../components/VueComponent.vue'; import SolidComponent from '../components/SolidComponent.jsx'; ---
``` Astro will render both frameworks as static HTML by default, with client-side interactivity only when needed. Both components can coexist on the same page without conflicts. Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/framework-components/

My Astro error component sometimes runs when the value handed to it isn't a real `Error` instance — it can be a plain string or nothing at all, and reading a property straight away blows up or prints something unexpected. How should the component handle that case while still avoiding disclosure?

In `src/components/GreetingHeadline.astro`, I destructure `const { greeting = 'Hello', name } = Astro.props;` and render `

{greeting}, {name}!

`. A parent passes ``. What does the component render if `userName` is `undefined` at call time, and why?

It renders `

Hi, !

`. The `greeting = 'Hello'` default only applies when no value is passed, and the parent explicitly passes `greeting="Hi"`, so the default is skipped. `name` has no default and `userName` is `undefined`, so `name` is `undefined` and the expression contributes nothing between the comma and `!`.
Can I rename the `src/styles` directory to `src/css` and still have Astro process my stylesheets correctly?

Yes. The `src/styles` directory is only a convention — Astro processes and optimizes stylesheets from anywhere inside `src/` as long as they are imported correctly (e.g., `import '../styles/utils.css'`). Renaming it to `src/css` works without configuration changes.

I'm tempted to put all of our marketing sections in plain `.html` files under src/pages/ so non-framework colleagues can edit them, including sections that need props from Astro. Why is that a bad fit, and what should I reach for instead — and what is the one HTML component limitation that isn't actually a limitation?

Plain `.html` files under `src/pages/` are static HTML with no Astro runtime: they lack frontmatter, server-side imports, and dynamic expressions, so you cannot pass or compute Astro props in them. For marketing sections that need props from Astro, use `.astro` components (or framework components with props passed from an `.astro` parent). The one apparent limitation that isn't actually a limitation is slots: a `<slot />` inside an HTML component works as an Astro slot (to use the native HTML Web Component `<slot>` instead, add `is:inline`).
In an Astro page or component that receives an `error` prop, what should I do before rendering anything from it, and why does the order matter?

Evaluate the `error` before rendering anything from it — the prop is typed `unknown`, so check `error instanceof Error` (or otherwise narrow it) first and return appropriate content based on the error thrown: ```astro --- interface Props { error: unknown; } const { error } = Astro.props; ---
{error instanceof Error ? error.message : "Unknown error"}
``` Order matters because evaluating first prevents both runtime errors from accessing properties on a non-`Error` value and the leaking of sensitive information — in particular, you should avoid displaying the error's stack, which reveals how your server code is structured. Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/astro-pages/

Do I have to buy a paid course to become productive with Astro, or can I get through the fundamentals on the free official tutorial alone? And if I do pay for a partner course, what happens to part of the money?

No — you can learn the fundamentals entirely through the **free official "Build a Blog" tutorial**. Paid partner courses are optional. If you purchase via Astro's affiliate links, **part of your purchase funds Astro open-source development** directly.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/astro-courses/
In what scenario would using a single-page application (SPA) approach be more appropriate than Astro's islands architecture?

An SPA is more appropriate when you need the simplicity and power of a full client-rendered application — for example, an app-like experience where the entire page is highly interactive, or an existing SPA embedded inside an Astro page (such as one migrated from Create React App). SPAs hydrate the whole site as one large JavaScript application, which causes page-load performance problems, and they lack the ability to selectively hydrate — making them a heavy-handed choice for most content-focused websites, where Astro's islands architecture wins.
When would I need to follow the 'Connect a headless CMS' guide versus just using Astro content collections directly? What does the CMS guide title tell you about the kind of service being integrated?

Follow the "Connect a headless CMS" guide when your content lives remotely in a CMS and you want to use the collections helper functions instead of writing `fetch()` calls or SDK integrations yourself; use content collections directly for local files (e.g. a directory of Markdown posts sharing frontmatter), for one-off pages, or when your data source ships its own incompatible client library. The word "headless" in the title signals the service is a content-only backend: it stores and delivers content via API without rendering its own frontend, so Astro stays the sole presentation layer. Either path lands you on the same collection APIs (`getCollection()`, build-time or live collections), so the guide changes where content is sourced, not how it is queried or rendered.
What is the difference between Astro content collections and just importing Markdown files manually, and why would I want type safety for my content?

Content collections organize sets of structurally identical documents behind a required `loader` and an optional Zod `schema`, giving you query APIs plus automatic TypeScript types, editor autocomplete, and validation—none of which you get from importing Markdown files one by one, where every frontmatter field is untyped and unchecked. Type safety matters because a schema guarantees each entry's data exists in a predictable form when you query it: a missing `title` or a string `pubDate` is caught and reported instead of failing silently at render time, and Astro generates the matching TypeScript interface so property access is checked in your editor.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/content-collections/

In an `.mdx` file under `src/pages/posts/`, what's the difference between declaring `layout: ../../layouts/BaseLayout.astro` in the frontmatter versus `import BaseLayout from '../../layouts/BaseLayout.astro'` and rendering `<BaseLayout>` myself? Specifically, which approach hands the layout `frontmatter` and `headings` for free, and what do I lose or gain in each case?

The frontmatter `layout` property passes `frontmatter` and `headings` (plus `file`, `url`, `rawContent()`, `compiledContent()`) to the layout automatically via `Astro.props`. A manually imported `<BaseLayout>` is just a normal Astro component: it receives no props automatically, so you must pass everything yourself — though you gain the ability to pass values that don't exist in frontmatter (JS exports like `fancyJsHelper`, computed props):

```mdx
import BaseLayout from '../../layouts/BaseLayout.astro';

<BaseLayout title={frontmatter.title} fancyJsHelper={fancyJsHelper}>
  Welcome to my new Astro blog!
</BaseLayout>
```

Both approaches require including `<meta charset="utf-8">` in the layout yourself.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/layouts/

I have `<slot />` inside an `.html` component and the slotted children render where I expect. But a child's CSS that targets the native HTML `<slot>` element doesn't behave as I anticipated. Why does Astro intercept my `<slot />` there, and how do I get the platform's Web Component `<slot>` behavior instead?

Astro intercepts `<slot />` even in `.html` components so it behaves as an Astro slot placeholder rather than the platform element. To get the native Web Component `<slot>` behavior instead, add `is:inline` to the element: `<slot is:inline>`. Slotted children still render where you expect either way; only the element's identity in the rendered output changes.

My CI pipeline needs to lint and format `.astro` files. I already have the Astro VS Code Extension installed on my machine — can I rely on it in CI, or do I need something else? Also, if I choose Biome instead of Prettier for `.astro` files, what exactly can Biome do with them today?

The Astro VS Code Extension is editor tooling, not a CLI, so it can't run in CI — use command-line tools instead: `prettier` with `prettier-plugin-astro` for formatting, the community `eslint-plugin-astro` for ESLint, `stylelint-config-html` for Stylelint, or Biome. Biome's `.astro` support is experimental: it can lint and format the frontmatter of `.astro` files, not the full template.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/editor-setup/

My `src/layouts/PageLayout.astro` receives a `head` slot and a default slot, then passes both to `BaseLayout.astro` using `` and ``. A page uses `Home

Welcome

`. What exact markup does `BaseLayout` receive for each slot, and why does the `head` slot need both attributes on the intermediate component?

`BaseLayout.astro` receives the `<title>` element in its named `head` slot and the `<h1>` element in its default slot.

The `head` slot uses both `name="head"` and `slot="head"` attributes to explicitly map the `head` slot from `PageLayout` to the corresponding `head` slot in `BaseLayout`. This is required because Astro's slot system supports transferring named slots between components, allowing you to rename or reorganize slots during layout nesting. Without specifying both attributes, Astro wouldn't know how to correctly route the content.

Example:
```astro
<!-- BaseLayout.astro -->
<html>
  <head><slot name="head" /></head>
  <body><slot /></body>
</html>

<!-- PageLayout.astro -->
<BaseLayout>
  <slot name="head" slot="head" />
  <slot />
</BaseLayout>
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/astro-components/#named-slots

I want to format `.astro` files with Prettier from the CLI in my Astro project. What packages do I install, and what does my `.prettierrc` need to contain so Prettier uses the correct parser for `.astro` files?

Install both packages as exact dev dependencies:

```
npm install --save-dev --save-exact prettier prettier-plugin-astro
```

Then create `.prettierrc` in the project root, registering the plugin and manually specifying the parser for Astro files:

```json
{
  "plugins": ["prettier-plugin-astro"],
  "overrides": [
    { "files": "*.astro", "options": { "parser": "astro" } }
  ]
}
```

Format from the CLI with `npx prettier . --write`. If you add other plugins (e.g. Tailwind), list them after `prettier-plugin-astro` in `plugins`.

In `MyFavoritePokemon.astro` I render an `<Avatar>` component that hits a slow API, and a `ReactPokemonComponent` that I only need once it scrolls into view. How do I delay the Avatar's rendering and give it a loading placeholder, and how do I make the React component hydrate only when it becomes visible?

Delay the Avatar with the `server:defer` directive and provide a placeholder in the `fallback` slot; hydrate the React component only in view with `client:visible`:

```astro
<Avatar server:defer>
  <svg slot="fallback" class="generic-avatar" transition:name="avatar">...</svg>
</Avatar>

<ReactPokemonComponent client:visible />
```

`server:defer` makes the Avatar a server island: its server rendering is deferred so it streams in when ready without delaying the page, showing the fallback until then. `client:visible` is a `client:*` hydration directive: the React component first renders to static HTML on the server, and its JavaScript (plus React itself) is not sent to the browser until the user scrolls the component into view.
When should you use API routes versus handling form submissions directly in Astro page frontmatter?

Handle submissions directly in page frontmatter for simple full-page POSTs: check `Astro.request.method === "POST"`, read the data with `await Astro.request.formData()`, then re-render the page — no client JavaScript needed (add `export const prerender = false` when not using `server` output mode). Use an API route when you need JavaScript to intercept the submit and send the data to an endpoint instead of causing a refresh or navigation, e.g. fetch-based partial updates; this requires an adapter for on-demand rendering and a UI framework integration. Prefer API routes for asynchronous, non-blocking submissions; frontmatter for classic no-JS form posts with server-side revalidation.
I placed a CSS file in `public/styles/main.css` and linked it in my HTML. Will this CSS be bundled and optimized like CSS in `src/`? What are the trade-offs?

No — a `<link>` to `public/styles/main.css` skips Astro's normal CSS processing, bundling, and optimizations. You get a consistent absolute URL and full manual control, but no minification, no per-page chunk splitting with shared-CSS reuse, and no automatic inlining of small stylesheets (production builds inline chunks under 4kB by default, controlled by `assetsInlineLimit` / `build.inlineStylesheets`). For bundling, import the stylesheet from `src/` in your component frontmatter: `import '../styles/utils.css';`. Also, relative `href` values are unsupported — the path must be absolute.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/styling/
When using a manually imported layout in an MDX file, why must you explicitly include <meta charset="utf-8"> in the layout component, and what happens if you omit it?

Astro 5.0 only adds `<meta charset="utf-8">` automatically for pages that don't use the `layout` frontmatter property or import a wrapping Layout component. With a manually imported layout, Astro skips this injection, so you must include the tag yourself. Omitting it may cause non-ASCII characters to render incorrectly.
How do I structure an Astro error component so it returns different, safe content depending on which kind of error was thrown, without ever exposing the server-side code structure?

Evaluate the `error` prop before rendering: type it as `unknown`, branch on what you detect (e.g. `error instanceof Error ? error.message : "Unknown error"`), and return different safe content per branch. Never render `error.stack`, which reveals server-side code structure; only output content you have deliberately chosen to expose.
What is the distinction between the React integration and the Partytown integration as described in the Astro 7 guide 'Add integrations like React and Partytown'?

Both are official Astro integrations set up via `npx astro add <name>` and registered in `astro.config.mjs`'s `integrations` array, but they serve different purposes: `@astrojs/react` is a front-end framework integration (listed under "Front-end frameworks") for building UI, while `@astrojs/partytown` is not a framework — it installs Partytown and enables it on every page so resource-intensive third-party scripts (analytics, ads) run in a web worker, off the main thread. Partytown needs no config (`partytown()`), with optional `config` for `debug`, `forward`, and `resolveUrl`; individual scripts opt in with `type="text/partytown"`.

In `src/components/ProfileCard.astro` I put an `await fetch('SOME_SECRET_API_URL/users')` call inside the `---` code fence and render `user.name` in the template below it. I don't see a `client:*` directive anywhere — can the secret API URL and its credentials still leak into the HTML or JS that reaches the browser, and where exactly is the boundary between the component script and the component template?

No. The `await fetch(...)` runs only inside the component script, and Astro's code fence guarantees that JavaScript is "fenced in": it executes on the server (at build time or on demand) and is stripped from the final page, so neither the URL nor the credentials reach the browser. The boundary is the `---` fence itself — everything above it is the component script (server-only), everything below is the component template that determines the HTML output. Only data you explicitly render from the script, such as `user.name`, appears in the HTML sent to visitors. Zero JavaScript is added by default since Astro components don't render on the client.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/astro-components/
Even if you write no TypeScript code, why does the manual setup require creating a tsconfig.json that extends astro/tsconfigs/base?

Even without writing TypeScript, a `tsconfig.json` extending `astro/tsconfigs/base` is required so that tools like Astro and VS Code can properly understand your project. Some features, such as npm package imports, are not fully supported in the editor without this configuration file.
Why might an Astro 7 site still exhibit a high Time to Interactive metric despite the framework's 'zero JavaScript by default' principle, and what default behavior could be responsible?

"Zero JavaScript by default" applies only to `.astro` components; hydrated UI framework components are the usual cause of a high Time to Interactive. Any framework component using a `client:*` directive ships that component's JavaScript plus its framework runtime (React, Svelte, etc.) to the browser, and with `client:load` the import begins as soon as the page loads, competing with interactivity for main-thread time. Choosing `client:visible`, `client:idle`, or `client:media` defers that cost, and skipping hydration entirely keeps it at zero. Note the framework bundle is shared: if multiple components use the same framework, it is sent only once.

A client island with `client:idle` never becomes interactive on a page where the user immediately starts scrolling. Why does this happen, and which directive would ensure it hydrates regardless of browser idle state?

`client:idle` hydrates only after the page finishes its initial load and the `requestIdleCallback` event fires (falling back to the document `load` event in browsers that lack `requestIdleCallback`). Continuous scrolling keeps the browser busy, so the idle callback may never fire and the component stays unhydrated. Use `client:load` instead: it loads and hydrates the component JavaScript immediately on page load, with high priority, regardless of browser idle state.

In a `Wrapper.astro` layout I already destructure `const { title } = Astro.props` from frontmatter, and I also wrap page content in `...

All about Fred

...`. What's actually different about the children between props and slots — when should I use `Astro.props` versus ``, and where does each one end up in the output?

**Props** (`Astro.props`) pass data (strings, numbers, objects) into the component for use anywhere in its template — e.g., `title` in `

{title}

`. **Slots** (``) inject **child HTML elements** at specific positions in the component's markup — e.g., `

All about Fred

` lands where `` sits. Use props for configurable values; slots for arbitrary child content. Named slots (``) target specific children via `slot="x"`. Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/astro-components/

I want to reuse an existing legacy `.html` snippet as an Astro component, but it needs to loop over a list of tags and conditionally add a class. Should I keep it as a `.html` file, and if not, what's the closest Astro-native approach?

Not if it needs a loop and a conditional class — `.html` components must contain only valid HTML and support no frontmatter, imports, or dynamic expressions. Rename it to `.astro` and use a component script; that's the closest Astro-native equivalent: ```astro --- const tags = ["astro", "docs", "css"]; ---
    {tags.map((tag) => (
  • {tag}
    • ))}
``` Keep `.html` only for markup you want to guarantee stays fully static.
I bumped my project from astro@7.3.4 to astro@7.3.5 and code that depended on unintended behavior stopped working, even though only the patch number changed. Is this a semver violation?

No, this is not a semver violation. According to Astro’s semantic versioning policy, patch releases can include bug fixes that may unintentionally break code relying on unintended or undesirable behavior, as long as those changes align with the documented functionality and expected behavior.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/upgrade-astro/#semantic-versioning
When connecting a headless CMS to Astro, what are the key architectural considerations for fetching and rendering content at build time vs. on-demand?

Astro prerenders every page and endpoint by default, so content fetched from a headless CMS at build time ships as static HTML—the most performant choice when data changes infrequently. For fresh or per-viewer content, opt routes into on-demand rendering: first add a server adapter for your runtime (e.g. `npx astro add netlify`; official adapters exist for Node, Netlify, Vercel, and Cloudflare), then add `export const prerender = false` on the individual pages or endpoints that need it. For a highly dynamic app, `output: 'server'` flips the default so everything renders on demand, with `export const prerender = true` opting individual routes back to static. Start in the default `'static'` mode until you know most pages need a server.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/on-demand-rendering/

I want a `TagList.astro` component that takes a `tags` array prop and renders one `<li>` per tag into a named slot, so each tag gets its own `<slot name="tag-{tag}" />` placeholder and the parent injects matching markup. Can I build the slot name with a template literal inside `tags.map()`, and if not, what's the right place to generate this kind of repeated, per-item markup?

No. Astro does not allow dynamically generating slot names (e.g., `slot="tag-{tag}"` inside a `.map()`). Generate the repeated markup directly in the component template instead, or use a framework component (React, Svelte, etc.) where dynamic slots are supported.

A personalized `<UserGreeting />` section on my page needs per-visitor data from a slow, authenticated request, but I don't want that request to block the rest of the HTML. I can either add a `client:load` framework island or a server directive to the component. When should I reach for a server island instead of a hydrated client island, and what changes about when the component's HTML actually gets generated and streamed?

Reach for a server island (`server:defer`) when the section is personalized server-rendered content that needs no client-side interactivity; a `client:load` island is for components that must be interactive in the browser, and it ships and hydrates framework JavaScript.

The timing differs: with `client:load`, the component's HTML is generated as part of the normal page render, and its JS bundle loads and hydrates afterward in the browser. With `server:defer`, generating that component's HTML is deferred — you provide fallback content (e.g. a `slot="fallback"`), and the component renders later in its own isolated context outside the page request, streaming its HTML in when the slow authenticated request resolves, without delaying the rest of the page.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/server-islands/
Besides the docs and courses, what channels exist for getting help from other Astro users, contributing back, and financially supporting the project — and are they the same thing?

Three distinct channels, linked at the bottom of most docs pages:
- **Community** (Discord) — real-time help, questions, showcases
- **Contribute** (GitHub) — code, docs, translations, PR reviews, triage
- **Sponsor** (OpenCollective) — financial support for the project
They are not the same: help/chat ≠ code/docs contributions ≠ monetary funding.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/contribute/

I'm building a custom Markdown layout in Astro and need to render a table of contents from the headings in my `.md` files. What is the exact shape of the data I receive in `Astro.props`, and can I call a `getHeadings()` function like I do in Markdown files?

`Astro.props` in a Markdown layout provides `headings` as an array of objects typed `{ depth: number; slug: string; text: string }[]`. You cannot call `getHeadings()`—the docs explicitly state heading information is available "via the `headings` array, rather than a `getHeadings()` function." Use `Astro.props.headings` directly to build your table of contents.

I moved my layout component out of src/layouts and into src/components/shared/PageShell.astro. The component still works, but I'm wondering: is there any Astro convention or routing behavior that would break if I colocate a layout alongside pages in src/pages, and what filename prefix prevents it from becoming a route?

Astro does not automatically treat components in `src/components` as routes, even when they are colocated with pages in `src/pages`. However, placing layouts directly inside `src/pages` will cause them to be treated as routes unless you use the `_` prefix.

To prevent a file from becoming a route in Astro, it must start with an underscore (`_`). For example, a layout named `_BaseLayout.astro` or `__BaseLayout.astro` would not be rendered as a page but can still be imported and used by other components or pages.

If you move your layout to `src/components/shared/PageShell.astro`, it will not become a route automatically because files in `src/components/` are not scanned for routing unless explicitly referenced from within another component or page. This is the standard convention for organizing shared components like layouts that should not be rendered as standalone pages.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/layouts/
In a manual Astro setup, what is the purpose of creating a public/robots.txt file, and how does Astro treat files placed in the public/ directory during builds?

`public/robots.txt` tells search bots how to crawl and index your site (e.g. `User-agent: *` with `Allow: /`), and Astro never processes anything in `public/`: those files are served at `/` during dev and copied to the build directory as-is, without transform or bundling (`publicDir` defaults to `"./public"`). That makes `public/` ideal for special files such as `robots.txt` and `manifest.webmanifest`, plus images and fonts needing no processing — CSS and JavaScript you write yourself belong in `src/`, since `public/` files ship unbundled.

How do you query the `src/content/posts` content collection in an Astro page and render the post titles?

Query it with `getCollection()` from `astro:content`, then map over the returned entries and read `post.data.title` in your template: ```astro --- import { getCollection } from 'astro:content' const posts = await getCollection('posts') ---
    {posts.map(post => (
  • {post.data.title}
    • ))}
``` `getCollection('posts')` returns an array of entries, each with a unique `id` and a `data` object containing your schema properties (including `title`). Note that the returned sort order is non-deterministic, so sort the array yourself if you need a specific order.
When rendering Strapi content in Astro, what's the difference between using `set:html`, rendering as plain text, and using a markdown component?

Plain text, ``, and a markdown component render the same string three different ways. `

{article.content}

` escapes the string and displays it literally, so any markup shows as visible characters. `` injects the string directly as live HTML — correct when Strapi already returns HTML, but check the `set:html` directive guidance for safety since the raw markup is executed. A markdown component (`{article.content}`) passes the string through a renderer that converts Markdown syntax to HTML. Choose to match the format your Strapi field actually stores: plain text for plain text, the markdown component for Markdown, `set:html` for pre-rendered HTML. What npm command installs Decap CMS in an Astro 7 project and what two files must be created to enable the admin interface?

Run `npm install decap-cms-app`, then create two files: `public/admin/config.yml`, which declares your collections (and optionally `media_folder`/`public_folder`), and `src/pages/admin.html`, the `/admin` route that loads the Decap script and links the config:

  </head>

  </body>

Then visit `yoursite.com/admin/`.
In Astro 7 Keystatic setup, I see @keystatic/core and @keystatic/astro listed as separate packages. What is the distinct role of @keystatic/astro versus @keystatic/core in the project configuration?

`@keystatic/astro` provides the Astro integration itself — you import it as `keystatic` and register it in the `integrations` array in `astro.config.mjs`, which mounts the Admin UI at `/keystatic`. `@keystatic/core` provides the content-modeling API — its `config`, `fields`, and `collection` exports are what you use in `keystatic.config.ts` to define storage and your collection schemas.

```js
// astro.config.mjs
import keystatic from '@keystatic/astro'
export default defineConfig({ integrations: [react(), markdoc(), keystatic()] })
```

```ts
// keystatic.config.ts
import { config, fields, collection } from '@keystatic/core'
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/cms/keystatic/

When building a blog with Storyblok in Astro, what is the key difference between creating static pages at build time versus using a dynamic [...slug].astro route with on-demand rendering for fetching blog post content?

With static generation, `getStaticPaths()` runs once at build time: it queries all stories and emits a page per story, so content updates require a full rebuild and unknown slugs produce no page at all. With on-demand rendering (adapter installed), `[...slug].astro` reads `Astro.params.slug` at request time, fetches that single story per visit, and can handle missing stories dynamically by returning `Astro.redirect('/404')` to a `src/pages/404.astro` page — serving fresh content without redeploying. In short: build-time = pre-generated, rebuild-to-update; on-demand = per-request fetch with runtime 404 handling.

When building a modular content block component in Astro that pulls a ‘Multiple-paragraph text’ field from DatoCMS, how should you define the Props interface and use the set:html directive, and what happens if the field type is not a simple string?
When building a static Astro site with WordPress data, what does `getStaticPaths()` in `src/pages/dinos/[slug].astro` return for each dinosaur post?

An array of objects, one per dinosaur post, each shaped as `{ params: { slug: post.slug }, props: { post: post } }`. The `params` key tells Astro which routes to build (the keys must match the `[slug]` filename, and values are strings), while `props` passes the full post object to the page template, where it's read via `Astro.props`. This function is required for static builds; SSR doesn't need it.

When fetching Contentful entries in an Astro component, explain the difference between using CONTENTFUL_DELIVERY_TOKEN and CONTENTFUL_PREVIEW_TOKEN, and which token to use for published versus unpublished content.

The delivery token consumes *published* content; the preview token consumes *unpublished* content. The standard client switches between them by mode:

```ts
export const contentfulClient = contentful.createClient({
  space: import.meta.env.CONTENTFUL_SPACE_ID,
  accessToken: import.meta.env.DEV
    ? import.meta.env.CONTENTFUL_PREVIEW_TOKEN
    : import.meta.env.CONTENTFUL_DELIVERY_TOKEN,
  host: import.meta.env.DEV ? "preview.contentful.com" : "cdn.contentful.com",
});
```

So in development you query the preview API (`preview.contentful.com`) and can see unpublished content from the Contentful web app, while at build time you query the delivery API (`cdn.contentful.com`) and only published content is available.

When deploying Decap CMS to a non-Netlify hosting provider, why must custom OAuth routes be created using on-demand rendered routes with an adapter, whereas on Netlify only the Identity Widget on the admin route and dashboard configuration are needed?

Netlify has first-class Decap support: you enable Identity in the Netlify dashboard and drop the Netlify Identity Widget onto the `admin` route, so authentication is handled by Netlify's hosted service and no server code of your own is required. On any other host, no such built-in service exists, so you must supply your own OAuth routes to complete the external OAuth client flow. Those routes must run server-side at request time — i.e. be on-demand rendered — and rendering any page on demand requires an adapter, which produces the script that runs your project on that specific runtime. Without an adapter, a statically built site cannot execute the OAuth exchange.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/on-demand-rendering/

To trigger automatic rebuilds of a static Astro site hosted on Netlify when content is published in Storyblok, what specific Netlify build hook URL must be added to Storyblok's Webhooks settings, and which Storyblok event should it be pasted into?

There is no fixed URL — you generate it in Netlify: site dashboard → **Build & deploy** → **Continuous Deployment** tab → **Build hooks** → **Add build hook**, name it, choose the branch, save, and copy the generated URL. Paste that URL into Storyblok's space **Settings** → **Webhooks** tab, in the **Story published & unpublished** field, then hit `Save`. Publishing or unpublishing a story then triggers a fresh Netlify build of your static Astro site.
