In `src/pages/index.astro`, why does the anchor tag use `set:html={post.title.rendered}` instead of interpolating `{post.title.rendered}` directly?

Because `title.rendered` contains HTML markup from WordPress: interpolating `{post.title.rendered}` would escape it and display the tags as literal text, while `set:html={post.title.rendered}` renders that HTML into the page. The same pattern is used for body content via `<Fragment set:html={post.content.rendered} />`.

My content team already edits files in a Git repository and reviews every change through pull requests, and they care most about editorial speed and security. When is a Git-based CMS the better fit than reaching for a dashboard-driven headless CMS like StudioCMS?

Choose a Git-based CMS (like CloudCannon, listed as "Git-based CMS built for speed, security, and zero headaches") when your team already uses Git workflows with pull requests and prioritizes editorial speed and security — it edits files directly in the repository rather than through a separate dashboard.

The guide warns that `set:html` inserts HTML without escaping. What specific step does the example take to mitigate XSS risk when rendering HackMD note content?

The example first passes the note through `markdown-it` with raw HTML disabled (`html: false`), so raw HTML in a note is escaped and rendered as literal text instead of being parsed, and only Markdown-generated markup reaches `set:html`. If you enable the `html` option for trusted authors, sanitize the rendered result before passing it to `set:html`.
What does the `populate=image` parameter do when fetching articles from Strapi in Astro, and when do I need to use it?

`populate=image` is a Strapi query parameter that tells the API to include the related image record in the response instead of returning an empty relation. Use it whenever you need the image data in Astro, e.g. `endpoint: 'articles?populate=image'` on the index page, or you won't have `article.image.data.url` available for ``. Plain field data such as `title`, `content`, and `slug` comes back without it. Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/cms/strapi/

In astro.config.mjs, the emdash integration is configured with a sqlite database using `url: "file:./data.db"` and local storage pointing to `./uploads`. What happens to uploaded media files when the project is deployed to a platform with an ephemeral filesystem?

EmDash's `local()` storage writes uploads to `./uploads` on the server's own disk, so on a platform with an ephemeral filesystem those media files do not persist: they are lost whenever the instance is recycled or redeployed, and other instances cannot serve them. For production, provision a persistent database and a dedicated media storage backend instead of local disk, as the EmDash deployment instructions advise.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/cms/emdash/

When retrieving only certain fields from Drupal JSON:API in Astro 7, what is the correct query string format to request the `title` and `body` fields for nodes of type `article`, and how does the `fields[node--article]` parameter differ from adding filters with `filter[status]`?

Use `GET /jsonapi/node/article?fields[node--article]=title,body` (the key is `fields--` style `{entity_type}--{bundle}`). The `fields[node--article]` parameter controls which attributes are included in each returned entity's response, while `filter[status]=1` (e.g. `?filter[status]=1`) controls which entities match and are returned at all; the two are independent and can be combined in one query string, as in `?fields[node--article]=title&filter[title]=Testing JSON:API`.

How can I set up my Astro site to automatically rebuild when I publish new content in Strapi?

In Astro's default static mode you must trigger a build yourself: create a build hook in your host — Netlify: **Build & deploy** → **Continuous Deployment** → **Build hooks** → **Add build hook**, name it, pick a branch, save, copy the URL; Vercel: **Settings** → **Git** → **Deploy Hooks**, name it, pick a branch, **Add**, copy the URL — then add that URL as a webhook in your Strapi admin panel following Strapi's webhooks guide. Publishing in Strapi then triggers a fresh build so your site updates. With on-demand rendering you don't need this, since pages fetch content at request time.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/cms/strapi/

Why might setting media_folder and public_folder to the same path 'src/assets/images' in public/admin/config.yml cause uploaded images to fail to display if the Astro project uses relative paths in content frontmatter?

Decap writes the `public_folder` value into your entry's frontmatter as the image `src`, while `media_folder` only decides where the file is committed. Setting both to `src/assets/images` therefore stores values like `src/assets/images/photo.jpg`, but content-collection image paths are resolved relative to the entry's own folder (e.g. `./firstpostcover.jpeg` in `src/content/blog/` resolves to `src/content/blog/firstpostcover.jpeg`), so a project-root path resolves to a non-existent file. It is also not a URL served by your site: files in `src/` are processed by Astro, not copied as static assets the way `public/` files are (those are referenced by their path relative to `public/`, e.g. `/images/cat.jpg`). Keep `media_folder` at `src/assets/images` for repo storage and set `public_folder` to a path that matches how the frontmatter value must be referenced.

If a Flotiq content object is deleted after the initial static build but the Astro site hasn't been rebuilt, how does the behavior differ between a page generated via `getStaticPaths` versus one using on-demand rendering with `Astro.params` when a user requests that slug?

A page generated via `getStaticPaths` is prerendered at build time into a static HTML file, so if the Flotiq object is deleted after build, requests still serve that stale static page until the site is rebuilt. By contrast, an on-demand page with `Astro.params` (rendered with `prerender = false` or `output: 'server'`) fetches data at request time and can detect the missing object, then return an appropriate `Response` (e.g. 404 or redirect), reflecting the current CMS state.

In `astro.config.mjs`, how must the `vite.define` block be configured to expose `process.env.APOS_HOST` and `process.env.APOS_EXTERNAL_FRONT_KEY` to the Astro build, and which Vite function is used to load these values from the `.env` file?
If your hosting provider supports webhooks, how can you automatically trigger a new Astro build when a HackMD note is updated, and what Astro output mode does this require?

Use your hosting provider's webhook functionality: configure a webhook that fires when HackMD sends a webhook event, and have it trigger a new build of your Astro site. This applies to projects using Astro's default static output mode, where pages are prerendered at build time, so an edited note is only published after a fresh build runs. Routes rendered on demand would instead read the updated note at request time without requiring a rebuild.
How do I create a dynamic blog page in Astro that generates a separate page for each article fetched from Strapi?

Create `src/pages/blog/[slug].astro` exporting `getStaticPaths()` that fetches articles from Strapi and returns an array of `{ params: { slug: article.slug }, props: article }`. The component then receives each article via `Astro.props` to render the page template.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/cms/strapi/
In `src/pages/index.astro`, why does the example filter notes with `note.readPermission === 'guest'` before rendering the list?

The HackMD access token can read private notes in your account. Filtering for `readPermission === 'guest'` ensures only publicly readable notes are included in the generated site, preventing accidental exposure of private content.
I'm setting up a new Astro 7 project with Keystatic and need to add the Markdoc and React integrations. Which Astro CLI command should I run, and which two packages must I install via npm/pnpm/yarn?

Run `npx astro add react markdoc` (or `pnpm astro add react markdoc` / `yarn astro add react markdoc`) — the React integration powers the Keystatic Admin UI dashboard and Markdoc handles content entries. Then install the two Keystatic packages: `npm install @keystatic/core @keystatic/astro` (or `pnpm add` / `yarn add`).

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/cms/keystatic/
In on-demand rendering mode with Flotiq, why does the code return `Astro.redirect('/404')` when `blogpostList.data?.[0]` is falsy, and what Astro API enables this redirect?

In on-demand rendering with Flotiq, `blogpostList.data?.[0]` being falsy means no matching blog post exists for the requested slug, so returning `Astro.redirect('/404')` sends users to a 404 page instead of rendering an empty or broken document. In on-demand rendering mode (Astro 7), a page can return a `Response` directly, and the Astro API that enables this is `Astro.redirect(path, status?)`, which creates a redirect response. The pattern matches the on-demand example where missing data triggers a redirect to a fallback route.

In an Astro page's frontmatter, you import the DeliveryClient from '../lib/kontent' and fetch blog posts. What method chain do you use to fetch all blog posts of a specific type using the generated content type codename and retrieve them as typed objects?

Chain `items()` with the generated type generic, `.type()` with the content type's codename, and `.toPromise()`; the typed items come back on `response.data.items`:

```astro
---
import { deliveryClient } from '../lib/kontent';
import type { BlogPost } from '../models';
import { contentTypes } from '../models/project/contentTypes';

const blogPosts = await deliveryClient
  .items<BlogPost>()
  .type(contentTypes.blog_post.codename)
  .toPromise();
---
```

Without model generation, use `deliveryClient.items().type("blogPost").toPromise()` with an untyped object and string literal.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/cms/kontent-ai/
If you switch from static generation to SSR for the dinosaur detail pages, which exported function from `src/pages/dinos/[slug].astro` becomes unnecessary and why?

`getStaticPaths()` becomes unnecessary. It exists only to prerender every route at build time, fetching all posts and returning `params`/`props` for each one. With on-demand (SSR) rendering, routes are created when requested instead: the page reads `slug` from `Astro.params` and fetches just that single post (or returns a 404/redirect when it doesn't exist), so there is no build-time list of paths to generate.

After deploying an Astro site to Cloudflare Workers, client-side hydration fails with the console error `Hydration completed but contains mismatches`. What Cloudflare setting is the likely cause, and how do you fix it?

Cloudflare's Auto Minify setting is the likely cause: it rewrites served assets, producing markup that mismatches the server-rendered HTML. Disable Auto Minify under your Cloudflare settings and redeploy/re-preview; hydration should then complete without mismatches.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/deploy/cloudflare/
What is the difference between deploying an Astro site as a static site versus a server-rendered site on Netlify?

A static Astro site is the default and needs no extra configuration on Netlify—you just set the build command (`astro build` or `npm run build`) and publish directory (`dist`). For a static site you only need the Netlify adapter if you use a deployment feature that requires it, such as the Netlify Image CDN or translating `redirects` config into a `_redirects` file. A server-rendered (on-demand rendered) site works the same way deployment-wise but uses the Netlify adapter (`npx astro add netlify`) to enable on-demand rendered routes and features like server islands, actions, and sessions; set `output: 'server'` to server-render all pages by default. Netlify also supports edge rendering as a third project type.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/deploy/netlify/
An Astro project is deployed to Fly.io as a static site by default. What additional package is required to deploy it as a server-side rendered (SSR) site instead?

The Node.js adapter. Add it with `npx astro add node` (or `pnpm astro add node` / `yarn astro add node`) to enable on-demand rendering; static deployment to Fly.io needs no extra configuration. Also ensure a `start` script runs the built server (e.g. `node ./dist/server/entry.mjs`).
What file would you create to attach custom HTTP response headers to your Astro deployment on Vercel, and what is its purpose?

Create a `vercel.json` file in your project root. Its purpose is to override Vercel's default behavior and configure additional settings, such as attaching custom HTTP response headers to your deployments.
What start script must exist in package.json for Hostinger to run a server-rendered Astro application?

For server-rendered Astro deployment on Hostinger, `package.json` must include a `start` script: `"start": "node ./dist/server/entry.mjs"`. This runs the built Node.js server after `npm run build`. The Hostinger Node.js application option uses this start command.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/deploy/hostinger/
You have an Astro static site deploying to Firebase Hosting. You now need SSR for dynamic pages. What two changes must you make before running `firebase deploy` again?
Add the Node.js adapter to your project and enable SSR by setting `output: 'server'` in `astro.config.mjs`.
I'm deploying my Astro site to GitLab Pages and I've set `site` to 'https://myuser.gitlab.io' but my links are broken. What should I also configure in `astro.config.mjs`?

You must also configure `base: '/<my-repo>'` in `astro.config.mjs` where `<my-repo>` is your repository name. GitLab Pages serves sites from a subpath, so `base` tells Astro the site root is `/my-repo` not `/`. Also set `outDir: 'public'` and `publicDir: 'static'`.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/deploy/gitlab/
Your Astro SSR deployment to Sevalla fails with a runtime error about a missing module. The module is listed in devDependencies in package.json. Why does this happen and how do you fix it?

Sevalla installs production dependencies only when building and running your app, so a package listed in `devDependencies` that's needed at runtime won't be present in the deployed environment, causing a missing-module error. Move the package to `dependencies` in `package.json` and redeploy. Astro's project structure guidance recommends keeping all dependencies in `dependencies`, since Astro needs them at build time anyway and only uses `devDependencies` for specific cases.

You are configuring an Astro project for on-demand rendering on Cloudflare Workers using the `@astrojs/cloudflare` adapter. The `wrangler.jsonc` requires a `main` entrypoint, specific `compatibility_flags`, and an `assets.binding`. What are the exact values for these three fields, and why is `nodejs_compat` required?
When deploying an Astro SSR site to Firebase Hosting, why does the deployment fail if you're on the Spark (free) plan?
Deploying an SSR Astro site to Firebase Hosting requires the Blaze (paid) plan or higher; the Spark (free) plan does not support SSR deployment.
After linking an SST Bucket named `MyBucket` in `sst.config.ts`, what import and syntax do you use in an `.astro` file to log the bucket's name at build time?

Import `Resource` from `"sst"` and access the linked resource by its identifier:

```astro
---
import { Resource } from "sst"
console.log(Resource.MyBucket.name)
---
```

This works because `MyBucket` is linked to the Astro app in `sst.config.ts` via `link: [bucket]` on the `sst.aws.Astro` component.
What happens if you try to use Astro's `output: 'server'` setting with a hosting provider that only supports static sites, and how can you avoid this issue?

The build fails with the `AdapterSupportOutputMismatch` error ("Adapter does not support server output"): "The `ADAPTER_NAME` adapter is configured to output a static website, but the project contains server-rendered pages." The currently configured adapter doesn't support server-side rendering, which your project setup requires. To fix it, install and configure the appropriate server adapter for your final deployment—adapters such as `@astrojs/netlify` enable on-demand/server rendering. Whether you can avoid it also depends on the host: on Hostinger, server-rendered deployment requires a plan that supports Node.js applications (e.g., Business Web Hosting or Cloud); static-only plans can't run server output. If your provider can't serve the output, either upgrade to a Node.js-capable plan or keep the site static by using `output: 'static'` or on-demand rendering per page.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/adapter-support-output-mismatch/

An Astro project is deployed to `https://username.github.io/my-repo/`. The `base` option in `astro.config.mjs` is set to `/my-repo`. A developer writes `About` in a component. Why will this link break in production?
With `base: '/my-repo'` configured, internal links must include the base; `/about` resolves to the domain root instead of `https://username.github.io/my-repo/about/`, so the link will 404.
What environment variables must be set in the zerops.yml run section for an Astro SSR site on Zerops, and why are both required?

Set `PORT: 3000` and `HOST: 0.0.0.0` in the `envVariables` section of `zerops.yml`. Both are required because the Node.js server (started via `node ./dist/server/entry.mjs`) needs to know which port to listen on and which network interface to bind to (0.0.0.0 listens on all interfaces).

You have a new Astro project with no adapter configured. You push to GitHub and import it in Vercel's dashboard. What deployment target does Vercel detect by default, and do you need to change any Astro configuration?
Vercel detects a static site by default. No Astro configuration changes are needed—Vercel automatically detects Astro and configures the right settings for a static deployment.
When deploying an on-demand rendered Astro site to Clever Cloud as a Node.js application, what start script should be configured in package.json to listen on the required port 8080?

Clever Cloud Node.js applications must listen on port 8080, so set:

```json
"scripts": {
  "start": "node ./dist/server/entry.mjs --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080"
}
```

This runs the built server from the Node adapter's output, binding to all interfaces on the required port.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/deploy/clever-cloud/
After running `npx astro add cloudflare`, what two changes are made to your Astro project automatically?

It installs the `@astrojs/cloudflare` adapter package and makes the corresponding changes to your `astro.config.mjs` in one step (adding the adapter import and registration), and it also creates a Wrangler configuration file (`wrangler.jsonc`) for you — you'd otherwise have to create it yourself.
An Astro project fails to build on Azion with the error 'Could not resolve "fs". The package "fs" wasn't found on the file system but is built into node.' What causes this and how should you fix it?

The package or import you're using isn't compatible with Azion's runtime APIs — Node.js built-ins aren't available as plain packages in the edge runtime. If you directly import a Node.js runtime API, consult Azion's Node.js compatibility documentation for resolution steps. If the import comes from a third-party package, check with the package author whether they support the `node:*` import syntax; if not, you may need to find an alternative package.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/deploy/azion/

I pressed Run on my Buddy pipeline, the Node.js action finished successfully, but my hosting provider still serves the old version of the Astro site. What's missing from the pipeline and why does the build alone not get the site live?

The pipeline is missing a deployment action. The Buddy Node.js action only builds the site (outputting to `dist/`). You must add a deployment action (FTP, SFTP, cloud provider, etc.) from Buddy's catalog and set its **Source path** to `dist` to actually push the built files to your hosting provider.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/deploy/buddy/
Your Astro project uses only static output (no SSR, no middleware, no server-only APIs). You are deploying to Zeabur. Should you install @zeabur/astro-adapter?

No. A static-only Astro site needs no extra configuration to deploy to Zeabur — the adapter is only required to enable SSR (`output: 'server'` with `@zeabur/astro-adapter/serverless`). Since your project uses static output, install nothing.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/deploy/zeabur/
Why must server.host be set to true in astro.config.mjs when deploying an Astro SSR app to Sevalla's Application Hosting?

Because `host: true` makes the dev/preview server listen on all network addresses instead of only localhost, which is required in Sevalla's containerized environment where traffic is routed to the container from outside. Without it the server binds only to a local interface and requests can't reach it.

An Astro site deployed via Flightcontrol returns 500 errors on dynamic routes after enabling SSR in astro.config.mjs. The Flightcontrol project was created using the 'Astro Static' preset. What configuration mismatch causes this?

The Flightcontrol project was created with the `Astro Static` preset, which configures a static deployment, while `astro.config.mjs` now enables SSR — the hosted infrastructure and the project's render mode disagree. Flightcontrol's static preset serves prebuilt static output and has no server to run on-demand routes. Recreate/select the `Astro SSR` configuration (GUI preset or `flightcontrol.json` SSR example) and set up the `@astrojs/node` adapter first; in static mode dynamic routes must instead export `getStaticPaths()`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/deploy/aws-via-flightcontrol/
What command adds the Vercel adapter to an Astro project for on-demand rendering?

```
npx astro add vercel
```
(`pnpm astro add vercel` or `yarn astro add vercel` also work.) The command installs the adapter and updates `astro.config.mjs` in one step; you then opt routes into on-demand rendering with `export const prerender = false`, or set `output: 'server'` to render everything on demand.

When using the Cloudflare adapter for on-demand rendering, a server build fails with '[Error] Could not resolve "XXXX". The package "XXXX" wasn't found on the file system but is built into node.' What does this error indicate and what are two possible resolutions?

The error means a server-side package or import you're using is not compatible with the Cloudflare runtime APIs: the module expects Node.js built-ins that aren't present on Workers' file system. Two resolutions: (1) if you are directly importing a Node.js runtime API, follow Astro's Cloudflare Node.js compatibility guidance to make it work on Cloudflare; (2) if the import comes from a package that itself imports a Node.js runtime API, check with the package author whether they support the `node:*` import syntax — if they don't, switch to an alternative package.
When deploying a static Astro site to Google Cloud Storage, which two files must be configured in the website configuration as the entrypoint and error page respectively?
`index.html` as the entrypoint and `404.html` as the error page, set in the bucket's website configuration.
What is the purpose of the `public/CNAME` file when configuring a custom domain for an Astro site on GitHub Pages?
The `public/CNAME` file tells GitHub Pages your custom domain (e.g. `sub.example.com`), so the site deploys to that domain instead of the default GitHub URL.
In my `.gitlab-ci.yml`, why must the artifacts path be exactly 'public' when deploying an Astro site to GitLab Pages?

The artifacts path must be `public` because that is the folder GitLab Pages requires for the exposed files it publishes. Astro's default build output is `dist`, which is why the guide has you set `outDir: 'public'` in `astro.config.mjs` ("This setting instructs Astro to put the static build output in a folder called `public`, which is the folder required by GitLab Pages for exposed files"). The `paths` in the `pages` job of `.gitlab-ci.yml` lists the built files to be published, and that folder "must be called `public`" for GitLab Pages to serve it. You match the two: `outDir: 'public'` so the build writes there, and `artifacts.paths: ['public']` so those files get deployed.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/deploy/gitlab/
An Astro site uses server-side rendering with dynamic routes. Why would Cloud Storage be an unsuitable deployment target, and which Google Cloud service should be used instead?

Cloud Storage is a static-only target (you upload the built `dist` folder and configure index/404 pages), so it cannot run server-rendered pages or dynamic routes. Use Cloud Run instead, which deploys both static and SSR sites by running your Astro app in a container built from a Dockerfile.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/deploy/google-cloud/

I dropped `banner.png` into `public/` and expected `<Image src="/banner.png" />` to fill in its width and height automatically. Why can't Astro do that?

Astro cannot automatically infer the dimensions of images in the `public/` folder because it treats them as static assets without processing. The `<Image />` component requires either an ESM-imported image or a remote URL to determine dimensions, which are needed for responsive image generation and layout stability.

To resolve this, import the image using ES modules:

```astro
---
import { Image } from 'astro:assets';
import banner from '../public/banner.png';
---

<Image src={banner} alt="Banner" />
```

Alternatively, specify `width` and `height` manually if you know the dimensions:

```astro
<Image src="/banner.png" width={800} height={600} alt="Banner" />
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/modules/astro-assets/

If I only need Actions for a single API route, do I still need to configure the entire project for server output with an adapter, or can I enable server rendering per-route?

You still need an adapter configured at the project level — `NoAdapterInstalled` is thrown without one. However, you can configure individual routes for on-demand rendering rather than switching the entire project to `output: 'server'`. The adapter is project-level; route rendering mode is per-route.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/no-adapter-installed/
Astro stops my build with the error "Failed to parse Markdown frontmatter." What part of the Markdown file failed to be processed, and what kinds of mistakes in it usually cause this?

Astro fails to parse the frontmatter section of a Markdown file when it encounters invalid syntax. Frontmatter must be valid YAML enclosed between `---` delimiters. Common causes include missing colons in key-value pairs, unmatched quotes, or incorrect indentation.

Example of problematic frontmatter:
```md
---
title: My Post
date: 2023-01-01
tags [invalid syntax]
---
```

Correct syntax should be:
```md
---
title: My Post
date: 2023-01-01
tags: [tag1, tag2]
---
```
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/markdown-frontmatter-parse-error/
I'm getting an error 'Could not process image metadata for `src/assets/example.png`' when building my Astro project. What should I check first?

Check first that `src/assets/example.png` is not a corrupted or malformed image — Astro could not read the file's metadata during import, and re-exporting the image from your image editor usually fixes it. If the file is valid and the build still fails, inspect the stack trace; a related "Could not transform image" error includes a stack trace that, depending on your configured image service, names the specific failure. Only after confirming the image data itself is intact should you investigate image service configuration.
I enabled the cache in my Astro config but `Astro.cache` still throws 'Cache is not enabled'. What could be wrong?

The error is thrown when the cache feature is not enabled in your Astro config. Even if you enabled caching, `cache.enabled` returns `false` when no cache provider is configured or when running in development mode. Ensure you have a cache provider properly configured and that you are running in production mode.
If my action handler returns a Date object or Map, will it trigger ActionsReturnedInvalidDataError?

No. Actions use the Devalue library which specifically supports Dates, Maps, Sets, and URLs. Returning a Map from an action handler will not trigger ActionsReturnedInvalidDataError, but returning a Date object may cause issues depending on how it's serialized. The error typically occurs when non-serializable data types like functions or circular references are returned.
What is the recommended way to organize server actions in Astro 7 projects, and how does it affect action resolution?
My middleware callback runs fine, sets context.locals.someData = false, and then Astro fails the request with 'MiddlewareNoDataOrNextCalled' — why does Astro reject code that clearly executed?

An `async` GET handler in my Astro project delegates to a helper that sometimes finishes without an explicit `return`, so the handler's promise resolves to `undefined`. Requests hitting that path throw `EndpointDidNotReturnAResponse` even though the function is async and typed as returning a `Response`. Why doesn't awaiting a promise satisfy Astro here?
How should I refactor a prerendered route that uses Astro.clientAddress to avoid the PrerenderClientAddressNotAvailable error?

Make the route on-demand rendered by adding `export const prerender = false;` to its frontmatter (not needed in `server` mode), so `Astro.clientAddress` is available at request time. Alternatively, keep the route static and fetch the IP client-side via an API like Ipify in a client-side script, or use a serverless function hosted on your provider.
Is there a way to configure Astro so it doesn't use any server adapters and can only generate static sites?

Yes. Static output is Astro's default (`output: 'static'`), and such projects need no adapter at all — you simply omit the `adapter` option from `astro.config.mjs`, and `astro build` emits only static files. Adapters are only required when you render pages on demand (SSR) or use server islands; without one, server-rendered pages fail with `NoAdapterInstalled` ("Cannot use server-rendered pages without an adapter"). Conversely, pairing a static-only adapter with server-rendered pages triggers `AdapterSupportOutputMismatch`, so a static-only project must also avoid server-rendered routes. Static sites may still install an adapter optionally for platform features (e.g. Netlify's Image CDN or `_redirects` translation), but it is never required.
Why does Astro throw an UnsupportedExternalRedirect error when using a URL like '//example.com/path' with Astro.redirect()?

Astro throws `UnsupportedExternalRedirect` because external redirects must start with `http` or `https` and be a valid URL. A protocol-relative URL like `//example.com/path` lacks an explicit scheme, so it does not meet this requirement and is rejected as an unsupported destination.

An entry fails validation with "date" must be a valid date even though the field is populated with a value. What kinds of mismatch between an entry's data and its collection schema produce this error?

My dynamic route /route/[id].astro throws GetStaticPathsInvalidRouteParam: Invalid getStaticPaths() route parameter for id. Expected a string or undefined, received number (2). Why is a numeric param rejected when I return { params: { id: 2 } }?
What should I do if I need to use both vector and raster images in my Astro project?

Avoid requesting conversions between the two kinds: Astro does not currently support converting between vector (SVG) and raster (PNG, JPEG) images. Use each image in its own format — render SVGs as SVGs and raster images as raster — and only request transformations (resize, format change) within the same category, or supply a pre-converted raster file yourself if you need one.

Why does Astro 7 throw an 'InvalidRedirectDestination' error when redirecting from /posts/[id] to /blog, even if /blog exists as a route?

Because a dynamic redirect destination must match an existing route pattern **and include all dynamic parameters from the source route**. `/posts/[id]` has a dynamic parameter, but `/blog` has fewer dynamic parameters than the source, so the destination doesn't correspond to a valid route — even though `/blog` itself exists — and Astro throws `InvalidRedirectDestination`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/invalid-redirect-destination/
What data types are supported by the devalue library for use in Astro's content config transform functions?

devalue supports strings, numbers, `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, `URL`, arrays, and plain objects — plus anything valid JSON can represent. These are the same types accepted by content collection transforms and sessions, since Astro serializes both with devalue. In a `transform()` you can therefore return nested plain objects containing `Date`s, `Map`s, and `Set`s directly; values outside this set (functions, class instances, symbols) will fail with `UnsupportedConfigTransformError`/`PARSE_ERROR`.
In Astro 7, when should I use server actions instead of client-side functions for handling form submissions?

Use server actions when you want the submission handled on the server with validation and zero-JS capability; use plain client-side functions only when no server work is needed. With an action, a `<form method="POST" action={actions.logout}>` submits without client JavaScript, and the server parses and validates the data via the action's `input` schema:

```astro
---
import { actions } from 'astro:actions';
---
<form method="POST" action={actions.logout}>
  <button>Log out</button>
</form>
```

The page calling the action via form `action` must be on-demand rendered (prerendering disabled). Client-side functions are still useful for in-browser behavior such as calling `actions.newsletter(formData)` then `navigate('/confirmation')` — but the actual mutation should live in the action.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/actions/

My Astro 7 build of src/pages/blog/[slug].astro fails with `GetStaticPathsRequired: getStaticPaths() function is required for dynamic routes.` Why does this error occur, and what do I need to change (or switch) so the build succeeds?
When should I NOT use live content collections in Astro 7 instead of regular markdown files?

You should not use live content collections when your content does not need to be fetched fresh at request time. Live collections run at request time (not build time), require an adapter configured for on-demand rendering, and have no built-in loaders—you must create a custom loader for your data source. If your content is static and can be processed at build time, regular build-time collections or plain markdown files are more appropriate, as they benefit from caching between builds and a performant data storage layer. Additionally, if you have only one or a small number of content pages, individual page components are simpler.

I'm encountering a 'No matching renderer found' error when trying to render a Vue component in Astro. What steps should I follow to resolve this issue?

The error means none of the renderers configured in `astro.config.mjs` can server-side render your component, so install and register the matching integration: for Vue, add `@astrojs/vue` (for Svelte, `@astrojs/svelte`; JSX/TSX uses `@astrojs/react`, `@astrojs/preact`, or `@astrojs/solid-js`). Integrations supply the renderer via `addRenderer`. Also confirm an import statement exists for the component and that the identifier matches the one used in the template — a mismatch produces "No import found for component" instead.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/renderer-reference/

My Astro page throws an `ImageMissingAlt` error saying 'Image missing "alt" property' when I render `<Image src={hero} alt={undefined} />`. I want the image to be purely decorative so screen readers skip it — what should I pass instead, and why doesn't omitting `alt` entirely work?

Pass `alt=""` to make an image purely decorative and skip it for screen readers. Omitting `alt` entirely or passing `alt={undefined}` fails because the Astro Image component requires the `alt` attribute to be present, even if empty.

Example:
```astro
<Image src={hero} alt="" />
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/image-missing-alt/
Why does `client:only` need an explicit renderer name like `client:only="react"`, while the same component hydrated with `client:load` doesn't supply one?

The `client:only` directive requires an explicit renderer name because it skips server-side rendering entirely. Astro needs to know which framework to use for client-side hydration and loading, since no server render occurs to infer this automatically.

In contrast, `client:load` and other directives first render the component on the server using Astro's built-in renderer (e.g., React or Vue), so Astro can detect the correct framework from the rendered output. This allows it to avoid requiring an explicit renderer name for hydration.

Example:
```astro
<!-- Requires explicit renderer -->
<SomeReactComponent client:only="react" />

<!-- Does not require explicit renderer -->
<SomeReactComponent client:load />
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/directives-reference/#clientonly

When calling an Astro Action from the client, I get an ActionsWithoutServerOutputError saying 'A server is required to create callable backend functions.' What two configuration changes are needed to fix this?

Two changes needed: 1) Add a server adapter to your Astro config (e.g., `@astrojs/node`, `@astrojs/vercel`), and 2) Configure your project for server-side rendering by setting `output: 'server'` in your Astro config or using `export const prerender = false` on pages that use actions.
My Astro dev server crashes with `FailedToLoadModuleSSR: Could not import './components/Card'`. What are the two causes this error points to?

Two causes: (1) the import path is wrong — the file does not exist or the path contains a typo; (2) a TypeScript type is imported without marking it as a type import, so the runtime tries to load a symbol that only exists at compile time. Fix the path, or use `import type { ... }` for type-only imports.
Can I return a Promise from getStaticPaths() in Astro 7, or must it be synchronous?

You can return a Promise from `getStaticPaths()` — declare it as `async function`. All documented examples use `export async function getStaticPaths()`, which inherently returns a Promise. The resolved value must be an array of objects with `params` properties.
How do I install Sharp manually in my Astro project using pnpm?
In Astro 7, why does attempting to set a status code in a component that's not a page component result in a ResponseSentError?

`ResponseSentError` means the response has already been sent to the browser and can no longer be altered: making changes to the response — setting headers, cookies, or the status code — is only allowed in page components. When you attempt to set a status code from a component that is not a page component, the page's response has already been committed/streamed to the client, so Astro throws this error. Move the status-code assignment into the page component (a file under `src/pages/`) that renders your component, and perform it before the response is sent.

My getStaticPaths() builds params from parsed frontmatter where id could be a number or an array. How do I structure the returned entries so Astro encodes them into valid URLs without throwing GetStaticPathsInvalidRouteParam?
Why does Astro throw an 'Attempted to render an undefined content collection entry' error when trying to display a non-existent post?

Astro throws `RenderUndefinedEntryError` when you attempt to render a content collection entry that is `undefined`. This happens if you try to display an entry that does not exist (e.g., querying by an incorrect `id`/slug or referencing a missing related entry). 

To fix it, ensure the entry exists before rendering by checking the result of `getEntry()`/`getCollection()` lookups, or guard against undefined in your template.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/render-undefined-entry-error/

What actually changes in my project when I set `i18n.routing.strategy` to `"manual"` instead of leaving it at its default?

When you set `i18n.routing.strategy` to `"manual"`, Astro disables its built-in i18n middleware, giving you full control over routing logic. You must handle locale detection, redirects, and fallbacks yourself using helper functions like `redirectToDefaultLocale()`, `notFound()`, or `redirectToFallback()`.

No other `routing` options (e.g., `prefixDefaultLocale`) can be used with `"manual"` strategy. You can still use the `middleware()` function manually to integrate Astro’s routing behavior alongside your custom logic, but you must manage all routing yourself otherwise.

Example config:
```js
i18n: {
  locales: ["es", "en", "fr"],
  defaultLocale: "en",
  routing: "manual"
}
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/internationalization/#routing

I have pages/blog/[id].astro and I want the build to produce site.com/blog/1. What does my getStaticPaths() need to return for that route to exist?

My Astro component calls `await getImage(myImage, { width: 300, height: 300 })` and fails with `ExpectedImageOptions: Expected getImage() parameter to be an object. Received myImage`. How should I restructure the call so `getImage()` from `astro:assets` accepts it?

You must pass the image options as a single object to `getImage()`, not as separate arguments.

Incorrect:
```ts
await getImage(myImage, { width: 300, height: 300 })
```

Correct:
```ts
await getImage({ src: myImage, width: 300, height: 300 })
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/modules/astro-assets/#getimage
What serializable data types are valid return values for an Astro action handler?

Valid return types for Astro action handlers are serializable data types: objects, arrays, strings, numbers, Dates, Maps, Sets, and URLs. The Devalue library handles serialization of Dates, Maps, Sets, and URLs. Action handlers cannot return a Response object.
Why does my Astro 7 project throw an InvalidGetStaticPathsEntry error when I return [ ['blog'], ['about'] ] from getStaticPaths()?

The error occurs because `getStaticPaths()` must return an array of objects, not an array of arrays. Your return value `[ ['blog'], ['about'] ]` is an array of arrays. Each entry must be an object with a `params` property, e.g., `[{ params: { id: 'blog' } }, { params: { id: 'about' } }]`.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/invalid-get-static-paths-entry/

I'm getting the error `InvalidComponentArgs: Invalid arguments passed to <MyAstroComponent> component.` from a line like `{items.map(MyAstroComponent)}` in my .astro file. Why does Astro throw this instead of just rendering each item, and what should I write instead?

Astro components cannot be rendered manually via a function call like `{items.map(MyAstroComponent)}` because Astro requires explicit component syntax for rendering. The error occurs because `MyAstroComponent` is treated as a function rather than a component tag.

Instead, use the component syntax with JSX-like syntax: `{items.map(item => <MyAstroComponent {...item} />)`.

Example:
```astro
---import MyAstroComponent from '../components/MyAstroComponent.astro';---
{items.map(item => <MyAstroComponent {...item} />)}
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/invalid-component-args/
How can I configure Astro 7 to automatically infer the dimensions of remote images when using the Image component, and what are the trade-offs involved?

Set `inferSize` to `true` on the `<Image />` component to fetch the remote image's original dimensions automatically. Trade-offs: if determining the remote image's dimensions fails — typically caused by an incorrect URL or attempting to infer the size of an image in the public folder, which is not possible — the build will throw a "Failed to retrieve remote image dimensions" error. Explicitly specifying `width` and `height` avoids this fetch and potential failure.
Why is it not allowed to return `null` from an Astro page?

Because only instances of `Response` can be returned from Astro files — any other value, including `null`, throws "Invalid type returned by Astro page" (`Route returned a RETURNED_VALUE`). Return an actual `Response` instead, e.g. `return new Response(null, { status: 404, statusText: 'Not found' })`, or `return Astro.redirect('/login')`, which itself returns an instance of `Response`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/only-response-can-be-returned/
What is the recommended approach for displaying unsupported formats in Astro?

Use a plain `` tag directly instead of the `` component or `getImage()`. Import the asset and pass its `src`, `width`, `height`, and `alt` attributes: ```astro --- import rocket from '../assets/images/rocket.gif'; --- ``` This skips the image service's optimization entirely while still letting you use `astro:assets` for authoring benefits such as no Cumulative Layout Shift and the enforced `alt` attribute. The same approach applies to vector images like SVGs, which cannot be converted to raster formats. Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/unsupported-image-format/
In Astro 7, what is the difference between passing an ESM-imported image directly to `getImage()` versus passing an object with a `src` property? Why does Astro require the object form?
Why does Astro 7 throw a 'Missing image dimensions' error when using a remote image with <Image> component without width and height?

For remote images, `width` and `height` cannot automatically be inferred from the original file. Both dimensions are required in order to avoid cumulative layout shift (CLS). To resolve the error, either specify the `width` and `height` properties explicitly, or set `inferSize` to `true` to fetch the remote image's original dimensions. If the image is inside your `src` folder, you probably meant to import it instead.
Why does the paginate() function throw a PageNumberParamNotFound error when using '/pages/[page].astro' as the filepath pattern?

`paginate()` assumes the page number parameter is named `page` and looks for it in the filepath pattern (`[page].astro` or `[...page].astro`). If that `page` param is missing from the filepath, it throws `PageNumberParamNotFound`.
How can I use an unsupported image format like GIF in Astro?

You can use unsupported image formats like GIFs directly with the `` tag instead of relying on Astro's built-in image optimization. ```astro --- import rocket from '../assets/images/rocket.gif'; --- ``` This approach bypasses Astro’s image services, which only support specific formats like JPEG, PNG, WebP, and AVIF. Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/unsupported-image-format/
In an Astro page, why does `Astro.response.headers = new Headers({ 'X-Custom': 'value' })` throw `AstroResponseHeadersReassigned`, and how do I set a custom header instead?

Because `Astro.response.headers` is a `readonly Headers` instance on the `ResponseInit` object: individual headers can be added to and removed from it, but it must not be replaced with another instance of `Headers` altogether — reassignment throws `AstroResponseHeadersReassigned`. Set the header by mutating the existing instance instead:

```astro
---
Astro.response.headers.set('X-Custom', 'value');
---
```

Do this in a page component before the response is sent, or you'll get `ResponseSentError`.
When is it correct to supply an empty `alt=""` instead of a descriptive alt string on Astro's Image component?

It is correct to supply an empty `alt=""` on Astro’s `<Image />` component when the image is purely decorative and does not contribute meaningful content or information to the page. This tells screen readers to ignore the image, improving accessibility for users who rely on assistive technologies.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/image-missing-alt/
Can I use Astro.callAction() inside a client-side component to invoke a server action, or does it only work in server contexts?

`Astro.callAction()` is for server-side use only — it works in Astro component scripts (the frontmatter) and server endpoints. It is not available inside client-side framework components. From the client, you call actions directly via the `actions` object (e.g. `await actions.logout({ userId: '123' })`), which returns the same `{ data, error }` shape. The `ActionCalledFromServerError` is thrown when server code calls an action without the `Astro.callAction()` wrapper.

My blog post at src/content/posts/hello.md has ![chart](chart.png) but the build fails with `ImageNotFound: Could not find requested image 'chart.png'. Does it exist?` — what's wrong with the path and how do I fix it?

The error occurs because `chart.png` in your Markdown is a bare filename without the required `./` prefix. In Markdown, local images in the same folder must use `./chart.png` (not `chart.png`). Fix by either:
1. Move `chart.png` next to `hello.md` and use `![chart](./chart.png)`
2. If in a subfolder like `images/`, use `![chart](./images/chart.png)`

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/image-not-found/
What's the distinction between ActionsCantBeLoaded and a runtime error thrown inside an action handler? At what point in the request lifecycle does each occur?

`ActionsCantBeLoaded` occurs at module load time in development, when the actions file itself fails to load — no request has been processed yet. A runtime error inside an action handler occurs later, during request execution, when the handler is actually invoked. Handler errors (including thrown `ActionError` instances) are caught and returned as the `error` property of the `{ data, error }` result, whereas `ActionsCantBeLoaded` prevents the actions module from loading entirely.
Why does Astro throw a LocalsNotAnObject error when I try to assign a number to context.locals in a middleware function?

Astro throws `LocalsNotAnObject` because `context.locals` must remain an object; assigning a non-object value (e.g. `context.locals = 1541`) overwrites it with something Astro rejects. Set properties on the existing object instead (`context.locals.title = "..."` or `Object.assign(ctx.locals, { one: 1 })`). Since Astro 5.0, replacing the whole object is also forbidden and throws `LocalsReassigned`, as that would wipe information stored by integrations or earlier middleware.

With `output: 'server'` in my Astro config, calling `Astro.rewrite('/about')` from an on-demand route fails with `ForbiddenRewrite`: "You tried to rewrite the on-demand route '/blog/[slug]' with the static route '/about', when using the 'server' output." Why does Astro refuse this rewrite, and what would I have to change about the target route for it to work?

Astro refuses the rewrite because `Astro.rewrite()` cannot map an on-demand route (like `/blog/[slug]`) to a static route (like `/about`) when using `"server"` output. Static routes are prerendered at build time into HTML files, which can't be dynamically served at runtime.

To fix this, make the target route (`/about`) also an on-demand route by using dynamic parameters or keeping it as a regular page that supports SSR. For example, rename `/about` to `/about/index.astro` or ensure it's not marked for prerendering in your config.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/forbidden-rewrite/

I need an API key available to browser-side code in my Astro project. Should I declare it with `access: "secret"` in `env.schema` and add its prefix to `vite.envPrefix` so Vite ships it to the client?
I'm migrating an older Astro site to Astro 7 and old collections still throw 'Content entry frontmatter does not match schema.' What does the deprecation of this error tell me about my migration?

The deprecation of the "Content entry frontmatter does not match schema" error indicates that legacy content collections, which were removed in Astro 6, are no longer supported. Since you're seeing this error in Astro 7, it means your site still contains old-style content collection definitions or usage that needs to be updated.

You must migrate from the deprecated `createCollection()` API and `content.collections` configuration to the new `defineCollection()` and `content.collection` APIs introduced in Astro 6. This involves updating your `src/content.config.*` file with the new syntax, ensuring all content entries match the new schema definitions, and replacing any references to old collection methods.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/invalid-content-entry-frontmatter-error/

How do I import a TypeScript-only interface from another file into an `.astro` component so Astro doesn't throw `FailedToLoadModuleSSR` at runtime?

Use a type-only import with the `import type` syntax, which erases the import at compile time so nothing is resolved at runtime:

```astro
---
import type { Props as CardProps } from "./types";
---
```

For contrast, a value import such as `import { getUser } from './user'` is emitted into the SSR module graph and will fail if the path is wrong or the export doesn't exist at runtime.

If a developer writes `const h = new Headers(Astro.response.headers); h.set('X-Foo', 'bar'); Astro.response.headers = h;`, will this throw `AstroResponseHeadersReassigned` even though the original headers were preserved?

Yes, it will throw `AstroResponseHeadersReassigned`. The error is triggered whenever a value is assigned to the `headers` field on `Astro.response`, regardless of whether the new `Headers` instance preserves the original headers. The check is on reassignment itself, not on content loss.
Why does Astro's <Image /> component throw an 'ExpectedImage' error when I pass a variable that might be undefined as the src prop?

Astro’s `<Image />` component throws an `ExpectedImage` error when the `src` prop is undefined because it requires the `src` to be either an ESM-imported image or a string. Passing `undefined` fails this requirement.

To avoid the error, ensure `src` is always a valid value:

```astro
<Image src={myImage ?? "/fallback.png"} alt="..." />
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/expected-image/

After upgrading my Astro project I get `ContentSchemaContainsSlugError` — "A content collection schema should not contain `slug` since it is reserved for slug generation. Remove this from your blog collection schema." How do I fix my `blog` collection schema while still keeping the custom slugs I already set in my entries' frontmatter?
Why am I getting a `PARSE_ERROR` when using a custom function in my content config?

Your custom `transform()` is returning a value that isn't valid JSON or devalue-serializable, which Astro reports as `UnsupportedConfigTransformError` with full error `PARSE_ERROR`. The fix is to return only supported types (strings, numbers, `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, `URL`, arrays, plain objects) — convert anything else to a serializable form before returning it. Note that live collections have a separate failure mode: their `schema` cannot be a function and must be a schema object (`LiveContentConfigError`).

After adding a 'date' field to fix '"date" is required', the same entry keeps failing with '"date" must be a valid date.' Why doesn't satisfying the required-field check clear the error?

The "date" field requirement is satisfied, but the value still fails validation because it's not in a valid date format. Content collections require dates to be RFC 3339 formatted strings (e.g., `"2024-12-01"`), or JavaScript `Date` objects.

If you're using a string like `"December 1, 2024"`, it won't pass validation even if the field is present. Update your frontmatter to use an RFC 3339 date format:

```md
---
title: "My Post"
date: "2024-12-01"
---
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/content-entry-data-error/

I'm building one reusable content loader that will feed several collections from a database whose keys are integers — what contract must it satisfy for every entry it returns so no collection load fails?
Where does Astro look for an image referenced in a Markdown file — relative to the site root, relative to the project, or relative to the .md file itself?

Astro looks for images referenced in Markdown files relative to the `.md` file itself.

For example, if your Markdown file is located at `src/pages/post-1.md`, then a local image path like `../assets/stars.png` is resolved relative to that file's location. Remote images use full URLs, and images in the `public/` folder are referenced relative to the `public/` directory.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/images/
What is the consequence of setting `prerenderConflictBehavior` to 'throw' and encountering a conflict?

`'throw'` is not a valid value: `prerenderConflictBehavior` accepts only `'error' | 'warn' | 'ignore'`. The behavior you describe is `'error'`, which fails the build and displays an error, forcing you to resolve the conflict. The default is `'warn'`, which logs a warning and builds using the highest-priority route.
How do I fix the `UnsupportedConfigTransformError` in Astro?

Fix `UnsupportedConfigTransformError` by making your content config `transform()` return only valid JSON or data types compatible with the devalue library — Dates, Maps, Sets, and other plain serializable values. Anything else (functions, class instances, or unsupported structures) fails serialization and surfaces as `PARSE_ERROR`. Rewrite the transform to convert unsupported values before returning, e.g. turn a custom object into a plain object, a Date-bearing record into plain fields plus `Date`, or a symbol/function into a string.
How do I properly export and import server actions in Astro 7 to avoid the ActionNotFoundError?
How can I resolve a 'PrerenderRouteConflict' error in Astro?

Two prerendered routes generate the same path, and a static path can only be produced by one route — adjust the conflicting routes (path, params, or filename) so only one emits that URL, keeping route priority order in mind. You can also control the outcome with `prerenderConflictBehavior` (added in `astro@6.0`, default `'warn'`): `'error'` fails the build, `'warn'` builds using the highest-priority route, `'ignore'` does so silently.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/configuration-reference/

I'm building a responsive layout where images sit in containers of unpredictable width, and I only want to serve my own predefined pixel widths to the browser. Which of `densities` or `widths` should I use, and is there a case where I should avoid `densities` entirely?

Use `widths` when you want to serve predefined pixel widths to the browser for responsive images in unpredictable container widths.

The `widths` prop generates a `srcset` with `w` descriptors (e.g., `100w`, `200w`) and requires a corresponding `sizes` attribute. This approach is ideal for your use case because it allows you to explicitly control the image sizes sent to the browser based on your layout needs.

You should avoid `densities` entirely when using predefined widths, as the two options are mutually exclusive and cannot be combined in a single `<Image>` component. Using both will result in an error: "Cannot set both densities and widths".

Example:
```astro
<Image
  src={myImage}
  widths={[300, 600, 900]}
  sizes="(max-width: 768px) 100vw, (max-width: 1200px) 50vw, 33vw"
  alt="A description of my image."
/>
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/modules/astro-assets/#widths
I'm getting an 'AdapterSupportOutputMismatch' error saying my adapter is configured for static output but my project contains server-rendered pages. How do I fix this?

The configured adapter only supports static output but your project uses server-side rendering. Switch to the adapter's server entrypoint (e.g., `@astrojs/vercel/serverless` instead of `@astrojs/vercel/static`) or install a server-compatible adapter for your deployment platform.
How can I handle complex data structures like nested objects with Dates and Sets in my Astro content transform?

You can return them as-is: nested plain objects containing `Date`s, `Map`s, and `Set`s are devalue-compatible and therefore valid `transform()` output. Astro serializes content config data with devalue, whose supported types include strings, numbers, `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, `URL`, arrays, and plain objects. Structure your transform so every nested value falls in that set — wrap fields into a plain object rather than a class instance — and only unsupported values (functions, symbols, class instances) need conversion to avoid `UnsupportedConfigTransformError`.

Is it possible to clone the request without affecting the original request in Astro?

Yes. Clone the request with `Request.clone()` before reading its body; the original stays untouched:

```
const data = await Astro.request.clone().formData();
Astro.rewrite("/target")
```

Reading the body consumes it, which is why `Astro.rewrite()` fails with `RewriteWithBodyUsed` if you read `Astro.request` directly — cloning first leaves the original request body usable for the subsequent rewrite or other handling.
What are the two valid ways an onRequest middleware can finish handling a request in Astro 7?
Can you explain how to choose the right server adapter for my deployment platform in Astro?

Install and configure an adapter for your deployment platform: server-rendered pages (and server islands) require one, otherwise Astro throws `NoAdapterInstalled` because it doesn't know how to emit the output your host expects. Pick the adapter matching your host and confirm it supports server output — an adapter configured for static output fails with `AdapterSupportOutputMismatch` when server-rendered pages exist. Some adapters expose separate entrypoints per output mode, e.g. `@astrojs/vercel/static` versus `@astrojs/vercel/serverless`, so choose the server entrypoint. Adapter features also vary, such as `middlewareMode` (`classic` or `edge`, added in `astro@6.0.0`) and `buildOutput`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/adapter-reference/
When should I use server-side rendering (SSR) versus static generation in Astro?

Use static generation (the default) for content identical for every visitor: it's prerendered at build time and served as plain HTML, so it's fastest and needs no server. Use SSR when pages must vary per request (cookies/sessions, logged-in users, fresh data) or when you need server endpoints — it requires an adapter for your host. Enable it selectively with `export const prerender = false`; for a mostly dynamic app set `output: 'server'` and opt individual pages back in with `export const prerender = true`. Start static, add SSR only where needed.
Why does Astro throw a 'NoAdapterInstalledServerIslands' error when I try to use server islands in my project?

`NoAdapterInstalledServerIslands` means server islands require an on-demand rendering adapter — the same constraints as SSR — and none is installed or configured. Install and configure the adapter for your final deployment target; the `server:defer` directive relies on the adapter to perform the delayed rendering. The pattern itself is portable across hosts (a Node.js server in Docker, or your chosen serverless provider), but an adapter must still be present for the island's deferred fetch, fallback replacement, and access to features like cookies.

What's the difference between returning a plain object versus a Response from an Astro action handler?

Action handlers must return serializable data (objects, arrays, strings, numbers, Dates, Maps, Sets, URLs) and cannot return a Response object. Middleware and endpoints (since Astro v3) must return a Response object directly. Returning a plain object from an action handler works; returning a Response throws ActionsReturnedInvalidDataError.
When using Astro's `file` loader to create a content collection from a CSV file, I get a 'FileParserNotFound: No parser was found for 'data.csv'' error. What causes this and how do I fix it?
My teammate suggests stripping the YAML frontmatter out of every Markdown file to get past "Failed to parse Markdown frontmatter." Is that the right fix, and what should I do instead?

No, stripping YAML frontmatter is not the correct fix. The error indicates invalid syntax in the frontmatter itself, which needs to be corrected.

Instead, inspect the Markdown files throwing the error for common issues like missing colons (`:`), unmatched quotes, or incorrect indentation in the frontmatter block. Fix these syntax errors so that the frontmatter parses correctly while preserving its content and structure.

Example of valid frontmatter:
```markdown
---
title: "My Page"
description: "A description"
---

# Content
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/markdown-frontmatter-parse-error/
In what scenarios should I avoid using remark/rehype plugins to modify frontmatter programmatically in Astro, and when is it better to handle such logic elsewhere?

Use remark/rehype frontmatter modification only for properties derived from the Markdown document itself (e.g., computing `title`-based values) that must be exposed via imported Markdown, `Astro.props.frontmatter`, or `remarkPluginFrontmatter`. Avoid it when the logic isn't about the document: it runs for every Markdown/MDX file, so site-wide or unrelated data is better computed elsewhere (e.g., in a content collection layer or component). Also avoid setting `astro.frontmatter` to `null`/`undefined`/invalid JSON, which throws `InvalidFrontmatterInjectionError`. Note metadata locations changed in v5 (`vfile.data.astro.frontmatter` is unchanged; headings/imagePaths moved under `vfile.data.astro`), and since v2 plugins receive the complete document frontmatter rather than an empty object.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/markdown-content/
How can I ensure that my component identifiers are correctly used in both the import statement and the component usage to avoid 'No import found for component' errors?

Use the identical identifier in both the import statement and the component tag: import in the frontmatter, then render with a tag whose name matches the imported binding and starts with an uppercase letter.

```astro
---
import GreetingHeadline from './GreetingHeadline.astro';
const name = 'Astro';
---
<GreetingHeadline greeting="Hi" name={name} />
```

If the import is missing or the names differ even slightly (`GreetingHeadline` vs `GreetingHeadline` with a typo), Astro cannot resolve the component and throws `NoMatchingImport`. The same rule applies in MDX: `import CustomCard from '../../components/CustomCard.astro';` then `<CustomCard>...</CustomCard>`. Starlight Markdoc is the exception, where `{% card %}` tags need no import.

Two of my Markdown files fail with different messages: "cannot read an implicit mapping pair; a colon is missed" on one and "unexpected end of the stream within a double quoted scalar" on the other. What distinct frontmatter mistakes do these two messages point to?

The error "cannot read an implicit mapping pair; a colon is missed" indicates a missing colon (`:`) in a key-value pair within the Markdown frontmatter, such as `title "My Title"` instead of `title: "My Title"`.

The error "unexpected end of the stream within a double quoted scalar" indicates an unclosed or mismatched quote in a string value, like `description: "This is a description` (missing closing quote).

Both errors stem from invalid YAML syntax in the frontmatter block. Ensure all key-value pairs have proper colons and that all strings are properly quoted.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/errors/markdown-frontmatter-parse-error/
Can I use a function call or complex expression as the value for prerender export in Astro 7, and why is static analysis required?

No, you cannot use function calls or complex expressions for the `prerender` export. Astro 7 only supports static values `true` or `false` with `export const prerender = true`. Static analysis is required because the compiler must determine the prerender setting at build time to generate the correct output — dynamic values were removed in v5.0.
What is the difference between using on-demand rendering and server islands in Astro, and when should you use each?

On-demand rendering (SSR) renders entire routes on the server per request, enabling cookies, status codes, headers, redirects, and fresh data for each viewer; server islands defer individual components (marked with `server:defer`) to render at request time, typically within an otherwise prerendered page. Both require an installed adapter — server islands throw `NoAdapterInstalledServerIslands` without one. No. `globalThis` exists in both server-side and client-side code, but its server-side value is not shared with the client — assigning `globalThis.myString` in an `.astro` component does not change what a browser `<script>` reads. The `declare var myString: string` in `src/env.d.ts` only supplies types for `globalThis.myString` and `window.myString` (`window` itself being client-only); it is a type declaration, not a value bridge between environments.

When passing named slots like slot="social-links" to a React component, what prop name does the component receive?

It arrives as a camelCase top-level prop: `props.socialLinks`. For React, Preact, and Solid, named slots are converted to props, and kebab-case slot names are converted to camelCase (`slot="social-links"` → `props.socialLinks`). Svelte and Vue instead keep the kebab-case name in a `<slot name="social-links">` element.
I want to run the dev server using a staging API endpoint defined in a .env.staging file. What command do I run, and which .env file does Astro load when I pass --mode staging?

Run `pnpm astro dev --mode staging` (npm: `npm run astro dev -- --mode staging`; yarn: `yarn astro dev --mode staging`). The `--mode` flag sets `mode` to `staging`, so Astro loads the matching `.env.staging` file from your project directory, giving you the staging API endpoint. `astro dev` and `astro build` default to `"development"` and `"production"` modes respectively; `--mode` is what overrides that and selects a different `.env.[mode]` file (e.g. `.env.testing`, `.env.staging`).
You import a local PNG image and pass it to ``. The original image is 1600x900. What does the rendered `` element contain in a prerendered build, and which format becomes the `` fallback?

In a prerendered build, `` renders a `` with two `` elements (AVIF first, then WebP) and an `` fallback using the original PNG format at 1600×900. The fallback format defaults to the source format (`.png` for static images). ```html ``` Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/images/
When would you choose to place an image in `public/assets/logo.png` and reference it as `/assets/logo.png` instead of importing it from `src/assets/logo.png`?

Use `public/assets/logo.png` when: the image must keep a stable, predictable URL (e.g., for external links, `manifest.json`, `og:image`); it shouldn't be optimized/transformed; or it's referenced outside Astro components (CSS `background-image`, JS fetch). Use `src/assets/logo.png` when you want Astro to optimize, hash, and transform the image via `<Image />` or `getImage()`, and you can import it in component code.
Why does my Playwright test fail with a timeout when running against my Astro dev server at localhost:4321?

The timeout occurs because you should run Playwright tests against your production build, not the dev server. The recommended workflow is to run `npm run build` first, then configure the `webServer` command to `npm run preview` in `playwright.config.ts`. The dev server is not intended as a test target — running tests against production code more closely resembles your live, deployed site and avoids dev-server-specific issues.
What's the difference between using `astro/tsconfigs/base` versus `astro/tsconfigs/strict` as the `extends` value in my `tsconfig.json`, and when would I choose one over the other?

`astro/tsconfigs/base` only enables support for modern JavaScript and serves as the foundation for the other templates, while `astro/tsconfigs/strict` builds on it with stricter checking. Choose `base` if you aren't writing TypeScript; choose `strict` (or `strictest`) if you are — Astro's `create astro` CLI defaults to `strict`. Note that `strict` and `strictest` already include the settings content collections need (`strictNullChecks`, `allowJs`); with `base` you must add those yourself to `compilerOptions`. Since Astro v3.0, `verbatimModuleSyntax` is enabled in every preset, so type-only imports must use `import type`.
What is the difference between using `getCollection()` and `getEntry()` when querying content in Astro?

`getCollection()` fetches an entire collection and returns an array of entries, while `getEntry()` fetches a single entry by collection name and `id` and may return `undefined` if it doesn't exist.

```astro
---
import { getCollection, getEntry } from 'astro:content';
const allBlogPosts = await getCollection('blog');          // array
const poodleData = await getEntry('dogs', 'poodle');       // one entry | undefined
---
```

`getCollection()` also accepts an optional `filter` callback to narrow results by `id` or `data` (e.g. `data.draft === true`); `getEntry()` takes no filter. Both return entries with a unique `id`, a `data` object, and a `body` with the raw document. `getCollection()` was added in `astro@2.0.0`, `getEntry()` in `astro@2.5.0`.
A team member reports the dev toolbar isn't appearing even though they haven't disabled it. What's the most likely cause and how do they fix it?

The dev toolbar was likely disabled either per-project (via `devToolbar: { enabled: false }` in `astro.config.mjs`) or per-user (via `astro preferences disable devToolbar`). Fix by removing the config setting or setting `enabled: true`, or by running `astro preferences enable devToolbar`.

What is the purpose of Astro Islands and how does it differ from traditional hydration approaches?

Astro Islands enable selective hydration by rendering most of a page as static HTML and only hydrating explicitly marked interactive components via `client:*` directives. Unlike traditional SPAs that hydrate the entire page as a single JavaScript application, islands load and hydrate each component independently with configurable priorities (`client:load`, `client:idle`, `client:visible`, `client:media`, `client:only`). This avoids monolithic JavaScript payloads, enables parallel loading of islands, and lets developers defer or skip hydration for components the user never sees. Server islands (`server:defer`) extend this pattern to dynamic server-rendered content, fetching personalized fragments at runtime while the static page shell loads instantly.

In my Astro 7 SSR project, I have an endpoint at `src/pages/api/data.json.ts` that exports a `GET` handler but no `HEAD` handler. A monitoring service sends HEAD requests to check endpoint health. What response will the monitoring service receive, and does the `GET` handler's response body get included?

The monitoring service receives the same status code and headers as the `GET` response, but with an empty body. Astro automatically handles `HEAD` by invoking the `GET` handler and stripping the response body.

How do I write blog posts in local Markdown files without any external CMS in Astro?

Create a `src/pages/posts/` folder and add Markdown files (e.g. `post-1.md`) with YAML frontmatter (like `title`, `pubDate`, `tags`) and Markdown body content; Astro automatically converts `.md` files to HTML pages at `/posts/<slug>/`. Then link to those posts from any page (such as `blog.astro`) using standard anchor tags.
Why does importing a browser-only NPM package like `chart.js` in an Astro component's frontmatter throw 'document is not defined', but importing it inside a `<script>` tag works?

Frontmatter runs at build time in Node.js (server environment), where browser globals like `document` don't exist. Code in `<script>` tags is sent to the browser and executes client-side where `document` is available. Importing a browser-only package in frontmatter executes its top-level code immediately in Node, causing the error.

You have an endpoint at `src/pages/api.js` that checks `context.locals.allowed` and calls `context.rewrite('/')` when false. How does this differ from returning `context.redirect('/')` in terms of browser behavior and request handling?

`context.rewrite('/')` keeps the original URL in the address bar and returns the `/` page's status code (typically 200), triggering a new rendering phase that re-executes middleware. `context.redirect('/')` sends a 302 response, causing the browser to navigate to `/` and update the address bar, without re-executing middleware for the original request.

A team is building a simple Astro 7 marketing site with a contact form that emails submissions to a single address. Based on the server-side needs listed in the documentation, why would integrating a full backend service be unnecessary for this use case?

A full backend service is unnecessary because backend services target complex server-side needs—user sign-ups/authentication, persistent data storage, user-uploaded asset storage, API generation, realtime communication, and application monitoring—and a single-address contact form requires none of these. Astro server endpoints can handle the form submission directly without adopting a cloud backend for databases or auth.
