What happens if a live collection entry fails Zod validation during getLiveEntry() and how should I handle the error?
When writing Markdown in Astro, you need to display a literal `<` character without it being interpreted as an HTML tag. What HTML entity should you use?
Use `<` to display a literal `<` character in Markdown without it being interpreted as the beginning of an HTML element.

When deciding between `server:defer` and `client:load` for a component that displays a user's notification count, what is the key architectural distinction in how each delivers interactivity, and why would `server:defer` be preferred if the count changes frequently and must be personalized per user?

`client:load` makes the component a client island: it renders to static HTML and runs a client-side runtime in the browser, so interactivity ships to the client. `server:defer` makes it a server island: at build time the component is swapped for a script plus `slot="fallback"` placeholder, and its HTML is fetched at run time from a special `/_server-islands/` route, rendered on demand outside the rest of the page.

`server:defer` is preferred for a frequently changing, per-user notification count because the count is computed on the server for each visitor while the outer shell and main content stay aggressively cacheable; the count needs no client runtime, and fallback content (a generic badge or spinner) renders immediately to prevent layout shift.
When nesting a hydrated Svelte button inside a hydrated React sidebar component in an .astro file, which component's client:* directive controls when the button's JavaScript loads?

The button's own `client:*` directive controls when its JavaScript loads. Each hydrated component's hydration is independently controlled by its own directive, even when nested inside another framework's component.

A developer considers enabling prefetch for all internal links on a high-traffic e-commerce site with many personalized, uncacheable pages. Why would enabling Astro's built-in prefetch be counterproductive in this scenario, and what is the recommended alternative approach for such pages?

Prefetching personalized, uncacheable pages wastes bandwidth since each prefetch generates a unique response that cannot be reused. The recommended approach is to enable `prefetchAll: true` globally, then opt out individual personalized links with `data-astro-prefetch="false"`. ```astro Dashboard ``` Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/prefetch/#prefetch-all-links-by-default

When should I use Astro.cache.set({maxAge:300, tags:['api','data']}) in an API route versus configuring a routeRule in astro.config.mjs with the same caching behavior, and what happens if both are present for the same route?

Use `routeRules` in `astro.config.mjs` to set declarative cache defaults for route groups, and `context.cache.set()` in an API route when a single request needs different or conditional options (custom `maxAge`/`tags`, or `cache.set(false)` to opt out). When both are present for the same route, they merge: per-route `cache.set()` calls can override or extend the values set by the matched config rule.

I have an Astro component with a script that uses querySelectorAll to attach event listeners. If I render this component multiple times on a page, will the event listeners be attached multiple times? How does Astro handle this?

No. Astro deduplicates processed `<script>` tags: if the component is rendered multiple times, the script is included and executed only once per page. Your `querySelectorAll` then finds every instance in the DOM and attaches a listener to each, so all buttons work without duplicate listeners.

For per-instance logic, wrap your markup in a custom element and do the work in `connectedCallback()` — the script still runs once, but the browser calls `connectedCallback()` for each element, letting you use `this.querySelector()` scoped to that instance.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/client-side-scripts/
After running `npm uninstall @astrojs/react`, what second step is required to fully remove the React integration from an Astro project?
Remove the integration from your `astro.config.mjs` file by deleting the import statement and the integration from the `integrations` array.

How does the debugging output location differ between an Astro component's frontmatter console.log() and a framework component's server-side render function when the framework component is hydrated with client:load?

An Astro component's frontmatter `console.log()` runs only during server rendering, so its output appears solely in the terminal running `astro build`/`astro dev` — Astro components are always rendered to static HTML and never run in the browser. A framework component with `client:load` renders on the server first (its log appears in the terminal), then hydrates and re-renders in the browser, so the same log also appears in the browser's developer console. `client:only` is the exception: it skips server rendering entirely, logging only in the browser.
What happens when you nest a client:idle Svelte component inside a client:load React component in the same Astro template?

Each island hydrates independently according to its own directive: the React component loads and hydrates its JavaScript on page load (`client:load`), while the Svelte component hydrates later, after the page finishes its initial load and `requestIdleCallback` fires (`client:idle`). Both are server-rendered to static HTML first (only `client:only` skips server rendering), and each framework's runtime is sent to the browser only once per page. Nesting hydrated framework components as children inside an Astro template is supported; a single framework component file (`.jsx`, `.svelte`) still cannot mix frameworks.
What command does the "Copy debug info" button in the Astro Menu app execute, and what does it copy to the clipboard?

It runs the `astro info` command and copies its output to your clipboard. The output reports your environment details—Astro, Vite, Node, system, package manager, output mode, adapter, and integrations—useful when opening an issue or asking for help. (The CLI equivalent is `astro info --copy`, which copies without prompting.)
In an Astro component, how do you pass arbitrary child content to a React component named MySidebar?

Place the content as children between the component tags; React receives it as `props.children`: ```astro --- import MySidebar from '../components/MySidebar.jsx'; ---

Here is a sidebar with some text and a button.

 ``` Named slots can also be used for grouping; for React they become top-level props.

When migrating a static endpoint to a server endpoint in Astro 7, I remove the `getStaticPaths()` export because the docs say server endpoints can access `params` without it. However, my dynamic route `src/pages/api/[slug].json.ts` now returns 404 for all requests. What configuration step am I missing to enable on-demand rendering for this route?

Enable on-demand rendering for the route. In `static` mode, add an opt-out to the endpoint file:

```ts
export const prerender = false;
```

In `server` mode, routes are rendered on demand by default, so no opt-out is needed. Without this step the endpoint is still prerendered at build time; a dynamic route with no `getStaticPaths()` produces no built files, so every request 404s. Once the route is on-demand, the server endpoint can read `params` without exporting `getStaticPaths`.
When should you avoid using the preload property on the <Font /> component, and what is the recommended strategy for above-the-fold text instead?

Avoid `preload` when preloading would block other important resources or download fonts not needed on the current page — preloading too many fonts harms performance. Instead, preload only the most essential fonts needed for above-the-fold text, and for finer control pass an array of objects selecting `weight`, `style`, or `subset` (e.g. `preload={[{ subset: "latin", style: "normal" }]}`) rather than preloading every file. For other text, let fonts load normally with Astro's automatic optimizations such as optimized fallbacks.
In astro.config.mjs, you set `prefetch: { defaultStrategy: 'viewport' }` but want a specific navigation link to prefetch on hover instead. What attribute do you add to that `<a>` tag?
Add `data-astro-prefetch="hover"` to that link: `About`. A value set on an individual link's `data-astro-prefetch` attribute overrides `prefetch.defaultStrategy` from your config.

Inside onRequest, I call return context.rewrite('/login') vs return next('/login') when using sequence(first, second). In the first case, does the entire middleware chain re-execute from the first function? In the second case, does second() receive the rewritten request?

- `return context.rewrite('/login')`: triggers a **new rendering phase**, so the **entire middleware chain re-executes from the first function**.
- `return next('/login')` inside `sequence(first, second)`: rewrites the request **in place without re-executing middleware**; `second()` receives the rewritten request with updated `context.url.pathname`.

Why does using `server:defer` on a component with large data objects as props prevent browser caching, and what alternative approach should you use?

Server island props are passed as an encrypted string in the URL query of a `GET` request, enabling browser caching via `Cache-Control`. However, browsers limit URLs to 2048 bytes. When large props exceed this limit, Astro switches to a `POST` request with props in the body. `POST` requests are not cached by browsers, breaking existing caching logic.

To preserve caching, pass only necessary props to your server islands and avoid sending entire data objects and arrays, keeping the query string small.

What HTML element does Astro's prefetch use in Chrome, and what API does it fall back to when that element isn't supported?
Astro's prefetch uses the `<link rel="prefetch">` HTML element in Chrome (and Firefox). When that element isn't supported by the browser (e.g. Safari), it falls back to the `fetch()` API.

When would you use `astro preferences disable devToolbar` versus setting `devToolbar: { enabled: false }` in astro.config.mjs?

Use `devToolbar: { enabled: false }` in `astro.config.mjs` when the whole team should stop seeing the toolbar: the setting is committed and scoped to the entire project. Use `astro preferences disable devToolbar` for a personal preference affecting only your user on that project (add `--global` to affect all your Astro projects on the machine), without changing the shared config.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/dev-toolbar/

A developer creates `src/pages/_astro/[...custom].astro` expecting it to handle requests to `/_astro/assets/main.css`, but the file is never invoked. Why does Astro ignore this user-defined route for the `_astro/` path?

The `_astro/` path is reserved for Astro's internal assets (compiled JS, CSS, hashed files). Astro intercepts requests to `/_astro/*` before user-defined routes can match, serving built assets directly. User routes under `src/pages/_astro/` are ignored.
How do you validate file uploads in an Astro action that accepts form data, and what Zod validator should you use for file inputs?

When I call `cache.invalidate({ tags: ['data'] })`, it removes all cached entries that have 'data' in their tags array. If I instead call `cache.invalidate({ path: '/api/data' })`, what exactly gets invalidated?

Path-based invalidation is exact-match only: only the single cached entry stored at exactly `/api/data` is purged. It supports no glob or wildcard patterns, unlike tag invalidation, which removes every entry whose tags include any of the provided tags.
In an Astro component, after defining a custom element class with a `connectedCallback()` method, what method must you call to register it with the browser, and what two arguments does it require?
Call `customElements.define(tagName, constructor)` with the custom element's tag name (e.g., `"astro-heart"`) and the class constructor (e.g., `AstroHeart`).
How do you call an Astro action from an HTML form to enable zero-JS form submissions, and what attribute must be set on the form element?

Set `method="POST"` on the `<form>` and set the form's `action` attribute to your action, e.g. `action={actions.logout}`. This enables zero-JS form submissions handled by the server. Import actions from `astro:actions`. The page must be on-demand rendered (prerendering disabled). Use `Astro.getActionResult()` on the server to read the result.

```astro
---
import { actions } from 'astro:actions';
---
<form method="POST" action={actions.logout}>
  <button>Log out</button>
</form>
```

For file uploads, also add `enctype="multipart/form-data"`.

When deciding between using an Astro action with accept: 'form' versus a traditional API endpoint for handling an HTML form submission, what specific boilerplate does the action eliminate, and what automatic validation behavior do you gain?

An `accept: 'form'` action eliminates the hand-written endpoint plumbing: you add only `<form method="POST" action={actions.newsletter}>` (the action's query string is handled by the server automatically) instead of writing a server endpoint, parsing `FormData` into an object yourself, and serializing responses. Astro parses the submission into an object keyed by each input's `name`, and you read the outcome with `Astro.getActionResult()` for redirects on success or error rendering on failure — including zero-JS submissions.

The automatic validation you gain: your Zod `input` schema validates the parsed object out of the box, with type-aware handling for `number`, `checkbox` (`z.coerce.boolean()`), `file` (`z.instanceof(File)`), arrays, and strings; empty values converted to `null` (except arrays/booleans); and `isInputError()` exposing per-field messages for UI feedback.
What are the exact steps to migrate an Astro project from Tailwind 3 (using `@astrojs/tailwind` integration) to Tailwind 4 (using `@tailwindcss/vite` plugin)?

1. Run `npx astro add tailwind` to install Tailwind 4 and the `@tailwindcss/vite` plugin, and update `astro.config.mjs`.
2. Uninstall the legacy integration: `npm uninstall @astrojs/tailwind`.
3. Remove `tailwind()` from the `integrations` array in `astro.config.mjs`. The CLI adds `tailwindcss()` to `vite.plugins` from `@tailwindcss/vite`.
4. Delete any old `tailwind.config.*` files if present.
5. Add `@import "tailwindcss";` to your global stylesheet (e.g. `src/styles/global.css`) and import it in your base layout.

In an Astro page that calls `auth.api.getSession({ headers: Astro.request.headers })` in the frontmatter, do I still need `export const prerender = false` if my project is already configured with `output: 'server'`?

No. With `output: 'server'`, pages are rendered on-demand by default, so `export const prerender = false` is redundant — the docs annotate it as “Not needed in 'server' mode.” The export only matters in projects that are not fully server-rendered, where it opts an individual page into on-demand rendering. Reading `Astro.request.headers` (as `auth.api.getSession()` does) works for any page that is not statically generated, so the frontmatter call behaves the same either way.
Since Astro does not ship a test runner, what is the recommended approach for testing an integration package during development?

Create a `fixtures` directory inside your demo project's `src/pages` (e.g. `demo/src/pages/__fixtures__/`) and add a new `.astro` page for every test case, each exercising a different usage of your component. Then run `astro build` to build the fixtures and compare the generated output in `dist/__fixtures__/` against what you expected. This build-and-compare workflow is Astro's current recommendation in the absence of a built-in test runner; you develop and test the package inside a demo project, since Astro has no dedicated "package mode."
What is the difference between setting `build.inlineStylesheets: 'never'` versus `build.inlineStylesheets: 'always'` in `astro.config.mjs`?

With `build.inlineStylesheets: 'always'`, Astro inlines all project styles into `<style>` tags in the HTML. With `build.inlineStylesheets: 'never'`, Astro sends all project styles as external CSS files (via `<link rel="stylesheet">`) instead of inlining them.
How does Chrome's support for `<script type="speculationrules">` enhance prefetching compared to the base `<link rel="prefetch">` approach used by Firefox and Safari?

Chrome supports `<link rel="prefetch">` like other browsers, but also fully supports `<script type="speculationrules">` from the Speculation Rules API, which lets you describe richer prefetching strategies and rules (via `eagerness` levels: `immediate`, `eager`, `moderate`, `conservative`) to balance load times against bandwidth, memory, and CPU costs. This functionality with `prefetch()` requires enabling the `clientPrerender` experiment. Firefox and Safari only get basic `<link rel="prefetch">` (Firefox) or the `fetch()` fallback (Safari), both of which depend on proper cache headers to work.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/prefetch/
When importing a TypeScript file in Astro, why does `import { getUser } from './user.ts'` fail while `import { getUser } from './user.js'` works?

Because TypeScript's module resolution rules forbid `.ts`/`.tsx` file extensions in import specifiers: you must write either the `.js`/`.jsx` extension or omit the extension entirely, and the specifier resolves to the corresponding TypeScript file (`./user.js` → `user.ts`). Using `./user.ts` is treated as a wrong path, surfacing `FailedToLoadModuleSSR: Could not import …` if the literal file doesn't match.

```ts
import { getUser } from './user.js'; // user.ts
import { getUser } from './user';    // also valid
```

Note that Astro itself performs no type checking; use `astro check` or your IDE for that.

You're creating a reusable `BlogPostImage.astro` component that wraps `<Image />` and applies consistent margins and border-radius via a `<style>` block. The component receives `alt` and `src` as props plus arbitrary additional attributes. How do you forward the remaining attributes to the underlying `<Image />` component?

After adding <ClientRouter /> to your Astro project, your bundled module scripts stop re-running on page navigation. Why does this happen, and what event can you listen for to run code after each navigation completes?

With `<ClientRouter />`, scripts that exist on both the old and new page are **kept in the DOM** during the head swap (to prevent FOUC), so they do not re-run. Listen for the `astro:page-load` event on `document` to run code after each navigation completes.

I want to apply stale-while-revalidate caching to all my API routes, a 1-hour maxAge to product pages, and 5-minute caching to blog posts — all without adding cache.set() calls in each file. How can I do this declaratively in astro.config.mjs?
Why do styles loaded via `<link rel="stylesheet">` tags in the HTML head have lower precedence than imported stylesheets and scoped styles in an Astro component?

Styles loaded via `<link rel="stylesheet">` tags are evaluated in order, before any other styles in an Astro file. Because they are processed first, they have lower precedence than imported stylesheets and scoped styles, which are injected afterward and therefore override them.
What content management features does a CMS provide that you don't get from writing Markdown files directly in your Astro project?

A CMS adds a visual content editor (WYSIWYG), the ability to define standard content types — including required fields, e.g. for product listings — collaboration with others, and asset management outside your project. Writing Markdown directly gives you only files with frontmatter that Astro's Markdown processor converts to HTML: no editing dashboard, no enforced required fields, no multi-author workflow.

When creating a JSON API endpoint in Astro 7, what file naming convention should I use for `src/pages/api/users/[id].json.ts` to ensure the response is served with the correct `Content-Type: application/json` header automatically, and does the `.json` segment in the filename affect routing or only the default response headers?

The `.json` segment affects routing: only the `.js`/`.ts` extension is stripped during the build, so `src/pages/api/users/[id].json.ts` serves `/api/users/<id>.json` — the `.json` becomes part of the URL path, and the bracketed parameter supports dynamic routing (`getStaticPaths()` in static mode, or any value matching the pattern when rendered on demand). The response's `Content-Type` comes from the `Response` you return, e.g. `headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }` or `Response.json()`. Note endpoints whose URLs include a file extension are only reachable without a trailing slash, regardless of `build.trailingSlash`.
How do you use `Astro.getActionResult()` to display a success message after a form submission, and what properties does the result object contain?
You have a remote image URL from an unauthorized domain. What happens when you pass it to `` versus ``?

Both render the original, unoptimized image — Astro never optimizes remote images from unauthorized domains — but `` still infers and sets `width` and `height` (plus `alt`, `loading`, `decoding`) on the resulting ``, reserving layout space and preventing CLS. A plain `` is passed through untouched: no processing, no inferred dimensions, only the attributes you write. So the visual output is the same, but with `` you get CLS risk unless you supply `width`/`height` yourself. Using `` for all images keeps authoring consistent and protects even unoptimized images.
When organizing actions into nested objects like `user.getUser` and `user.createUser`, what file structure and import pattern enables calling them as `actions.user.getUser()` from the client?
What happens if I don't use `import type` for type-only imports when `verbatimModuleSyntax: true` is set in tsconfig.json?

TypeScript errors: with `verbatimModuleSyntax: true` (enabled by default in all Astro tsconfig presets since v3.0), the compiler checks your imports and reports an error telling you to use `import type` for type-only imports. Beyond the error, skipping type imports risks edge cases where Astro's bundler may try to bundle your imported types as if they were JavaScript. Use inline type specifiers where needed:

```astro
---
import { type CollectionEntry, getEntry } from "astro:content";
---
```

If it causes issues, you can opt out with `"verbatimModuleSyntax": false` in `tsconfig.json`.

I'm migrating a NuxtJS app that uses Tailwind CSS. The migration guide says I can reuse my CSS stylesheets — does this mean my existing Tailwind config (tailwind.config.js) works unchanged, or does Astro 7 require its own Tailwind integration setup?

No, your existing `tailwind.config.js` from Nuxt will not work unchanged. Astro 7 requires its own Tailwind integration setup via `npx astro add tailwind`, which installs the `@tailwindcss/vite` Vite plugin (for Tailwind v4) and creates `src/styles/global.css` with `@import "tailwindcss"`. For Starlight projects, you must also install `@astrojs/starlight-tailwind` and configure `customCss` in `astro.config.mjs`. Legacy Tailwind v3 used the `@astrojs/tailwind` integration, which must be removed when upgrading to v4.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/styling/

You have a dynamic route file `src/pages/[org]/[repo]/tree/[branch]/[...file].astro`. In `getStaticPaths()`, what shape must the `params` objects have to generate a route like `/withastro/astro/tree/main/docs/public/favicon.svg`?

In a React component inside an Astro project, I import `./styles.module.scss` but the styles don't apply. The file exists and uses valid SCSS. What naming convention must the file follow for CSS Modules to work with Sass in React/Preact components?

The file must use the CSS Modules naming convention: it must end in `.module.scss` (likewise `.module.css` or `.module.sass`) — e.g. `styles.module.scss`, so the name contains `[name].module.scss`.

```jsx
import './global.css'; // global CSS
import Styles from './styles.module.scss'; // must end in `.module.css`, `.module.scss`, or `.module.sass`!
```

React/Preact `.jsx` files support both global CSS and CSS Modules; a file lacking the `.module.` segment is treated as global CSS, so no scoped `styles` object mapping is exported.
Why does a CSS rule defined in an imported stylesheet take precedence over a scoped style in the same component when both have equal specificity, and how can I ensure my scoped styles win?

The premise is inverted: at equal specificity, scoped styles win, not imported styles. Astro evaluates CSS in this order of appearance: `<link>` tags in the head (lowest precedence), then imported styles, then scoped styles (highest precedence). When specificity is equal, the last rule wins, so scoped styles override imported ones. An imported rule only wins when it has higher specificity (e.g. an ID selector beats an element selector). To ensure your scoped styles win, set `scopedStyleStrategy: 'class'` or `'attribute'` in your Astro config — both add +1 specificity to scoped selectors, letting element selectors override global defaults. Use `'where'` only if you want no specificity increase and plan to control precedence manually.
When using `<ClientRouter />` for view transitions, prefetching is enabled by default with `prefetchAll: true`. How do you disable prefetching entirely while keeping view transitions active?
When an action returns an error, how can you check the `error.code` property to handle specific error types like 'UNAUTHORIZED' in your UI?

Await the action call and compare `error?.code` to the status code, e.g. `if (error?.code === 'UNAUTHORIZED') setShowLogin(true);`. The `error` on the result is an `ActionError` carrying a human-readable `code` (like `"UNAUTHORIZED"`, `"NOT_FOUND"`) plus an optional `message`; you can also narrow with `if (error instanceof ActionError)` before reading `error.code`.

In dev mode, I call `Astro.cache.set({ maxAge: 3600, tags: ['products'] })` in my page and see no warnings or errors. When I build and preview, caching works. Why does my caching logic appear to work in dev but not actually cache anything, and what property should I check to gate caching logic correctly?
In an Astro server action defined with `defineAction`, how do you safely read an existing session value like 'cart' and append a new product ID before saving it back?

Use optional chaining with a fallback empty array: `const cart = await context.session?.get('cart') || [];`. Then push the product ID and save: `cart.push(input.productId); await context.session?.set('cart', cart);`. This prevents errors if the cart doesn't exist yet. Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/actions/
How do I prevent a personalized dashboard page from being cached when a route rule in my config would otherwise apply caching to it?

When rendering images in a React component (`.jsx`) inside an Astro project, why must you import the local image file first and access its `.src` property, rather than passing the import directly to ``?

Astro components (``, ``) cannot be used inside UI framework components (React, Svelte, etc.) because "a client island must contain only valid code for its own framework." In `.jsx`/`.tsx`, you must use the framework's native `` tag. Importing the image gives an `ImageMetadata` object; you access its `.src` property (the optimized URL) to pass to ``.

My astro build fails with a validation error for a missing secret API_KEY, even though the only code that uses it is inside an if (import.meta.env.PROD) block that's false during staging builds. Why does Astro validate all schema-defined secrets at build time regardless of code reachability?

Because validation is triggered by module import, not by runtime reachability: by default, all secrets defined in your `env.schema` are validated whenever anything is imported from the `astro:env/server` module, and the docs note that secrets "may be validated even when they are not imported." A branch like `if (import.meta.env.PROD)` is irrelevant — validation covers the entire schema during `astro build`. To make a staging build pass, supply a dummy `API_KEY` in the build environment, or read the raw value with `getSecret("API_KEY")` from `astro:env/server`. Setting `validateSecrets: true` instead validates secrets on start.
What prop types are supported when passing data to a framework component that uses client:visible for hydration?

The supported prop types for hydrated framework components (including `client:visible`) are: plain object, `number`, `string`, `Array`, `Map`, `Set`, `RegExp`, `Date`, `BigInt`, `URL`, `Uint8Array`, `Uint16Array`, `Uint32Array`, and `Infinity`. Functions and custom class instances are not supported because they cannot be serialized for client hydration.

In an Astro 7 project, you create src/actions/index.ts with a getGreeting action that accepts a name string and returns a greeting. How do you call this action from a <script> tag in an .astro page component and handle the returned result?
How do you define a simple action using defineAction in src/actions/index.ts and then call actions.getGreeting({ name: "Houston" }) from a script tag in an Astro page?

After calling actions.likePost({ postId }) from a client component, the error object may lack a code property; what is the recommended way to safely check for an authentication error before accessing error.code, and why might code be undefined?

Use optional chaining: `if (error?.code === 'UNAUTHORIZED')`, followed by `else if (error)` to early-return on unexpected errors — the pattern used in the `LikeButton` example. `code` can be undefined because `error` itself may be undefined: the result only contains `error` when the action actually failed, and `Astro.getActionResult()` returns `undefined` if the action was not called during the request. Optional chaining short-circuits before reading `code`, so you only compare when a real `ActionError` (with `code` and `message`) is present.

What is the difference between using `defineMiddleware` in a `.ts` file versus annotating a plain function with `@type {import("astro").MiddlewareHandler}` in a `.js` file — specifically regarding type inference for `context.locals`?

No functional difference for `context.locals` inference. Both `defineMiddleware` (in `.ts`) and `@type {import("astro").MiddlewareHandler}` (in `.js`) automatically type `context` and `next`, including `context.locals: App.Locals`. The `.ts` version uses native TypeScript; the `.js` version uses JSDoc. Both provide identical type safety and autocompletion for `locals` properties declared in `env.d.ts`.
Why does the Astro 7 Sentry integration guide appear as a stub without step-by-step setup instructions?

Because it is one of the backend service pages that Astro marks as a stub — the backend guides index notes that "many of these pages are stubs: they're collections of resources waiting for your contribution," and the Sentry, Supabase, Firebase, and Scalekit pages contain only the "More backend service guides" listing rather than written setup steps. Until a contributor fills it in, you'd use the community-maintained integrations directory or Sentry's own documentation for the actual setup.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/backend/
What VS Code setting and extension do I need to associate Astro's generated schema with all YAML files in src/content/authors/?
How do you delete a cookie named 'session' in an Astro page using on-demand rendering?

To delete a cookie named 'session' in an on-demand rendered Astro page, use `Astro.cookies.delete('session')` in the frontmatter. The page must opt out of prerendering with `export const prerender = false`.

```astro
---
export const prerender = false;
Astro.cookies.delete('session');
---
<html>...</html>
```

This invalidates the cookie by setting its expiration to Unix epoch (0). Options like `domain`, `path`, `httpOnly`, `sameSite`, and `secure` can be passed as a second argument.
How do I invalidate only the cached response for a specific product entry when that product is updated in my CMS, without clearing the entire cache?

Tag the response when caching, then invalidate by that tag alone. In the page, `Astro.cache.set({ maxAge: 3600, tags: ['product:' + id] })` (use `context.cache` in API routes/middleware); on a CMS update, call `await context.cache.invalidate({ tags: ['product:123'] })` from an API route. Only entries with that tag are purged; path invalidation is exact-match only (no wildcards), and all of this requires a configured cache provider — guard with `cache.enabled`, since `invalidate()` throws otherwise.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/caching/

My middleware tries to replace the entire locals object with context.locals = { user: { id: 1, name: 'John' } }. Astro throws an error at runtime. Why does this happen, and what's the correct pattern for setting multiple properties on locals?

In src/pages/api/debug.ts I destructure const {maxAge, swr, tags} = context.cache.options but the values are undefined at runtime; why might the options be unavailable and how can I verify the current cache configuration?

Options may be missing because no `cache.provider` is configured or the app is running in dev mode—`context.cache.enabled` is `false` in both cases, `cache.set()` and `cache.options` only warn, and accumulated options only exist after a `cache.set()` call in that request; `context.cache` itself is typed `object | undefined`. Verify with `if (context.cache.enabled)` before reading `cache.options`, configure `cache: { provider: memoryCache() }`, and build + preview to test outside dev.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/configuration-reference/

In an Astro project using Clerk, you set `export const onRequest = clerkMiddleware()` in `src/middleware.ts`. How do you then access the authentication state in a page component to conditionally render content or redirect unauthenticated users?

In an Astro project using Clerk, after setting `export const onRequest = clerkMiddleware()` in `src/middleware.ts`, you can access the authentication state in a page component via `Astro.locals.auth()`. This function returns an object with properties like `isAuthenticated` and `redirectToSignIn()` that let you conditionally render content or redirect unauthenticated users. For example, to protect a dashboard page: ```astro --- const { isAuthenticated, redirectToSignIn } = Astro.locals.auth(); if (!isAuthenticated) return redirectToSignIn(); ---

Dashboard

``` Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/authentication/
In an Astro component script, how do you call an action using Astro.callAction() and then check whether the error.code is 'UNAUTHORIZED' to conditionally show a login link?
How do I disable the dev toolbar for all developers working on a specific Astro project?
In dev mode, Astro's cache API is available but `cache.enabled` returns `false` and `cache.set()`/`cache.invalidate()` are no-ops. How should you test your caching logic locally before deploying?

Build the site (`astro build`) then run the preview server (`astro preview`). The preview command starts a production-like server with the configured cache provider active, allowing real caching behavior to be tested locally. Dev mode (`astro dev`) never caches — `cache.enabled` is `false` and cache methods are no-ops.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/caching/

A project uses `import.meta.glob("../pages/**/*.md")` to load hundreds of blog posts. The build slows down and type checking becomes sluggish. What Astro 7 API should replace this for better performance and content-focused querying?
Why do images placed in the public/ folder not receive responsive image optimization or srcset generation, even when image.layout is configured globally?

Because images in `public/` are never processed or optimized by Astro — they are served exactly as they exist on disk, so no responsive variants can be generated. Even when `image.layout` is configured globally, that setting applies only to image components (`<Image />`, `<Picture />`) and to local/remote images written with Markdown `![]()` syntax, which Astro analyzes and transforms at build time (or on demand for SSR). Public folder files bypass this pipeline entirely: "Images in your `public/` folder are never optimized, and responsive images are not supported." To get `srcset`/`sizes` generation, move the image into `src/` and reference it via an import.
How do you validate a date input from an HTML form in an Astro action using z.coerce.date() when the action is configured with accept: 'form'?
My middleware calls cache.invalidate() but it throws an error in certain environments. What condition causes this, and what check should I add before calling cache methods to prevent it?
My Eleventy project uses a custom Markdown plugin pipeline. Does Astro 7's configurable Markdown processor support the same plugin ecosystem, or will I need to find Astro-specific alternatives?

Astro 7 supports the same remark/rehype plugin ecosystem via the Unified processor, but Sätteri (the new v7 default) uses a different, Rust-based plugin system. To keep your Eleventy Markdown plugins, configure `markdown.processor: unified({ remarkPlugins, rehypePlugins })` in `astro.config.mjs` using `@astrojs/markdown-remark`. Sätteri does not support remark/rehype plugins.

The Netlify adapter's `cacheNetlify()` provider sets `Netlify-CDN-Cache-Control` and `Netlify-Cache-Tag` headers and uses Netlify's durable cache. What is the practical benefit of the durable cache compared to a standard edge cache?

The practical benefit is that cached responses are shared across all edge nodes instead of being confined to a single one, so cache hits are served straight from the CDN regardless of which node receives the request. This reduces function invocations compared to a standard edge cache. The `cacheNetlify()` provider enables this by setting `Netlify-CDN-Cache-Control` and `Netlify-Cache-Tag` headers via Netlify's durable cache, and it supports both tag-based and path-based invalidation.
How do you configure the <ClientRouter /> component to immediately replace the old page with the new one without any animation in browsers that don't support the View Transitions API?

To immediately replace the old page with the new one without any animation in browsers that don't support the View Transitions API, configure the `<ClientRouter />` component with the `fallback="swap"` prop. For example: `<ClientRouter fallback="swap" />`. The `swap` fallback strategy does not attempt to animate; it replaces the old page content with the new page content immediately in non-supporting browsers.

I have a dynamic route `src/pages/posts/[...id].astro` with a `getStaticPaths()` function that returns `params: { id: string }` and `props: { draft: boolean; title: string }`. Using the `satisfies GetStaticPaths` constraint, how do I extract the exact `Astro.params` and `Astro.props` types for use in the component frontmatter?
Your middleware calls `context.rewrite('/')` when `response.status === 404`. The rewritten `/` page itself returns a 404. What happens, and why?

An infinite loop occurs. The middleware rewrites to `/` on 404, triggering a new rendering phase that re-executes the middleware. If `/` also returns 404, the middleware rewrites again, repeating indefinitely.
In an MDX file, what are the three different syntaxes available for displaying a local image stored in src/assets/, and which one requires importing both the component and the image?

The three syntaxes are: (1) the `` or `` component, (2) the JSX `` tag, and (3) standard Markdown `![alt](src)` syntax. Only the `` (and ``) component requires importing both the component and the image: ```mdx import { Image } from 'astro:assets'; import rocket from '../assets/rocket.png'; ![A rocketship in space](../assets/rocket.png) ``` The `` tag needs only the image import (used unprocessed via `rocket.src`), while Markdown `![]()` with a relative path to `src/assets/` requires no import at all.

I have an API route at `src/pages/api/events.ts` that exports both a `POST` handler and an `ALL` handler. A client sends a POST request to this endpoint. Which handler executes, and what determines the priority between specific method handlers and the `ALL` catch-all?
The `POST` handler executes. Astro matches requests to specific method handlers first (`GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, etc.); `ALL` only catches methods that have no corresponding exported handler.
When using `transition:name="hero"` on an `<aside>` element in two different pages, what constraint must you follow regarding the name's usage on each page?

The `transition:name` value can only be used once on each page — apply `transition:name="hero"` to exactly one element per page so Astro can pair the `<aside>` on the old page with the corresponding one on the new page. Using the same name twice on a single page violates this constraint; names are meant to identify a unique pair of DOM elements across navigation.
When should I use per-route cache.set() calls versus config-level routeRules, and what happens when both are present for the same route?

Use config-level `routeRules` for broad, declarative defaults (e.g., all `/api/[...path]` routes get `swr: 600`). Use per-route `cache.set()` in `.astro` pages or API routes to override or extend those defaults for specific requests (e.g., disable caching for personalized content with `cache.set(false)`). When both apply, per-route calls merge with and take precedence over config rules.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/caching/
What core responsibility does a backend service handle that allows Astro developers to focus on building their applications?

A backend service manages your backend infrastructure as a cloud-based system — providing tools for databases, user authentication, and other server-side functionality. Owning that underlying infrastructure is the responsibility that frees you to focus on building your application, covering concerns such as sign-ups, persistent data storage, uploaded-asset storage, API generation, realtime communication, and monitoring.
In astro.config.mjs, what does the `base` option do when set to `/docs` and how does it affect generated URLs?

With `base: '/docs'`, every generated URL is prefixed with that path. Since Astro 5.0, `paginate()` URLs (`page.url.prev`, `page.url.next`, etc.) include `base` automatically, so you must remove any manual `"/docs" +` concatenation you added under v4.x. Public-directory assets are not rewritten for you: you must prefix them yourself (``), and since Astro 4.0 the dev/preview server returns 404 (no more 301 redirect) for public assets missing the base prefix. Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/upgrade-to/v5/
When using an external Redis store for sessions in Astro 7, why must the driver configuration be moved to a separate entrypoint file instead of being defined directly in astro.config.mjs?

A deployment serves static prerendered pages without explicit Cache-Control headers. In Firefox, prefetch requests error with NS_BINDING_ABORTED. Why does the prefetch still work on subsequent navigation despite the error?

Even though the prefetch errors with `NS_BINDING_ABORTED` in Firefox, the response is still cached if it has a proper `ETag` header. On subsequent navigation, the browser reuses that cached response, so the prefetch effectively works despite the error. For static or prerendered pages, the `ETag` header is often automatically set by the deployment platform and is expected to work out of the box. Without an `ETag` (or other cache headers), the prefetch will not work.

Your Astro site uses Hono middleware with astro/hono to require authentication on every route under /dashboard. When would it be inappropriate to use this pattern, and what is the simpler Astro‑native alternative for protecting a single page that already needs session data?
What happens to a page's prerender setting when using output: 'server' and not explicitly setting prerender = true or false?

With `output: 'server'`, all pages are server-rendered on demand by default — it's equivalent to opting out of prerendering on every page, so a page without an explicit `export const prerender` is rendered on demand. You can then add `export const prerender = true` to individual pages or endpoints that don't require a server. Note that `'server'` mode adds no functionality; it only switches the default rendering behavior.
Can a single .jsx file contain both React and Solid components, and why or why not?

No. Framework component files (`.jsx`, `.svelte`, etc.) cannot mix multiple frameworks. A single `.jsx` file must belong to either React or Solid, configured via `include`/`exclude` patterns in `astro.config.mjs` for each framework integration. Only `.astro` components can contain components from multiple frameworks.

I'm building a `<Button>` component and a separate `<Link>` component that should accept all valid `<a>` tag attributes. What's the difference between typing `<Link>`'s props with `HTMLAttributes<"a">` from `astro/types` versus using `ComponentProps<typeof Button>` to reuse `<Button>`'s prop types?

`HTMLAttributes<"a">` gives `<Link>` a props type describing every attribute valid on a native `<a>` element, independent of any component. `ComponentProps<typeof Button>` instead resolves to the exact `Props` type `<Button>` declares — even if the component doesn't export it — so `<Link>` would inherit `<Button>`'s custom props and constraints rather than the standard element attribute set.

```astro
---
import type { ComponentProps } from 'astro/types';
type ButtonProps = ComponentProps<typeof Button>;
---
```

Use `ComponentProps` when wrapping or extending an existing component so changes to it propagate automatically; use `HTMLAttributes<"a">` when the component should mirror the standard `<a>` contract (the pattern behind Starlight's `<LinkButton>`, which accepts `href`, `variant`, `icon`, plus any other `<a>` attributes).

In a large Astro project, how can you organize related actions into a separate file such as src/actions/user.ts and namespace them under a top‑level key in src/actions/index.ts, and what is the impact on importing and calling those actions from component scripts?
What does the defineConfig helper from "astro/config" provide when used in astro.config.mjs?

`defineConfig()`, imported from `astro/config`, configures your project with type safety in a supported Astro configuration file (`astro.config.mjs`, `astro.config.ts`, or `astro.config.js`). Its type is `(config: AstroUserConfig) => AstroUserConfig`, so it accepts your plain config object and returns it typed — its main benefit being automatic IntelliSense and editor autocomplete for all configuration options (integrations, build, server, env schema, and more) when you write `export default defineConfig({ ... })`.

I'm adding Better Auth to my Astro project. I created src/pages/api/auth/[...all].ts with `export const ALL: APIRoute = async (ctx) => { return auth.handler(ctx.request); }`. The docs show `export const prerender = false` above it with a comment 'Not needed in server mode'. In which Astro output mode is this line required, and what happens to my auth endpoints if I omit it in that mode?

`export const prerender = false` is required in any output mode other than `server` — i.e., in the default static mode where routes are prerendered — and is redundant in server mode, as the comment says. If you omit it there, the catch-all endpoint is built as a prerendered route instead of being rendered on demand, so `auth.handler(ctx.request)` never runs against live requests and your auth endpoints won't function at runtime. Keep the line unless the whole project uses `output: 'server'`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/authentication/
The documentation recommends starting with the default `'static'` output mode. What specific condition should be met before switching to `output: 'server'`?

Switch to `output: 'server'` only when you are sure that **most or all** of your pages will be rendered on demand. The default `'static'` mode is recommended until that condition is met to keep the site as performant as possible.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/on-demand-rendering/

My Astro site uses on-demand rendering and I deployed to Netlify via CLI without running `npx astro add netlify` first. The deployment succeeds but server-side features like API routes return 404s. What step did I miss?

You skipped installing the Netlify adapter: on-demand rendering requires it, so without `npx astro add netlify` (or a manual `@astrojs/netlify` install plus `adapter: netlify()` in `astro.config.mjs`), your server routes, API endpoints, server islands, actions, and sessions are not built for Netlify and 404 at runtime. A static site needs no adapter, but an on-demand rendered site does.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/integrations-guide/netlify/
If a project has no astro.config.mjs file at all, which Astro features will still work and which will not?

Astro works with its defaults: `.astro` components, the dev server, prerendered static builds, build-time content collections (`src/content.config.ts`), and fetching headless CMS content all function, since the config file "is only required if you have something to configure." What does not work is anything you would declare there: integrations (e.g. a CMS integration such as Storyblok's), an adapter for on-demand rendering, and custom build or server options. Add `astro.config.mjs` (or `.js`/`.ts`) with `defineConfig()` to enable those.
My Astro component's <script> tag throws "Cannot use import statement outside a module" in the browser. What changed about how the script is loaded, and how do I fix it?

The script is being emitted unprocessed: Astro only processes `<script>` tags with no attributes other than `src` (and never `is:inline`), so without processing it isn't converted to `type="module"` or bundled, and the browser hits raw `import` syntax. Remove any extra attributes (including `is:inline`) so Astro processes the script, or load local code via `<script src="../scripts/menu.js"></script>`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/client-side-scripts/
In a live collection loader, which two methods must I implement instead of the single `load` method used by build-time collections?

Implement `loadCollection` and `loadEntry` instead of `load`. Live loaders return data directly at request time rather than storing it in the persistent data store, and are defined with `defineLiveCollection()` in `src/live.config.ts`.

When the router performs a swap, it replaces the entire <body> but selectively keeps certain <head> elements. Which three types of head elements are preserved during the swap, and what attribute controls preservation of other head elements?

The three types of head elements preserved during the swap are: (1) stylesheet DOM nodes, (2) scripts, and (3) any other head elements marked with `transition:persist` that have a corresponding element in the new page. The `transition:persist` attribute controls preservation of other head elements.
The Audit app in the dev toolbar reports no performance or accessibility issues on my page — is that enough to ship, or should I still run dedicated audits?

No, the dev toolbar Audit app is not a replacement for dedicated audits. It only catches common issues during development. You should still run dedicated tools like Pa11y or Lighthouse, and ideally involve human testers, before shipping.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/dev-toolbar/

In a Playwright configuration for an Astro project, what does setting `webServer: { command: 'npm run preview', reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI }` accomplish when running tests locally versus in a CI environment?

Setting `reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI` makes Playwright reuse an already-running preview server locally (avoiding startup delay), but always starts a fresh server in CI where `process.env.CI` is truthy. Locally, you can run `npm run preview` once and rerun tests instantly. In CI, a clean server ensures isolation between test runs.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/testing/

In an Astro component, I have a scoped `<style>` block targeting `.button { color: red; }`. I also render a child Astro component that contains a `<button class="button">`. Why doesn't the parent's scoped style apply to the child's button, and what are two ways to make it apply?

Astro scoped styles only match elements carrying the parent's `data-astro-cid-*` scope attribute, and HTML attributes like `class` don't automatically pass through to child components — so the child's `<button class="button">` sits outside the parent's scope and `.button { color: red; }` never matches it. Two fixes:

1. Accept the class in the child, rename it (it's a reserved word), and spread the rest of the props so the scope attribute is forwarded:

```astro
---
const { class: className, ...rest } = Astro.props;
---
<button class={className} {...rest}><slot /></button>
```

Pass it from the parent as `<MyComponent class="button">`. The forwarded `data-astro-cid-*` attribute includes the child in its parent's scope, so styles cascade from parent to child (use unique class names in the child to avoid side effects).

2. Change `scopedStyleStrategy` to `'class'` or `'where'`; then passing only `class` works and the `...rest` spread isn't necessary.
What is the difference between using `Astro.cache.set()` in a `.astro` page component versus `context.cache.set()` in an API route or middleware?

There is no functional difference—both `Astro.cache.set()` in `.astro` pages and `context.cache.set()` in API routes/middleware use the same `Cache` API. The only difference is the accessor: `Astro.cache` is available in page components, while `context.cache` is available in API routes and middleware. Both accept identical options (`maxAge`, `swr`, `tags`, etc.) and merge with route rules.

A server island's fallback content includes a `<button>` that calls a JavaScript function to trigger an analytics event. The button works in the fallback but stops working after the island hydrates. Why does this happen, and what pattern should you use to ensure the analytics handler persists across the fallback-to-island transition?

The fallback is only temporary static markup: at build time Astro omits the `server:defer` component and injects a script plus your `slot="fallback"` content, then at runtime the fetched HTML from the island's special endpoint replaces that fallback node — taking the fallback `<button>` and any listeners bound to it out of the DOM. Keep the analytics handler outside the island: register one delegated listener on `document` (or an ancestor above the island) from a persistent `<script>`, so it still fires when the hydrated island renders its own version of the button.

Why doesn't Astro support secret client variables (context: 'client', access: 'secret') in the env schema, and what would be the security implication if it did?

Because there is no safe way to send secret data to the client: client-context variables are bundled into client-side JavaScript, so anyone could read the value in the browser — it would no longer be secret. Therefore `context: "client"` with `access: "secret"` cannot be configured in `env.schema`. The same principle drives the `EnvPrefixConflictsWithSecret` error: a `vite.envPrefix` matching a secret's name would expose that secret in client bundles, bypassing `access: "secret"` protection.
How do I configure a custom output directory for my Astro build when deploying to hosts that require a specific publish directory?

Set the `outDir` configuration option in `astro.config.mjs`; the default is `dist/`, and changing it moves the entire build output so you can point the host's publish directory at the new location:

```js
import { defineConfig } from 'astro/config'
export default defineConfig({
  outDir: './build'
})
```

Then set your host's publish directory to match. Files from `public/` are still copied directly into that output directory.

What's the difference between using `.orThrow()` on an action call versus checking the `error` property, and when would you choose one over the other?

`.orThrow()` throws on failure and returns the action's `data` directly (typed, e.g. `number`), skipping the `error` property — use it when prototyping or when a surrounding library already catches errors. Checking `error` instead returns a result object with either `data` or `error`, letting you show targeted user-facing feedback and ensuring `data` is defined without `undefined` checks — the right choice for production UI handling.
When should you use `astro add` for integrations versus installing packages directly with your package manager?

Use `astro add` for official Astro integrations (e.g., `@astrojs/preact`, `@astrojs/tailwind`) as it automates installation, configuration, and peer dependency handling. Use your package manager directly for non-integration packages, community integrations, or when you need manual control over configuration.

Typically reusable without rewriting: `public/` folder (static assets), UI framework components (React, Vue, etc.), CSS stylesheets/libraries including Tailwind, Markdown/MDX files (with Astro's configurable Markdown processor), and CMS content via integrations or API. Next.js `pages/` and other source files go into `src/` following Astro's structure.

I'm creating a server endpoint at `src/pages/api/users/[id].json.ts` in an Astro 7 project using SSR mode. Do I need to export a `getStaticPaths()` function for the dynamic `id` parameter to work, or can I access `params.id` directly in the `GET` handler?

No—`getStaticPaths()` is only needed for build-time (prerendered) routes. In SSR/on-demand mode, server endpoints can access `params` without exporting `getStaticPaths()`, so you can read `params.id` directly in your `GET` handler.
What is the difference between getEntry() and getLiveEntry() when accessing content in Astro 7, and when should I use each one?

`getEntry()` (added in astro@2.5.0) queries build-time collections, returning `Promise<CollectionEntry | undefined>` from the data store at build time; `getLiveEntry()` (added in astro@6.0.0) fetches a single entry from a live collection at request time, returning `{ entry, error }` and requiring an on-demand-rendering adapter. Use `getEntry()` for static/build-time content; use `getLiveEntry()` when data must be fresh per request (CMS, API, database), with live collections defined in `src/live.config.ts` via `defineLiveCollection()`. `getLiveEntry()` accepts an `id` string or a type-safe filter object.

```astro
---
const { entry } = await getEntry("blog", "my-post");
const { entry: live, error } = await getLiveEntry("blog", Astro.params.id);
---
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/modules/astro-content/
When should I avoid using a custom element in Astro and instead use a standard Astro component with a processed `<script>` tag?

Avoid a custom element when your interactivity doesn't need per-instance scoping or lifecycle — a plain processed `<script>` is simpler. Processed scripts are TypeScript, bundled, auto-inlined when small, and deduplicated: included once per page even if the component appears many times, so `querySelectorAll` + `addEventListener` already wires up every instance. Reach for a custom element only when you need `this.querySelector()` to query within one instance, or need `connectedCallback()` to run for each occurrence despite the single script execution.

Why would a developer set `session: false` in their Astro 7 config, and which adapters' default drivers does this disable?

Setting `session: false` (added in `astro@7.2.0`) opts the project out of session support entirely. It tells adapters that normally provide a default session driver—**Node**, **Cloudflare**, and **Netlify**—not to configure one. This is useful for serverless and edge runtimes where a smaller bundle reduces cold start time. The session runtime is already excluded from the server bundle when no driver is configured; `session: false` additionally prevents the adapter from injecting its own default.

A second `astro dev` command fails to start a new dev server for the same project. What file mechanism prevents this, and what information does it store?

A lock file — `.astro/dev.json` for `astro dev` (or `.astro/preview.json` for `astro preview`) — prevents duplicate servers. It records the running server's URL, port, and PID. If a background server is already running for the project, the command prints the existing server's info and exits; use `--force` to stop it and start a new one, or `--ignore-lock` to start without checking or writing the lock file.

How does the custom element pattern in Astro enable you to write component logic that executes independently for each instance of a repeated component, solving the limitation of `<script>` tags that only run once?

A `<script>` tag runs once per page, but `connectedCallback()` runs for every instance of the custom element. Using `this.querySelector()` inside `connectedCallback()` scopes logic to each individual instance, enabling independent state and behavior per component occurrence.
When should I choose a build-time content collection over a live content collection for my product catalog?

Choose a build-time collection when your catalog can be fetched once when the site is built: the built-in `glob()` and `file()` loaders (or a custom build-time loader) populate a persistent data store, so queries are served from performant storage between builds with no rebuild required for reads. Choose a live collection when up-to-the-moment data matters more than that cached store—live collections run at request time, are defined in `src/live.config.ts` with `defineLiveCollection()`, return data directly via `getLiveCollection()`/`getLiveEntry()`, and require an adapter configured for on-demand rendering.

What's the difference between calling `auth.api.getSession({ headers: Astro.request.headers })` inside a page's frontmatter versus calling it inside a Hono middleware's `requireAuth` function with `c.req.raw.headers`? When would I use each approach?

Both call the same session lookup, but at different stages and with different headers objects: in page frontmatter you pass `Astro.request.headers` and receive the `session` value to use while rendering; in Hono middleware you pass `c.req.raw.headers` — the raw `Request` Hono wraps, since `Astro.request` doesn’t exist there — and use the result only to decide between `next()` and `c.redirect()`.

Use the frontmatter call when you aren’t guarding the route and just need the data, e.g. personalizing content with `session.user?.name`. Use the middleware `requireAuth` when you need to block unauthenticated requests to a set of routes before Astro’s pipeline handles them; protected pages can still read the session themselves if they need it.
What is the difference between scoped styles and global styles in Astro, and how do you explicitly opt an element out of scoping?

Scoped styles in Astro are automatically compiled to apply only to HTML within the same component, using `data-` attributes by default (configurable via `scopedStyleStrategy`). They don't leak to other components or the rest of the site. Global styles apply site-wide and are delivered as-is to the browser. To explicitly opt out of scoping, use `<style is:global>` for an entire style block, or the `:global()` selector within a scoped `<style>` tag to target specific elements globally (e.g., `article :global(h1)`). Scoped styles won't apply to child components; wrap them in a `<div>` to style them.
What happens to a framework component's HTML and JavaScript when it is rendered in Astro without any client:* directive?

Without a `client:*` directive, a framework component is not hydrated: its HTML is rendered onto the page, but no JavaScript is sent to the browser for that component, so it stays static and non-interactive. The component renders on the server (unlike `client:only`), but none of its event handlers or reactivity run. Adding any directive (`client:load`, `client:idle`, `client:visible`, `client:media`, `client:only`) sends the component's JavaScript—and the framework runtime, shared across components of the same framework—so it can hydrate and become interactive.
What is the difference between the `forwards` and `backwards` properties in a custom transition animation object, and when does each apply during navigation?

`forwards` and `backwards` are the two properties of a `TransitionDirectionalAnimations` object, each holding a `TransitionAnimationPair` (with `old` and `new` animation definitions). `forwards` applies during forward navigation (e.g. clicking an internal link), while `backwards` applies during backward navigation (e.g. clicking the browser's back button). The router tags the navigation with `data-astro-transition="forward"` or `"back"` and runs the corresponding pair, letting you define different keyframe behavior for each direction.
When using `client:visible` on a framework component in Astro, when does the component's JavaScript get sent to the browser?

Only once the component has entered the user's viewport. `client:visible` uses an `IntersectionObserver` to track visibility, and the component's JavaScript (along with its framework's JavaScript) is sent to the browser at that point, then the component hydrates. An optional `rootMargin` value can trigger hydration slightly before the element is actually visible.

Why does a Playwright test configured with `webServer: { command: 'npm run preview', url: 'http://localhost:4321/' }` fail with a connection error if you run `npm run test:e2e` without first executing `npm run build`?

The `webServer` command `npm run preview` serves the production build from `dist/`. Without running `npm run build` first, no production output exists for the preview server to serve, so the URL at `http://localhost:4321/` never becomes available and the test fails with a connection error. You must run `npm run build` before `npm run test:e2e`.

Your project uses Tailwind 4 and you've enabled Astro's default responsive image styles. You notice Astro's `width: 100%; height: auto;` rules are overriding your Tailwind utility classes on `<Image />` components. Why does this happen, and how do you fix it without disabling responsive behavior entirely?

Tailwind 4 uses cascade layers, so its rules are always lower precedence than unlayered rules — including Astro's responsive styles — and Astro's `width: 100%; height: auto` wins even though Astro's own selectors use `:where()` (specificity 0). Fix it by leaving `image.responsiveStyles` at its default `false`, so Astro's global styles are not emitted, and styling `<Image />` with Tailwind utilities yourself. Responsive behavior is not lost: when a `layout` is set, Astro still generates `srcset`/`sizes`, and you can still set per-image `fit`/`position` props. Note that since Astro 6 these styles are emitted as a hash class plus `data-astro-fit`/`data-astro-pos` attributes rather than inline `style` values.
What global configuration option enables Astro's default responsive image styles, and what CSS specificity do these styles have that makes them easy to override?

Set `image.responsiveStyles: true` in your Astro config (default is `false`; added in `astro@5.10.0`). These global styles are wrapped in the `:where()` pseudo-class, which has a CSS specificity of 0, so any selector you write will have higher specificity and easily override them. The styles target `[data-astro-image]` (applying `object-fit`/`object-position`) plus layout-specific rules such as `:where([data-astro-image='constrained']) { max-width: 100%; }`. You can also override `object-fit` and `object-position` per image with the `fit` and `position` props on `<Image />` or `<Picture />`.

How can I inspect the current cache configuration (maxAge, swr, tags) that's been accumulated for a request in Astro 7?

Read `Astro.cache.options` (or `context.cache.options` in API routes/middleware). It returns a read-only snapshot of the merged cache configuration:
```
const { maxAge, swr, tags } = Astro.cache.options;
```
The object includes all accumulated `maxAge`, `swr`, `etag`, `lastModified`, and `tags` values from route rules and per-request `cache.set()` calls.
If a page has three React components hydrated with `client:load`, `client:idle`, and `client:visible`, how many times will the React framework JavaScript be sent to the browser?
Once. The React framework JavaScript is sent only once per page regardless of how many React components use different `client:*` directives.
Why does the guide require placing the `<Font cssVariable="--font-distant-galaxy" />` component inside the `<head>` element of your layout, and what happens if you put it in `<body>` instead?

The `<Font />` component outputs `<style>` and `<link rel="preload">` tags that must be in `<head>` for valid HTML and proper font loading. Placing it in `<body>` outputs these tags in the body, which is invalid HTML and can cause font loading/rendering issues.

I need to load a third-party analytics script from a CDN in my Astro project. I tried `<script src="https://analytics.example.com/script.js"></script>` but it's not being processed or bundled. What's the correct way to include external scripts from another server?

Include it with the `is:inline` directive: scripts living outside your project's `src/` folder (in `public/` or on a CDN) must skip Astro's processing, bundling, and optimizations.

```astro
<!-- absolute path to a script at `public/my-script.js` -->
<script is:inline src="/my-script.js"></script>
<!-- full URL to a script on a remote server -->
<script is:inline src="https://my-analytics.com/script.js"></script>
```

The tag is rendered into the final HTML exactly as written—no transformation, no import resolution, and no deduplication. A third-party analytics snippet doesn't need bundling; it just needs to load as-is.

An architect is deciding between using Astro's built-in API routes versus integrating a backend service like Supabase or Firebase for a new project. What key architectural factor from the documentation should drive this decision?

Whether the project has complex server-side needs. A backend service is worth integrating when you need managed infrastructure for features such as user sign-ups and authentication, persistent data storage, user-uploaded asset storage, API generation, realtime communication, or application monitoring — it lets you focus on the application without managing the underlying infrastructure. Simpler needs stay within Astro itself; for anything beyond that, pick a service guide covering your use case (Appwrite, Firebase, Neon, Prisma Postgres, Scalekit, Sentry, Supabase, Turso, Xata).

I have a global `<style is:global>` block in one Astro component and a scoped `<style>` block in another component, both targeting `h1 { color: red; }`. The global style wins even though the scoped component renders later. Why does the global style take precedence despite source order?

The two rules aren't competing on the same element. Astro compiles a scoped `<style>` to selectors carrying that component's `data-astro-cid-*` attribute (e.g. `h1[data-astro-cid-hhnqfkh6]`), so it only matches HTML written inside that same component and won't apply to `h1`s elsewhere — the `is:global` rule is the only one matching them.

Where both rules do match an element, the browser resolves the conflict by specificity first and only then by order of appearance, so component render order alone never decides the winner.

When defining a custom session driver entrypoint that reads environment variables like `REDIS_HOST`, why must you declare those variables in the `env.schema` in astro.config.mjs using `envField` with `context: 'server'`?

Session drivers execute on the server, so they require server-scoped environment variables. Declaring `REDIS_HOST` with `envField` and `context: 'server'` ensures the variable is only available in the server bundle (via `astro:env/server`), never exposed to the client. For sensitive values like Redis credentials, use `access: 'secret'` to exclude them from the final bundle entirely.

When using Vercel's `cacheVercel()` provider, tag invalidation marks cached responses as stale and revalidates them in the background using `stale-while-revalidate`. In what scenario would you choose NOT to use this provider despite deploying to Vercel?

Choose NOT to use `cacheVercel()` when you need hard, immediate invalidation: its tag invalidation is a soft invalidation, where cached responses are only marked as stale and revalidated in the background using stale-while-revalidate. After you invalidate, stale responses can still be served while revalidation runs. If invalidated content must stop being served right away, this provider's behavior is insufficient. Also note that during the experimental phase these providers must be manually enabled.
I have a route rule that caches all responses, but I need to opt out for personalized content. How do I use `Astro.cache.set(false)` to prevent caching on specific requests?

Wrap the opt-out in a conditional check inside the page/component:
```
---if (isPersonalized) {  Astro.cache.set(false);}---
```
Calling `cache.set(false)` explicitly disables caching for that request, overriding any matching route rule.
