In a project using @astrojs/alpinejs, why are Alpine.js directives automatically available in every Astro component without needing client:* directives?

Alpine.js directives are automatically available in every Astro component without client directives because the `@astrojs/alpinejs` integration automatically adds and enables the Alpine.js script on every page of your website. The integration injects Alpine.js globally, making its directives (like `x-data`, `x-show`, `@click`) work directly in any Astro component's template without requiring hydration directives like `client:load`. Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/integrations-guide/alpinejs/
You set `extensions: ['.svelte', '.svx']` in both `astro.config.mjs` (inside the svelte() integration call) and `svelte.config.js`. Which value takes effect at build time and why?
The `astro.config.mjs` value takes effect. Options passed to the `svelte()` integration in `astro.config.mjs` take precedence over `svelte.config.js` when both are present.
Why does the `withState` wrapper preserve metadata for progressive enhancement, and what happens to the form submission when JavaScript is disabled on the user's device?

`withState` preserves hidden form metadata (action name, serialized state) that enables the form to submit as a standard HTML POST request when JavaScript is disabled. With JS disabled, the browser submits the form to the action endpoint server-side; Astro executes the action handler, re-renders the page with updated state, and returns full HTML — progressive enhancement without client-side React.
What two tsconfig.json compiler options are required when adding @astrojs/solid-js to an Astro project?

When adding `@astrojs/solid-js` to an Astro project, the two required `tsconfig.json` compiler options are:

```json
{
  "jsx": "preserve",
  "jsxImportSource": "solid-js"
}
```

These settings ensure TypeScript properly handles SolidJS JSX syntax and knows to import JSX factories from `solid-js`.

When should I extend Alpine through a custom entrypoint file configured with the entrypoint option instead of just dropping a plugin's CDN <script> tag into my page <head>? What does each approach give me that the other doesn't?

Use a custom entrypoint (configured via `entrypoint: '/src/entrypoint'` in the `@astrojs/alpinejs` integration) when you need to register plugins or directives programmatically before Alpine starts, e.g., `Alpine.plugin(intersect)`. This runs once at startup and works for any plugin imported via npm. The CDN `<script>` approach in `<head>` loads plugins globally at runtime but cannot register them with the Astro-managed Alpine instance before it initializes; it only works for plugins that auto-register on the global `Alpine` object.
What is the trade-off of setting `experimentalDisableStreaming: true` in the React integration?

You lose the performance benefits of HTML streaming — Astro normally streams React component output to the browser as it becomes available for faster page loading, but disabling streaming makes React components render synchronously, blocking the full HTML response until all components are ready.
How does the `maxDuration` option in the Vercel adapter affect serverless function execution time?
When defining a custom Markdoc tag that renders an Astro component from an npm package with a named export, what is the correct signature for the `component()` function?
What `Cache-Control` header does the standalone server automatically apply to assets in `dist/client/_astro/`, and why is that header appropriate for those files?

The standalone server applies `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` to assets in `dist/client/_astro/`. This is appropriate because those assets are content-hashed (filename includes a hash), so they are immutable and safe to cache for a year.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/integrations-guide/node/
I'm deploying a static Astro site to Netlify. Do I need to install the @astrojs/netlify adapter, and if so, when?

You do not need the `@astrojs/netlify` adapter for a basic static site (`output: 'static'`). Install it only when you need Netlify-specific features: the Netlify Image CDN (for on-the-fly image optimization) or to translate Astro's `redirects` config into Netlify's `_redirects` file format.
How do I configure the Netlify adapter to opt out of Netlify's Image CDN for remote image optimization?
A React library I'm importing via preact/compat fails at build time with an ESM-related error. What astro.config.mjs change can resolve this, and why does it only affect certain libraries?

An existing project uses `@astrojs/svelte@5` for Svelte 4 components. What version must you install to migrate to Svelte 5, and what breaking change does the migration guide imply about the integration version number?
Install `@astrojs/svelte` (latest, currently v9.0.1). The major version jumps from 5 to 9 for Svelte 5 support — `@astrojs/svelte@5` is for Svelte 3/4 only.
You have a Solid component rendered with client:only='solid'. The component uses a Lazy component from Solid. Will the lazy component's HTML be included in the initial server-rendered page?

No, the lazy component's HTML will not be included in the initial server-rendered page when using `client:only='solid'`.

Components with the `client:only` directive are rendered only on the client and are not processed during server-side rendering. As a result, any asynchronous operations or lazy-loaded components within them are also not executed or included in the initial HTML output.

Astro's automatic Suspense wrapping applies to server-rendered components (like those using `client:transparent` or `client:load`) but does not apply to `client:only` components. Therefore, even if a `client:only` Solid component uses lazy components, their HTML is not included in the initial SSR output.

Example:
```tsx
// This will NOT include the lazy component's HTML in SSR
<MySolidComponent client:only="solid" />
```

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/directives-reference/#clientonly
How do I use `withState()` with React's `useActionState()` hook to handle form submissions in Astro?

I have a custom workerEntryPoint configured in my astro.config.mjs that exports a Durable Object. After upgrading to @astrojs/cloudflare v13, what three changes are required to migrate to the new Wrangler-based entrypoint approach?

1. Remove `workerEntryPoint` from the adapter config in `astro.config.mjs`. 2. Add `"main": "./src/worker.ts"` to `wrangler.jsonc`. 3. Update `src/worker.ts` to export a standard Worker object using `handle` from `@astrojs/cloudflare/handler` alongside custom exports like Durable Objects.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/integrations-guide/cloudflare/
I added './data/**/*.json' to includeFiles but my new data file isn't available in the deployed Netlify Function. What's a likely cause related to how the adapter traces dependencies?

The Netlify adapter automatically traces dependencies via static imports/requires, but does not detect files loaded dynamically through `fs` operations (e.g., `fs.readFile('./data/file.json')`). Data files accessed this way must be explicitly declared in `includeFiles` with glob patterns relative to the project root. If a new file isn't included, verify the glob pattern matches its path from root and that the file is actually read via `fs` at runtime.
What Wrangler configuration flag enables Node.js runtime APIs like `node:buffer` and `node:crypto` in Cloudflare Workers?

Add the `nodejs_compat` flag to the `compatibility_flags` array in `wrangler.jsonc`:

```json
{
  "compatibility_flags": ["nodejs_compat"]
}
```

This enables Node.js runtime APIs like `node:buffer`, `node:crypto`, and `node:path` in Cloudflare Workers.
What TypeScript declaration do I need to add to src/env.d.ts to get IDE autocompletion for the Alpine global on the window object?
When enabling `allowHTML: true` in the `@astrojs/markdoc` integration config, what security risk does the documentation explicitly warn about, and why does it occur?
You want to use a React component inside a Markdoc tag. Why must you wrap it in an `.astro` component with a `client:` directive instead of passing the React component directly to the `render` prop?

Tags and nodes are restricted to `.astro` files. React components require a `client:` directive for hydration, which only works in `.astro` components. The wrapper `.astro` component passes props and applies the `client:` directive:

```astro
// src/components/ClientAside.astro
---
import Aside from './Aside';
---
<Aside {...Astro.props} client:load />
```

This Astro wrapper is then passed to `render` in the Markdoc config. Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/integrations-guide/markdoc/
What configuration enables Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR) for on-demand rendered pages in the Vercel adapter, and what is the default behavior of middleware when ISR is enabled?

Why does a remote image like `![A picture of a dog](https://example.com/dog.jpg)` render as an unoptimized `` tag instead of using Astro's `` component when you've configured a custom MarkdocImage.astro component?

The `` component requires `width` and `height` for remote images, which cannot be provided via the `![]()` Markdoc syntax. To avoid errors, the custom `MarkdocImage.astro` component must detect string `src` (remote URLs) and render a standard `` tag instead of ``.

I need to access the user's geolocation (city) in an Astro component deployed to Netlify with the adapter. What TypeScript types should I add to src/env.d.ts to get proper typing for Astro.locals.netlify.context?
When security.csp is enabled in Astro config, what is the difference in CSP header delivery between setting staticHeaders: true versus leaving it as the default false?

With `staticHeaders: false` (default), CSP is delivered via a `<meta http-equiv="content-security-policy">` tag in each page's HTML `<head>`. With `staticHeaders: true`, the adapter writes CSP as an actual HTTP response header in the platform's configuration (Netlify `_headers` or Vercel `vercel.json`), and the `<meta>` tag is omitted from static pages.

In a custom worker entrypoint (src/worker.ts), I want to use the advanced routing Fetch API with Cloudflare-specific bindings like ASSETS and cf-connecting-ip. What two functions from @astrojs/cloudflare/fetch do I need, and in what order should I call them?

Use `cf()` first to handle static assets and Cloudflare bindings, then `finalize()` to apply cookies and CDN cache headers. Import both from `@astrojs/cloudflare/fetch`. Call `cf(state, env, ctx)` and if it returns a Response, return it; otherwise pass the Astro response to `finalize(state, response)`. 

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/integrations-guide/cloudflare/
When should you disable the `collectionsBackwardsCompat` flag in Astro?

Disable the `collectionsBackwardsCompat` flag after migrating your collections to the Content Layer API. The flag is explicitly described as a "temporary migration helper" that should be disabled once migration is complete.
Why must you set `export const prerender = false` in an API route that returns ImageKit upload authentication parameters?

The endpoint must run on-demand (not at build time) to generate fresh, short-lived authentication tokens for each upload request. The guide states: "This requires an adapter so the endpoint runs on demand" and shows `export const prerender = false; // Not needed in 'server' mode`. Without this, the route would be prerendered at build time, producing a single static token that would expire and fail for subsequent uploads.

Pelican uses Jinja templates with `{% extends 'base.html' %}` and `{% block content %}` for layout inheritance. In Astro, what is the equivalent mechanism for wrapping Markdown pages with a shared layout that injects the rendered Markdown content?

Astro uses a per-file frontmatter `layout` property in each Markdown file (e.g., `layout: ../layouts/BlogPostLayout.astro`) pointing to an `.astro` layout component. That component receives the Markdown content via a default `<slot />` where rendered HTML is injected. The layout also accesses frontmatter through `Astro.props.frontmatter`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/layouts/

A Nuxt project stores images in `static/images/logo.png`. After migrating to Astro, the image 404s in production. What directory should the image be moved to, and why does Astro use a different convention than Nuxt for static assets?

Move the image to `public/images/logo.png`. Astro uses the `public/` directory for static assets that are served as-is without optimization, whereas Nuxt uses `static/`. During migration, the guide instructs: "Move the contents of Nuxt's `static/` folder into `public/`." Assets in `public/` are copied directly to the build output root.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/migrate-to-astro/from-nuxtjs/

In Eleventy, the input directory can be configured arbitrarily, but Astro requires all source files to live under src/ with pages in src/pages/. If an Eleventy project has content in a custom folder like content/posts/, how must it be restructured for Astro's file-based routing to generate routes automatically?

Move content files from `content/posts/` into `src/pages/` or a subdirectory like `src/pages/posts/`. Astro's file-based routing only generates routes from files inside the required `src/pages/` directory. Restructure Markdown posts as `src/pages/posts/[slug].astro` (dynamic routes) or static `.astro`/`.md` files under `src/pages/` so Astro's router can generate URLs automatically.

A SvelteKit app uses client-side navigation by default as a SPA with SSR. When migrating to Astro, what architectural difference means Astro sites are multi-page apps (MPAs) by default, and how does this affect interactivity strategy for content-driven sites?

Astro uses **Islands Architecture** (selective hydration) by default, rendering pages as static HTML with interactive "islands" only where needed, whereas SvelteKit defaults to a SPA with client-side navigation. This means content-driven sites in Astro serve fast static HTML by default, and you explicitly opt into interactivity per-component using directives like `client:load` or `client:visible`, avoiding the monolithic JavaScript payload of SPAs.

An existing CRA project uses Jest and React Testing Library for component tests. After migrating to Astro, the docs suggest end-to-end tests can run against the build output. What architectural difference between CRA (SPA) and Astro (MPA) makes this testing approach viable, and what limitation might arise for tests that relied on client-side routing behavior?

Astro's multi-page architecture (MPA) outputs raw HTML for each route at build time, unlike CRA's single-page architecture (SPA) which relies on client-side routing and JavaScript to render pages. This makes end-to-end testing against build output viable since every page exists as static HTML. However, tests depending on client-side routing behavior — such as navigation without full reloads, route transitions, or SPA-specific state persistence — will not work identically because Astro defaults to full-page navigation between routes unless explicitly configured as an SPA.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/migrate-to-astro/from-create-react-app/

I'm converting a Pelican site that mixes a documentation section, a blog, and a portfolio, and Pelican's built-in blog features (article indexes, tag pages) won't come along. How should I bootstrap the Astro project so I'm not rebuilding all of that from scratch, and what do I use if I later need to add features like MDX support?

Bootstrap with `npm create astro@latest -- --template starlight` for the documentation section, and use additional starters from astro.new for blog and portfolio. Copy existing Markdown files into `src/pages/` to leverage file-based routing. For MDX support and other features later, add official integrations from the Astro Integrations Directory (e.g., `@astrojs/mdx`). Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/migrate-to-astro/from-pelican/

In the migration example, the `<App client:load />` directive is used on the root React component. What would happen if you omitted the client directive entirely, and how does this reflect Astro's default rendering behavior for framework components?

If you omit the client directive, the React component's HTML renders on the server but no JavaScript is sent to the browser — the component remains static and non-interactive. This reflects Astro's default zero-JS behavior: framework components are server-rendered to HTML without hydration unless explicitly opted in via a `client:*` directive.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/directives-reference/
When converting a Nuxt page that uses `<NuxtLink to="/pokemon/bulbasaur">`, what is the correct Astro equivalent for the link component and its href attribute?

Replace `` with a standard HTML anchor: ```astro Bulbasaur ``` Astro has no built-in link component; `href` replaces `to`. You can create a custom `` component if desired: ```astro --- const { to } = Astro.props --- ``` Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/migrate-to-astro/from-nuxtjs/

After syncing GitBook content to `src/content/docs/en` via Git Sync with 'GitBook to GitHub' priority, why do custom GitBook components fail to render in Astro, and what are the two approaches to handle them in Markdoc?

Custom GitBook components fail because they don't exist in Astro. Handle them by either creating the components and registering them via Markdoc's config `tags` attribute, or removing the component references from your files.

Gridsome uses GraphQL to query local project files, while Astro uses ESM imports and import.meta.glob(). What is the key architectural difference this reflects between how the two frameworks handle local data at build time?

Gridsome uses a GraphQL data layer to query local files at build time (SPA architecture), while Astro uses direct ESM imports and Vite's `import.meta.glob()` for local files (multi-page architecture with direct file imports).
When migrating from WordPress, what are the two main approaches for handling existing content, and what is a key difference in where content lives between them?

Two approaches: (1) Keep WordPress as a headless CMS — content remains in WordPress's database and Astro fetches it at build or request time. (2) Export all content to local Markdown/MDX files in the Astro project (e.g., via `wordpress-export-to-markdown`). Key difference: WordPress stores content in a database; Astro stores content as files in the project directory (or fetches from a CMS).

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/migrate-to-astro/from-wordpress/

In Jekyll, tags and categories are built-in features for organizing blog posts. In a minimal Astro project, these features are absent. What are two distinct approaches to add tag/category functionality in Astro, and what trade-offs does each involve?

Two approaches: (1) Build tag/category functionality yourself using content collections and dynamic routing, giving full control but requiring implementation effort. (2) Use an Astro blog starter theme that includes tags/categories pre-built, which is faster but may include unwanted features or styling. The Jekyll migration guide notes these features "are not included in a minimal Astro project" and recommends either building them or choosing "a blog starter template theme that includes these features."
When migrating a Next.js project to Astro, how do you replace a Next.js `<Link to="/blog">Blog</Link>` component with Astro's native approach?

Replace `Blog` with a native HTML anchor tag: `Blog`. For better UX, you can also use Astro's built-in `` component from `astro:link` which provides client-side navigation and prefetching. A Gridsome site uses vue-router for SPA navigation and vue-meta for head management. After migrating to Astro, you notice full page reloads on navigation instead of client-side transitions. A Jekyll site uses the `permalink` frontmatter property with placeholders like `/blog/:year/:month/:day/:title/` to generate URLs. After migrating to Astro, the same URLs return 404. Why does this happen and how do you preserve the URL structure?

You have 50 product images in `src/assets/products/`. A colleague suggests statically importing each with `import img1 from './assets/products/p1.jpg'` instead of using `import.meta.glob`. What is the key maintenance disadvantage of static imports in this scenario that dynamic imports solve?

Nano Stores in .astro frontmatter won't work because Astro components are server-side only with no client-side runtime. Writing to a store from frontmatter doesn't affect client-side components, you can't pass stores as props to hydrated components, and Astro components don't re-render on store changes. Nano Stores are built for client-side reactivity only. Use `<script>` tags in .astro files or framework components instead.

In the multi-stage Dockerfile for SSR, why does copying only package.json and package-lock.json in the base stage allow Docker to skip the npm install steps when only source code changes?

Why would you choose the Unified processor with `rehype-external-links` over the Sätteri processor with a custom hast plugin for adding external link icons?

Why does using promises directly in the template allow Astro to stream HTML before data is resolved, and how does it differ from blocking component renders?

Because Astro's SSR streams HTML to the browser as each piece becomes available, a promise placed directly in a template expression is resolved in parallel while streaming continues: only the markup that comes after it waits, so surrounding HTML (e.g. `

A name

`) renders while the data loads. Blocking is different: an `await` in a page's or component's frontmatter makes Astro wait for the fetch to resolve before sending any of that markup, so every element after it is delayed. Moving fetches into separate components or using inline promises both unblock the earlier HTML. Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/recipes/streaming-improve-page-performance/

The component's props accept `string | ImageMetadata` for image URLs. What does `ImageMetadata` represent, and why is this union type necessary when passing imported local images versus remote URLs?

`ImageMetadata` is the type describing an imported local image collected during import, with properties including `src` (the absolute filesystem path reference), `width`, `height`, `format`, and optional `orientation`. The union `string | ImageMetadata` allows the prop to accept either a remote image URL (string) or an imported local image (full `ImageMetadata` object), since Astro requires local images to be passed as the imported object rather than a string filepath.

Files from `public/` are copied directly to the output directory and are not processed by Rollup. How do I access the `lastModified` frontmatter property added by a markdown plugin when using content collections in Astro?

Yes, `/api/hello` remains exposed as a real HTTP route. Importing and calling `GET(Astro)` directly in a page component does not change the endpoint's routing behavior—the file at `src/pages/api/hello.ts` still creates the `/api/hello` route that outside clients can hit independently.
What error occurs if I try to use JSX syntax directly in a dev toolbar app without compiling it first, and why does this happen?

Using JSX directly in a dev toolbar app without compiling it first will not work because Astro does not preprocess JSX code in dev toolbar apps. A build step (TypeScript, Babel, Rollup, or ESBuild) is required to compile JSX to JavaScript before Astro can execute it. The entrypoint in your integration must point to the compiled output file (e.g., `app.js`), not the `.tsx` source.

Import the endpoint's `GET` export and call it directly with the `Astro` global as its context, then read the JSON — no HTTP fetch involved: ```astro --- import { GET } from './api/hello.ts' let response = await GET(Astro) const data = await response.json() ---

The `showDefaultLang` option in `src/i18n/ui.ts` controls this behavior. Setting `export const showDefaultLang = false;` hides the default language from URLs, so `/blog/post-1` serves the default language while `/fr/blog/post-1` serves French.

My Astro 7 project uses on-demand rendering. After building with rollup-plugin-visualizer, I see two stats.html files — one in dist/client and one in dist/server. Why are there two files and what does each represent?

Two files are generated because on-demand rendering produces separate client and server bundles. The `dist/client/stats.html` visualizes the client-side JavaScript bundle (hydration scripts, islands, shared components). The `dist/server/stats.html` visualizes the server-side bundle (page render logic, API endpoints, middleware). This split mirrors Astro's architecture: client assets are served statically, while server code runs on-demand via the adapter.
When should I choose to build a dev toolbar app with a UI framework like Preact over using plain JavaScript with `h` or `htm`?

Choose a UI framework like Preact with JSX when you want a more declarative, maintainable, and readable way to build complex UI for your toolbar app. Use plain JavaScript with `h` or `htm` when you want to avoid a build step entirely — both approaches work without compilation. The tradeoff is JSX requires a build step (tsc, Babel, etc.), while `h`/`htm` run directly in the browser.
When using Astro.redirect in src/pages/index.astro to send users to the default language, why does this approach only work with an SSR adapter and not in static output mode?

`Astro.redirect` in a page requires on-demand rendering because the redirect decision depends on the request's `Accept-Language` header (accessed via `Astro.preferredLocale` / `Astro.preferredLocaleList`), which is only available at request time. In static output mode (`buildOutput: "static"`), pages are prerendered at build time and no server logic runs per request, so the redirect cannot be evaluated. The adapter reference confirms that `buildOutput: "static"` produces static files with no server-side execution, while `buildOutput: "server"` (the default) enables request-time rendering.

What is the difference between awaiting fetch calls in a page's frontmatter versus moving them into child components for better rendering performance?

Awaiting fetches in a page's frontmatter blocks the whole response: Astro waits for all `fetch` calls to resolve before sending any HTML. Moving the fetches into child components lets Astro's HTML streaming work for you — the page shell (`<head>`, `<body>`, headings) renders immediately, then the child fetches run in parallel and their HTML streams to the browser as each resolves. Why might a component not update when subscribing to a Nano Stores atom in Astro?

Because Astro components render only once and never re-render, so a subscription started in server-side code has nothing to update. Specifically, you cannot subscribe to store changes from a `.astro` file's frontmatter, writing to a store from a `.astro` file or non-hydrated component will not affect client-side components, and a Nano Store cannot be passed as a prop to a client component. Because each value in the `images` object is a lazy import loader — `() => import('./assets/avatar-1.jpg')` — not the image itself. `<Image src>` needs the imported module's image metadata (the `default` export typed as `ImageMetadata`), so invoking the function resolves the dynamic import and produces the value Astro can render. Why is it recommended to use Maps over Atoms for managing cart items in Astro 7 when dealing with frequently updated objects, and what performance benefits does this provide?

For a cart with frequently changing items, `cartItems.setKey(id, { ...existing, quantity: existing.quantity + 1 })` touches only that entry, rather than replacing the entire cart object that a whole-value `set()` would require on every change. The related performance habit from the cart example: read with `.get()` in event handlers and reserve `useStore` — which exists to trigger component re-renders — for store values actually rendered to the UI, so re-renders stay limited to the components displaying them.

I configured `redirects: { '/old-page': '/blog/[...slug]' }` in my astro.config.mjs, but Astro throws an error on build. Why does this redirect fail even though both paths exist in my project?

Redirects only work between the same kind of route: a static route like `/old-page` cannot redirect to a dynamic route such as `/blog/[...slug]`. Dynamic-to-dynamic redirects are allowed only when both routes contain the same parameters (e.g. `'/blog/[...slug]': '/articles/[...slug]'`), and a dynamic destination must match an existing route pattern with all of the source route's parameters — otherwise Astro raises `InvalidRedirectDestination` because the destination doesn't correspond to any page in your project, even if a similarly named page exists.

If a `DataEntry` has `rendered.html` populated but `body` is `undefined`, and I call the `render()` function on that entry, does it use the pre-rendered HTML or try to re-render from `body`?

It uses the pre-rendered HTML. When `rendered` is populated, `render()` returns a component that renders `rendered.html` directly; `body` is optional and is not used internally, so an undefined `body` is neither re-rendered nor an error. The `RenderUndefinedEntryError` only occurs when the entry itself is undefined (e.g. rendering an entry that does not exist), not when its `body` is missing. `rendered` has been available since `astro@5.0.0`.

On Windows, the server stays in the foreground so the agent can manage the process directly. The contributor can opt in explicitly by passing `--background` manually (e.g. `astro dev --background`). Can I use `client:idle` on a component rendered via a dynamic tag like `<MyComponent client:idle />` where `MyComponent` is a variable? If not, what's the limitation?

No. Hydration directives such as `client:idle` are not supported when a component is rendered through a dynamic tag (a variable like `<Component />`). Astro needs to know at build time which components to bundle for production, and the dynamic tag pattern prevents that from working — so the directive is ignored. Use a directly imported component tag (`<MyComponent client:idle />`) whenever you need island hydration; reserve dynamic tags for plain elements or non-hydrated components. Why might I see a deprecation warning when using setAdapter() with entrypointResolution: 'explicit' in Astro 7, and how should I migrate?

`entrypointResolution: "explicit"` is the default value that mimics Astro 5.x adapter API behavior (using `createExports()` and `start()`). It is deprecated and will be removed in a future major version in favor of `entrypointResolution: "auto"`.

To migrate:
1. Set `entrypointResolution: "auto"` in `setAdapter()` and remove `exports` and `args`.
2. Replace `createExports()` in your server entrypoint with `createApp()` from `astro/app/entrypoint`.
3. If you had a `start()` function, call its code directly in the entrypoint.
4. If you relied on `args`, create a virtual module to pass build-time configuration and import from it instead.

I'm using a dynamic tag variable `const Element = 'div'` in my Astro template. Why does `<element>Hello</element>` (lowercase) render as a literal `<element>` tag instead of a `<div>`, and what naming rule must I follow?

Rename the variable and use it capitalized: ```astro --- const Element = 'div' --- Hello! ``` Two further restrictions apply to dynamic tags: `client:*` hydration directives are not supported (Astro can't statically determine which components to bundle), and `define:vars` is not supported — add values manually, e.g. `style={`--myVar:${value}`}` on the element.

`Astro.currentLocale` resolves to `'en'`. When the URL contains no `/[locale]/` prefix, `currentLocale` (type `string | undefined`, added in `astro@3.5.6`) defaults to the value of `i18n.defaultLocale`, which is `'en'` in your configuration. Nothing — it is valid and expected. `astro:config:done` is typed `(options: {...}) => void | Promise<void>`, so it returns no value and an `undefined` return is ignored; do your work through the hook's options (`config`, `setAdapter()`, `injectTypes()`, `buildOutput`, `logger`) rather than through a return value.

My component's scoped `<style>` rules don't affect elements rendered inside a nested framework component, and someone suggested `is:global`. What does `is:global` actually change about how Astro handles my CSS, and how is that different from `is:inline`, which leaves the tag as-is in the final output?

`is:global` opts a `<style>` block out of Astro's automatic CSS scoping, so its rules apply globally without the unique scoping attribute added to selectors. This lets styles reach into nested framework components (React, Svelte, etc.) that otherwise ignore scoped rules. `is:inline` does the opposite: it skips Astro's CSS extraction and bundling entirely, leaving the `<style>` tag as-is in the final HTML output (useful for critical CSS or third-party snippets). Both directives go on the `<style>` tag: `<style is:global>` or `<style is:inline>`.

`page.url.prev` is `string | undefined` — it holds the previous page's URL, or `undefined` when on page 1 — so render a link only when it exists: ```astro {page.url.prev ? Previous : null} ``` Since Astro 5.0, a configured `base` is already included in `page.url`, so no manual prepending is needed.
`astro dev` and `astro preview` both serve my site locally — what is each one actually for, and is `astro preview` intended for production hosting?

`astro dev` runs the development server with hot module replacement for live editing. `astro preview` serves the static `dist/` output from `astro build` to verify the production build locally. `astro preview` is **not** intended for production hosting. What is the difference between 'redirect' and 'rewrite' strategies for fallback locales?

With `fallbackType: "redirect"` (default), the browser navigates to the fallback locale's URL, changing the address bar. With `fallbackType: "rewrite"`, Astro renders the fallback page's content at the originally requested URL without redirecting. For example, if `fr` falls back to `es` and `/fr/about` doesn't exist, "redirect" sends the user to `/es/about`, while "rewrite" shows the Spanish content at `/fr/about`.

I'm using `client:idle` on a notification widget, but on slow devices it sometimes takes several seconds to become interactive. Is there a way to cap how long the browser waits before hydrating? What option do I pass and what does it control?

Pass a `timeout` option to `client:idle` (added in `astro@4.15.0`):

```astro
<NotificationWidget client:idle={{ timeout: 500 }} />
```

It sets the maximum time to wait, in milliseconds, before hydrating the component even if the page has not finished its initial load, forwarding the value to the `timeout` option of `requestIdleCallback()`. Without it, hydration waits for the page's initial load plus the `requestIdleCallback` event, which can be arbitrarily late on slow devices.

When Astro calls my CDN provider's `setHeaders()` method, at what point in the response lifecycle does this happen, and why are the headers it returns stripped from the final response sent to the client?

`setHeaders(options, request)` is called after the response has been rendered but before it is sent to the client. The returned headers are stripped from the final response because they are internal, CDN-facing directives (e.g., `CDN-Cache-Control`, `Cache-Tag`) meant for the CDN or reverse proxy layer to act on; once translated, they are removed so they never reach the browser.

My statically-generated Astro site with no adapter installed serves redirects via a meta refresh tag instead of a real HTTP status code. Why does this happen, and what do I need to change to get proper 301/308 responses?

Static sites without an adapter use client-side `<meta http-equiv="refresh">` redirects because there's no server to emit HTTP status codes. To get real 301/308 responses, enable SSR (`output: 'server'`) or add a static adapter (e.g., `@astrojs/netlify`, `@astrojs/vercel`) with `output: 'static'`. Adapters provide the server infrastructure needed to serve proper HTTP redirects.

I need a strict Content Security Policy and my pages render code blocks with Astro's default syntax highlighter, but scripts stop loading correctly once I enable security.csp. What should I not rely on here, and what's the recommended alternative for highlighting?

Do not rely on inline `<script>` or `unsafe-inline` for syntax highlighting when using a strict CSP. The default Shiki highlighter outputs inline styles. Use the `<Code />` component (powered by Shiki) with a pre-generated CSS theme, or use the `<Prism />` component with an external stylesheet to avoid inline scripts/styles. For Shiki, generate CSS themes and include them via `<style is:global>` or `<link>`. For Prism, install `@astrojs/prism`, add a stylesheet to your project's `public/` directory, and load it in `<head>`.
What payload does Astro validate against `security.serverIslandBodySizeLimit`, and what should I consider before raising the default 1 MB cap for my server islands?

Astro validates the server island request body, which contains the encrypted props and slot HTML passed to the island component. The default 1 MB (1048576 bytes) limit exists to prevent abuse. Before raising it, consider that a larger limit increases exposure to abuse from oversized payloads. Also ensure your island props remain serializable—functions and objects with circular references cannot be passed to `server:defer` components.

The adapter may not provide a preview server when it doesn't implement a `previewEntrypoint` (required for hybrid or server output modes). Static output adapters don't need a preview entrypoint. `strictDynamic` is written to `script-src`, but when you scope script resources or hashes to `script-src-elem` (using `kind: "element"`), Astro inherits `strict-dynamic` into `script-src-elem`. On a server-rendered page I need to pick a language for the visitor. What's the difference between `Astro.preferredLocale` and `Astro.currentLocale`, and which one reflects the locale in the URL versus the browser's Accept-Language header?

`Astro.preferredLocale` reflects the browser: it's computed by matching the visitor's `Accept-Language` header against your configured `i18n.locales`, producing the best supported match (or `undefined` if none exists). It's only available on routes rendered on demand. `Astro.currentLocale` reflects the URL: it's computed from the current URL path using your `locales` syntax, falling back to `i18n.defaultLocale` when the URL has no `/[locale]/` prefix. Unlike the others, `Astro.currentLocale` is available on all pages, including prerendered static pages. So use `preferredLocale` for browser language detection (server-rendered pages only) and `currentLocale` to know which locale segment the visitor is browsing.

To fix this, open the toolbar Settings app in your browser and reset the placement there, or clear the relevant `localStorage` entry. The config value only applies when no user preference has been saved.
I have a sidebar toggle that should only be interactive on narrow screens. Should I use `client:media` or `client:visible`? What's the difference in when each one triggers hydration?

Use `client:media`, which is specifically recommended for sidebar toggles: it loads and hydrates the component JavaScript once a CSS media query is met, e.g. `<SidebarToggle client:media="(max-width: 50em)" />`.

`client:visible` instead hydrates when the component enters the user's viewport, tracked with an `IntersectionObserver`, regardless of screen width. Both are low priority. The caveat: if your toggle is already hidden and shown by a media query in your CSS, it's easier to just use `client:visible` without repeating that same query in the directive.

Our CI step runs `astro check --minimumFailingSeverity hint` and exits with code 1 even though the console only shows hint-level diagnostics and no errors. Why does it fail, and what should I change?

`--minimumFailingSeverity hint` sets the lowest diagnostic severity that still exits with code 1, so hint-level diagnostics alone fail the run. Use `--minimumFailingSeverity error` (the default) if only errors should fail CI; `--minimumSeverity` separately controls which diagnostics are printed (defaults to `hint`).

My loader calls `store.set()` with a fresh `DataEntry` object every build, but it always returns `false` and the entry never updates. What causes this, and how does the digest comparison work internally?

`store.set()` returns `false` because the `digest` you supply matches the digest of the existing entry with the same ID: the entry only updates when the digest differs from the stored one, so a fresh `DataEntry` with an unchanged (or identical) digest is skipped. Digest comparison is a plain string comparison — the entry's `digest` string is compared against the stored entry's `digest`, and only a mismatch triggers the update; the format is loader-defined but must change when the data changes. Use `generateDigest(data)` to compute it:

```ts
const digest = generateDigest(data);
store.set({ id, data, digest });
```

If data changed but `set()` still returns `false`, the digest is not actually reflecting that change.

What is the purpose of the `astro:config` helpers (`validateConfig` and `mergeConfig`) in Astro's programmatic API?

The `astro:config` helpers `validateConfig()` and `mergeConfig()` programmatically validate and merge Astro configurations before passing them to CLI commands. `mergeConfig()` combines a default config with overrides using recursive merging for objects, concatenation for arrays, and Vite's mergeConfig for Vite options. `validateConfig()` validates a config object as if exported from `astro.config.mjs`, applying defaults for the specified command (`build`, `dev`, `sync`) and project root.

What happens when `client:idle` is used in a browser that doesn't support `requestIdleCallback`?

The component hydrates on the document `load` event instead: `client:idle` waits for initial page load plus the `requestIdleCallback` event, and falls back to `window` `load` in browsers without `requestIdleCallback` support. Since `astro@4.15.0` you can also pass `client:idle={{timeout: 500}}` to cap the wait in milliseconds regardless of load state.
When should I NOT set build.format to 'file' even though I want .html URLs, and how does this choice affect Astro.url.pathname during the build?

Don't use `'file'` if you have pages that should resolve as directory indexes (e.g. `src/pages/about/index.astro` should serve at `/about/`, not `/about.html`). With `'file'`, every route gets a `.html` extension. Use `'preserve'` instead—it generates `.html` for non-index pages and directory-style `index.html` for index pages, matching your source structure.

With `build.format: 'file'`, `Astro.url.pathname` includes `.html` (e.g. `/foo.html`). With `'preserve'`, index pages get a trailing slash (`/foo/`) and non-index pages get `.html` (`/foo.html`).
When should I avoid using experimental flags in production, and what are the potential risks?

Avoid experimental flags in production because experimental features are not guaranteed to be stable and may include breaking changes even in small `patch` releases while the feature is actively developed. Enabling a flag means your project can break on any update, and the experimental feature documentation is only updated for the current released version, so older configs may drift from reality. To mitigate risk, update Astro frequently and watch the Astro changelog for changes needed in your project code. Note that flags are routinely removed across major versions as features stabilize: `env`, `serverIslands`, `contentLayer`, and others in v5; `csp`, `fonts`, `liveContentCollections`, `preserveScriptOrder`, `staticImportMetaEnv`, `headingIdCompat`, `failOnPrerenderConflict` in v6 — so remove obsolete flags when upgrading.

My session driver config uses process.env.REDIS_URL but the value is undefined at runtime. Why does this happen and how can I fix it?

The `session.driver.config` you set in `astro.config.mjs` is evaluated when the project is built and serialized into the build output, so `process.env.REDIS_URL` is read in the build environment - where it is typically unset - and that `undefined` value is what your deployed server receives. Read the variable at runtime instead: access `process.env.REDIS_URL` inside your driver implementation module (the `entrypoint` you registered), which runs on the server where the variable is set.

On the first page of my paginated Astro route, `page.url.prev` is undefined. Why, and which other `page.url` values can also be undefined?

On the first page of a paginated route, `page.url.prev` is `undefined` because there is no previous page before the first one.

Similarly, `page.url.first` is also `undefined` on the first page since it's redundant to link to the first page when already on it.

The following `page.url` properties can be `undefined`:

- `page.url.prev`: When on the first page.
- `page.url.next`: When on the last page.
- `page.url.first`: When on the first page.
- `page.url.last`: When on the last page.

These values are only present when a corresponding adjacent page exists.

I'm calling `Astro.rewrite()` inside a route after reading the request body with `await Astro.request.json()`, and I get `RewriteWithBodyUsed`. Why does Astro forbid this, and what's the correct pattern?

Astro forbids `rewrite()` after reading the request body because the body stream is consumed. The correct pattern is to clone the request first: `const data = await Astro.request.clone().json();` then call `Astro.rewrite('/target')`. This ensures the original request body remains available for the rewrite operation.

What is the `key` property in Astro's SSRManifest, and how is it used when encrypting server island props?

`SSRManifest.key` (type `Promise<CryptoKey>`, added in `astro@4.13.4`) is the cryptographic key used for encrypting server island props, protecting sensitive data from accidental exposure. Astro generates a new random key on each build and embeds it in the server bundle; in the serialized manifest handed to `astro:build:ssr`, the same property is a `string`. If your frontend (encrypting) and backend (decrypting) can fall out of sync — rolling deployments, multi-region hosting, CDN-cached pages — run `astro create-key` and set the resulting `ASTRO_KEY` environment variable so the same key is reused at build time.
What does the `beforeTogglingOff()` function in a `defineToolbarApp()` configuration do, and what happens with its return value when the user clicks to toggle the app off?

`beforeTogglingOff()` is an optional hook that runs when the user clicks the app icon to toggle the app off, letting you perform cleanup or ask for confirmation first. It receives the app's `canvas` ShadowRoot and may return a boolean or a `Promise<boolean>`. A falsy return value cancels the action, so the toggling off is cancelled and the app stays enabled; a truthy value lets the toggle proceed. Example: return `window.confirm("Really exit?")` so the user can decline.

How can I inject a script into every page that runs on the server side only using Astro?

Use the `injectScript()` callback provided by the `astro:config:setup` hook in your integration, with the `"page-ssr"` stage: `injectScript('page-ssr', 'import "your-script.js";')`. This injects your content as a separate module imported in the frontmatter of every Astro page component, so it executes only on the server during rendering. Because the script is imported, the `Astro` global is not available inside it, and it runs once when the `import` is first evaluated. The other stages (`"head-inline"`, `"before-hydration"`, `"page"`) produce client-side output and would not be server-only.

I store responses from my provider's onRequest() hook in a Map, but the second request for the same URL receives an empty or already-consumed body. How should I store the response so later requests can replay it?

When you store a `Response` in a `Map` and later return it, the body stream is already consumed on the first read. To replay it for subsequent requests, **store a clone** of the response and return the original (or return clones consistently). In your `onRequest()` hook, call `cache.set(url, response.clone())` after receiving it from `next()`, and return the original `response` for that request while returning the cached clone for later ones. This preserves the body for both the current and future requests.

What is the purpose of the `supportsAstroStaticSlot` option in a renderer, and how should it be used?

`supportsAstroStaticSlot` (added in `astro@2.5.0`) is a boolean on `SSRLoadedRendererValue` indicating whether the renderer supports Astro's static slot optimization; when `true`, Astro prevents the removal of nested slots within islands. Set it only if your renderer handles that optimized representation — such renderers can then use the `astroStaticSlot: true` flag on `AstroComponentMetadata` together with `hydrate` to decide how to render slots.
How do I implement the getURL() hook to return an endpoint URL for local image processing in Astro 7.3.5, and what parameters does it receive?

For a local service, `getURL()` returns the URL of the endpoint that generates your image, used for on-demand rendering and dev mode (unused during build); that endpoint may call both `parseURL()` and `transform()`. Its type is `(options: ImageTransform, imageConfig: AstroConfig['image'], logger: AstroRuntimeLogger) => string | Promise<string>` — `options` are the user's `<Image />` attributes or `getImage()` options, plus the image configuration and, since Astro v7.3.0, a logger. Typically you build query params (e.g. `href`, `w`, `h`, `q`, `f`) and return `/my_custom_endpoint?${searchParams}` or the built-in `/_image?${searchParams}`.

What does setting i18n.routing to 'manual' do to Astro's built-in i18n middleware, and what am I responsible for handling myself when I use this mode?

Setting `i18n.routing: "manual"` disables Astro's built-in i18n middleware so you can implement your own custom logic; no other `routing` options (e.g. `prefixDefaultLocale`) may be combined with it. You are responsible for providing your own middleware file — Astro throws `MissingMiddlewareForInternationalization` if none exists. You can write your own routing logic from scratch, or execute Astro's i18n middleware manually via the `middleware()` function from `astro:i18n` (combined with your own middleware using `sequence()`). Helper functions are available for your middleware: `redirectToDefaultLocale()`, `notFound()`, and `redirectToFallback()`.

I want my Astro memory cache to include every single query parameter in the cache key, including tracking parameters like utm_source and fbclid that are normally excluded. How do I override the default exclusion list?
How do I inject a new route into my Astro project using the `injectRoute` option in Astro 7?

`injectRoute()` is a callback on the `astro:config:setup` hook, typed `({ pattern: string; entrypoint: string | URL; prerender?: boolean }) => void`, for injecting `.astro` pages or `.js`/`.ts` route handlers:

```js
injectRoute({
  pattern: '/subfolder/[dynamic]',
  entrypoint: './src/dynamic-page.astro',
  prerender: false,
});
```

- `pattern` is the output path and uses Astro's filepath syntax for dynamic routes (`/foo/[bar]`, `/foo/[...bar]`); no file extension.
- `entrypoint` is a bare module specifier; since `astro@5.0.0` it may also be a `URL`, e.g. `new URL('./dashboard.astro', import.meta.url)`.
- `prerender` is only a fallback for when Astro can't detect your `prerender` export.

For a published package, reference the entrypoint by package name (`'@fancy/dashboard/dashboard.astro'`) and expose it via `package.json` `"exports"`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/integrations-reference/

I want to pull in a theme stylesheet installed as an npm package from inside a component's `<style is:inline>` block with `@import`. Is that the right approach, and what actually happens to that import?

No — an `@import` inside `<style is:inline>` is left untouched: the tag is rendered exactly as authored, its `import`/`@import`/`url()` references are not resolved relative to your `.astro` file, and nothing is bundled or optimized, so the browser receives a bare `package-name/...` specifier it cannot load. Import the stylesheet from the component's frontmatter instead, and Astro will bundle and optimize it:

```astro
---
import 'package-name/styles.css';
---
```

If the package omits the file extension, add it to `vite.ssr.noExternal` in `astro.config.mjs` first.

I'm building a custom CDN cache provider for Astro and need to generate cache tags for path-based invalidation. Which helper from `astro/cache/provider-utils` creates a tag like `astro-path:/blog/post-1`, and what's its signature?

`pathTag()` from `astro/cache/provider-utils` generates that tag, with signature `(path: string) => string`. It produces `astro-path:{path}` (e.g., `astro-path:/blog/post-1`) and is used to support `invalidate({ path })` on platforms that only offer tag-based purging rather than native path purges.

In `tests/Card.test.js` I want to render `src/components/Card.astro`, whose frontmatter declares `interface Props { name: string }` and destructures `const { name } = Astro.props`, and assert the output contains "Hello, world!". How do I supply that prop through the experimental Container API?

I added `data-analytics-id` to a `<script>` tag in my `.astro` file and suddenly the script stopped being bundled — the raw code showed up verbatim in the built HTML instead. Why does adding any attribute other than `src` change how Astro handles the script?

Because Astro only processes a `<script>` tag that has no attributes other than `src`. Processing — TypeScript compilation, import bundling of local/npm files, automatic `type="module"`, deduplication across component instances, and inlining small scripts — applies only to such tags. The moment you add `data-analytics-id`, the tag counts as attributed, so Astro treats it as unprocessed: it is rendered into the HTML exactly as written, with no TypeScript transformation or import resolution (the same behavior as an intentional `is:inline`). To keep bundling, drop the extra attribute; to keep the attribute, opt in explicitly with `is:inline` and accept the raw output.

My Astro project sets `base: '/docs'`, and my paginated route builds a canonical link from `page.url.current`. What do `page.url.current`, `page.url.prev`, and `page.url.first` return in that setup, including on the very first page?

In an Astro project with `base: '/docs'`, the pagination URLs returned by `page.url.*` include the base path automatically starting from Astro 5.0. For a paginated route like `/posts/[page].astro`: - `page.url.current` returns the full URL including the base, e.g., `/docs/posts/1`. - `page.url.prev` returns the previous page’s URL or `undefined` on the first page. - `page.url.first` returns the first page's URL, e.g., `/docs/posts/1`. Example: ``` ---export async function getStaticPaths({ paginate }) { const data = Array.from({ length: 50 }, (_, i) => ({ id: i + 1 })); return paginate(data, { pageSize: 10 }); } const { page } = Astro.props; --- Previous First Page ``` Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/routing-reference/#paginatetion-page-prop
