I tried to set up a redirect from '/product1/' to '/product1' in my redirects config but Astro says this isn't supported. What's the exact limitation with trailing slashes in redirect source paths?

Redirect source paths with trailing slashes are not supported. In the `redirects` config, a key like `'/product1/'` is invalid — Astro explicitly notes this case as unsupported. Use the path without the trailing slash (`'/product1'`) as the redirect key instead. Redirects must map a route to the same kind of route (static to static, dynamic to dynamic with matching parameters).
I want my integration to both register a toolbar app and later push data to it while the dev server is running. Which hooks do I hook into, and what objects do I use on each side of that channel?

Use two integration hooks:

1. **`astro:config:setup`** — call `addDevToolbarApp({ id: 'my-app', entrypoint: './app.ts' })` to register the app.
2. **`astro:server:setup`** — receive a `toolbar` object with `send()`, `on()`, `onAppInitialized()`, `onAppToggled()` to push data to the client and listen for messages.

On the client side (inside `defineToolbarApp`), the third `init` argument `server: ToolbarServerHelpers` provides `server.send(event, payload)` and `server.on(event, callback)` for bidirectional communication.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/dev-toolbar-app-reference/
What's the practical difference between container.renderComponent(Card) and container.renderToString(Card), and why does the former require importing the component as Card.astro?container?

`renderComponent()` returns HTML **including inlined scripts and styles** from the component, while `renderToString()` returns only the rendered HTML/content without scripts or styles. The `?container` query import (`Card.astro?container`) provides a component factory that exposes the necessary metadata for the container to extract and inline those scripts and styles. Without `?container`, the component is treated as a regular factory and `renderComponent()` falls back to `renderToString()` behavior.
Both my integration and my toolbar app's client code can react to the user toggling my app. When should I use toolbar.onAppToggled on the server versus app.onToggled inside defineToolbarApp?

Use `toolbar.onAppToggled()` on the server when your integration code (Node-side) must react to the toggle — e.g. to start/stop dev-only server behavior, log, or send messages to the client via `toolbar.send()`. It's registered in the `astro:server:setup` hook and receives `{ state }`.

Use `app.onToggled()` inside `defineToolbarApp` when the reaction is UI or browser-side — updating the app's own `canvas`, reading client state. It runs in the browser within your toolbar app's `init()`.

In short: server-side effects → `toolbar.onAppToggled`; client-side rendering/DOM → `app.onToggled`. Both fire on the same user click, so choose based on where the logic must execute.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/dev-toolbar-app-reference/
How do you configure Astro to suppress all log output using the logger configuration?
How can you enable on-demand rendering for all pages in your Astro project by default?

First add an adapter for your server runtime (e.g. `npx astro add netlify`), then set `output: 'server'` in `astro.config.mjs` — this server-renders all pages by default, the equivalent of opting out of prerendering on every page. Individual static pages can then re-enable prerendering with `export const prerender = true`. This mode requires an adapter; it adds no functionality, only switches the default rendering behavior.

```astro
---
export const prerender = true
---
```

If only some routes need server rendering, keep the default `'static'` mode instead and add `export const prerender = false` per route. The docs recommend starting with `'static'` until most pages actually require on-demand rendering.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/on-demand-rendering/
My integration wants to push a message to my toolbar app as soon as the dev server is reachable. Is listening to Vite's built-in `connection` event a reliable way to do that?
I set `image.objectFit: 'contain'` in astro.config.mjs, but my responsive images still come out cropped the way `cover` behaves. What am I missing for this setting to take effect?

`image.objectFit` **requires `image.layout` to be set** (globally in config or per-component via the `layout` prop). Without a layout value, responsive image styles aren't generated, so `objectFit` has no effect. Add `image.layout: 'constrained'` (or `'full-width'`) to your config.
How does the `rendered` property on `LiveDataEntry` enable the `<Content />` component and `render()` function for a live-loaded Markdown entry?

When a live loader's `loadEntry()` returns a `LiveDataEntry` with the optional `rendered` property set to `{ html: string }`, that HTML is stored with the entry, which enables both `render()` and `<Content />` for rendering the body in a page:

```astro
---
import { getLiveEntry, render } from 'astro:content';
const entry = await getLiveEntry('posts', 'welcome');
const { Content } = await render(entry);
---
<Content />
```

If `rendered` is omitted, `<Content />` renders nothing. Since `rendered` was added in `astro@6.0.0`, this applies to live loaders in Astro 6+.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/content-loader-reference/

I need my Dev Toolbar app to send a custom message to my Astro integration and receive a response back. What methods do I call on the client side inside `init()`, and what hook do I use on the server side to handle those messages?

On the client, use the `server` object passed as the third argument to `init()`: call `server.send('my-app:my-message', payload)` to send a message, and register `server.on('server-message', (data) => {...})` to receive the response. Prefix client event names with your app ID to avoid conflicts. On the server, use the `astro:server:setup` integration hook's `toolbar` object: `toolbar.on('my-app:my-message', callback)` handles incoming messages, and `toolbar.send('server-message', payload)` sends the response back. If you need to message the app only after it loads, use `toolbar.onAppInitialized(appId, callback)`.
What is the difference between `astro preview` and the `preview()` function in Astro's programmatic API?

`astro preview` is a CLI command that serves the built static directory (`dist/`) with terminal hotkeys (`o` to open browser, `q` to quit). The `preview()` function is a programmatic API that returns a `PreviewServer` instance for programmatic control (e.g., `await previewServer.stop()`). Both serve the same build output, but the CLI is for interactive use while the function enables integration in scripts/tests.
What is the difference between setting 'debug' as the log level and enabling verbose logging via the --debug CLI flag in Astro?

There is no behavioral difference: the `debug` log level is equivalent to the `--debug` CLI flag, and both enable verbose logging, including Vite logging. `debug` is one of the `AstroLoggerLevel` values (`'debug' | 'info' | 'warn' | 'error' | 'silent'`) you set in the `logger` configuration (added in `astro@7.0.0`), while `--debug` is the command-line flag that turns on the same verbose output.
How do you pass custom `locals` (e.g., user authentication data) to a component when rendering with the Container API?
Which method in the `SSRLoadedRendererValue` interface is called to inject page-level hydration setup code?

`renderHydrationScript()` (added in `astro@4.1.0`) on `SSRLoadedRendererValue`. Typed `() => string`, it returns an HTML string that Astro injects once per page before the first hydrated component handled by that renderer — meant for renderers that need page-level hydration setup.
Inside init(canvas, app) I call app.toggleNotification({}) with no options object properties. What does the user see on my app's icon, and why?

The app icon shows an "error"-level notification highlight: a dark pink circle. With no properties passed, `toggleNotification({})` assumes `state: true`, so the icon is highlighted, and `level: 'error'`, which determines the color and shape of the highlight (dark pink circle for error, gold triangle for warning, blue square for info).
In what scenario would you use `--root` and `--config` together, and how does Astro resolve the config file path when both are provided?

Use both when running the CLI from outside the project's directory and the config file isn't at the default name/location — for example, from a monorepo root targeting a site whose config lives in a subfolder with a custom name. `--root` sets the project root (resolved against your current working directory if relative), and that root is what Astro uses to locate the config file. `--config`'s path is then resolved relative to that project root, defaulting to `astro.config.mjs`; if the file doesn't exist there, Astro throws ConfigNotFound (`Unable to resolve --config "CONFIG_FILE". Does the file exist?`).

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/cli-reference/
Why does Astro ship some features behind an experimental flag rather than just releasing them as stable APIs?

Astro uses experimental flags to safely test new features with early adopters before making them stable, allowing feedback and changes without affecting the general user base. These flags enable developers to try out upcoming functionality while Astro maintains flexibility for breaking updates during active development.

Experimental features may be removed or modified between versions until they are finalized. This approach helps Astro iterate quickly on ideas and gather real-world usage data from users who opt-in, ensuring that only polished and well-tested features become part of stable releases.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/experimental-flags/
My design requires the injected content to sit inside an element carrying a `class` that I style from my stylesheet. Is `<Fragment />` the right tool for that job?

No. `<Fragment />` renders no element of its own — that's precisely its purpose, avoiding wrapper elements — so there is nothing for a `class` attribute to live on and nothing for your stylesheet to target. Use a real wrapper element instead:

```
<div class="injected" set:html={content} />
```

then style `.injected` from your stylesheet.

How does Astro handle the order of execution for integrations when multiple integrations are configured, and what should I consider when writing a custom integration that might need to run before or after others?

All integrations run in the order they are configured in the `integrations` array. For `[react(), svelte()]`, `react` runs before `svelte`. Your integration should ideally run in any order; if not possible, document that it needs to come first or last in the user's configuration array.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/integrations-reference/

I've got Markdown files sitting in `src/data/pages` and I want them exposed as a content collection in `src/content.config.ts`. What does the `glob()` loader call look like, and relative to what directory must the `pattern` be written?
In my `astro.config.mjs` I want Astro's JSON logger to print logs across multiple lines and only emit `warn` and `error` messages. What does the `logger` option look like?

All URLs generated from src/pages/en/blog/[slug].astro report the same routePattern even though their paths differ — how can I use that to collect metrics grouped by route template rather than by individual page?

Group by `Astro.routePattern` instead of the request URL: every page generated from `src/pages/en/blog/[slug].astro` (e.g. `/en/blog/post-1/`, `/en/blog/post-2/`) shares the same value, `/en/blog/[slug]` (added in `astro@5.0.0`), so it works as the metric label for the whole route template while `Astro.params`/the URL identify individual pages. For prerendered routes, `routePattern` is also available in `getStaticPaths()` options (added in `astro@5.14.0`) if you need it while building paths.
What is the difference between 'auto' and 'explicit' entrypointResolution values when setting up an Astro adapter?
What is the role of the `clientEntrypoint` in an Astro renderer, and how does it differ from the `serverEntrypoint`?

The `clientEntrypoint` is a renderer's browser-side module: a default-exported function that receives the island element and returns an async hydrator `(Component, props, slots, { client })`, used to hydrate components according to their `client:*` directive. The `serverEntrypoint` is the server module imported during development and production builds that renders component syntax to HTML, default-exporting an object implementing `SSRLoadedRendererValue` (`check`, `renderToStaticMarkup`). The client entrypoint is optional; without one, a component with a `client:` directive fails with `NoClientEntrypoint`. (An adapter's `serverEntrypoint` is unrelated — it defines the adapter's on-demand rendering entrypoint.)
What is the role of the `validateOptions()` hook in Astro image services, and how can it set defaults or warn about invalid options?

`validateOptions()` is an optional hook for both local and external services (added in `astro@2.1.4`) that validates and augments the options the user passed to `<Image />`, `<Picture />`, or `getImage()`, returning the corrected `ImageTransform`. It receives `(options, imageConfig, logger)`; the `logger` parameter was added in Astro v7.3.0, so you can warn about invalid options, e.g. clamp an oversized width and call `logger.warn(...)` while falling back to `imageConfig.service.config.maxWidth`. It's the standard place for setting defaults or enforcing required parameters before `getURL()`/`transform()` run.
What is the purpose of the `entrypoint` property in a session driver config, and how should it be defined?

The `entrypoint` property in a session driver config defines the runtime entrypoint for the driver implementation. It must be a string or URL pointing to the module that exports the `SessionDriver` implementation (with `setItem`, `getItem`, `removeItem` methods). In the config function, it's typically set using `new URL('./runtime.js', import.meta.url)` to reference a local runtime file, or a string like `"unstorage/drivers/redis"` for Unstorage drivers. The entrypoint is required and was added in `astro@6.0.0`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/session-driver-reference/

In Astro 7, when using paginate() with a format function like { format: (url) => `${url}.html` }, what is the purpose of the format option and how does it differ from the default URL generation behavior?

The `format` option (added in Astro v7.1.0) is a function that lets you rewrite each computed pagination URL before it is rendered, e.g. `` (url) => `${url}.html` `` appends an extension to every generated page URL. By default, no transformation is applied: `paginate()` builds URLs straight from the `page` param, so `/posts/[page].astro` yields `/posts/1`, `/posts/2`, … and `/posts/[...page].astro` yields `/posts`, `/posts/2`, … — with `format` you control that final shape yourself.
Is adding `--site https://example.com` to the `build` script in package.json a good way to set the canonical site URL for the project, or should that value live in `astro.config.mjs` instead?

The canonical site URL should live in `astro.config.mjs`. The `--site` CLI flag is documented as an override: "Passing this flag will override the `site` value in your `astro.config.mjs` file, if one exists." Use the config file for the project's permanent setting; reserve the flag for temporary overrides or CI environments.
What's the difference between setting markdown.syntaxHighlight to 'prism' versus configuring markdown.shikiConfig, and when would I use one over the other?

`markdown.syntaxHighlight: 'prism'` switches the highlighter to Prism, which emits CSS classes requiring a separate Prism stylesheet. `markdown.shikiConfig` configures the default Shiki highlighter (inline styles, no extra CSS, zero-runtime JS). Use Shiki for simpler setup and smaller output; use Prism if you need CSS-class-based theming or existing Prism themes.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/syntax-highlighting/
How can you configure a route to be rendered on-demand instead of being prerendered at build time in Astro?

Add `export const prerender = false` at the top of a page or endpoint to opt out of static prerendering and enable on-demand server rendering. This requires an adapter integration (e.g., `@astrojs/netlify`, `@astrojs/vercel`) configured in `astro.config.mjs`.

```astro
---export const prerender = false---<html>
  <body>Server-rendered on each request</body>
</html>
```
For fully dynamic apps, set `output: 'server'` in `astro.config.mjs` to render all pages on demand by default, then use `export const prerender = true` for static pages.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/on-demand-rendering/
Why would `astro preview --background` fail to start a new server if one is already running, and what flag would you add to force a restart?

`--background` writes a lock file (`.astro/dev.json` or `.astro/preview.json`) recording the running server's URL, port, and PID to prevent duplicate servers for the same project; if one already exists, the command prints the existing server's info and exits without starting a new one. Add `--force` to stop the existing server and start a new one:

```
astro preview --background --force
```

(Alternatively, `--ignore-lock` lets a new server start alongside an existing one, but it errors when combined with `--background`, which relies on the lock file.)
I have a monorepo where my Astro project lives in a subdirectory, not the repo root. How do I run `astro check` against that subdirectory, and what flag do I use to point it at the right location?

Use the `--root` flag: `astro check --root ./path/to/subdirectory` specifies a different root directory to check; it defaults to the current working directory, so you can also `cd` into the subdirectory and run `astro check` normally.

I defined a variable `count = 0` in my Astro component's frontmatter and display it in the template as `{count}`. Later in the same component, I update `count = 5` in a script block. Why does the rendered HTML still show `0` instead of `5`?

Because the component template is evaluated once, server-side, to produce the HTML output — at that moment `count` is `0`, so `0` is baked into the rendered markup. `<script>` blocks are client-side scripts: they run in the browser after the HTML already exists, and they don't re-run the component's frontmatter or re-render the template, so assigning `count = 5` there only changes the browser-side variable, never the server-rendered HTML. Astro templates have no reactivity to frontmatter variables; if you need the displayed value to change, have the script update the DOM directly (e.g. set `textContent` on an element) or use a hydrated framework component with a `client:` directive.
What is the difference between `page.url.prev` and `page.url.next`, and how do they behave on the first and last pages?

`page.url.prev` returns the previous page's URL (or `undefined` on page 1). `page.url.next` returns the next page's URL (or `undefined` on the last page). Both prepend the `base` config if set. ```astro ---const { page } = Astro.props;--- {page.url.prev && Previous} {page.url.next && Next} ``` Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/routing-reference/

In astro.config.mjs I call myCache({ apiKey: '...' }) and the factory in my runtime module receives that apiKey as its argument. How does the value travel from the config file to the factory at runtime?

The config travels via Astro's cache provider configuration. Your config helper returns a `CacheProviderConfig` with `entrypoint: 'my-provider/runtime'` and `config: options` (e.g. `{ apiKey: '...' }`). Astro serializes that `config` object at build/config time and passes it as the argument to your runtime module's **default-exported `CacheProviderFactory` function** at runtime. The factory receives that serialized `config` and returns the `CacheProvider` instance that uses it.

In an Astro component I have `const visible = true` in my frontmatter. How do I render a `

` element only when `visible` is true, and what are the two JSX-like expression forms I can use for this?

Use either the logical AND form `{visible &&

Show me!

}` or the ternary form `{visible ?

Show me!

:

Else show me!

}`. Both are valid JSX-like expressions in Astro templates for conditional rendering.
Every other attribute I put on a `<style>` tag forces inline behavior, but `define:vars` doesn't. What does that mean for how my component's styles are processed when I use `define:vars`?

`define:vars` is the exception to the rule that any extra attribute on `<style>` implies `is:inline` — so your styles are still processed normally: bundled, optimized, and scoped to the component, rather than left as-is in the final HTML. The frontmatter values are serialized with `JSON.stringify()` and injected as CSS custom properties, which you consume with `var(--name)`:

```astro
<style define:vars={{ textColor: foregroundColor, backgroundColor }}>
  h1 { background-color: var(--backgroundColor); color: var(--textColor); }
</style>
```

(The `<script>` tag behaves differently: `define:vars` there does imply `is:inline`, so scripts are not bundled.)
In an Astro component, I have a wrapper `<aside>` that should only render when a named slot 'more' has content. Which utility do I use to check for slot content before rendering the wrapper?

Use the `Astro.slots` utility functions in your component frontmatter to test whether the named slot `more` received content, and render the `<aside>` only when it does. Note that fallback content alone can't detect this: Astro renders an empty slot when a slot element exists but has nothing to pass, and fallback content is only shown when no matching slot element is found.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/astro-components/
What does the 'silent' log level do in Astro, and how is it different from setting the '--silent' CLI flag?

The `'silent'` log level suppresses all logging output (the server runs with no console output). It is equivalent to the `--silent` CLI flag; the difference is only how you configure it (via logger configuration in `astro.config.mjs` versus passing the `--silent` flag to the Astro CLI).
What is the purpose of the `Loader.name` property on a build-time loader object, and where does Astro use it during the build process?

`Loader.name` is a unique string identifier for your build-time loader (added in `astro@5.0.0`). Astro uses it in logs and for conditional loading — specifically the `refreshContent` option of integrations, which can target loaders by name to decide which collections to reload. It is one of the two required properties of a `Loader` object, alongside `load()`.
I ran `astro telemetry disable` while experimenting and now want telemetry back on. What command re-enables it, and is that setting stored per project or per CLI user?

Run `astro telemetry enable` to turn telemetry back on. The setting is stored per CLI user, not per project: `astro telemetry` sets telemetry configuration for the current CLI user, so the enabled/disabled state applies across all of your projects on that machine. The anonymous data it reports gives the Astro team insight into which Astro features are most used.
How should a team structure its dependency policy for an Astro project that relies on an experimental flag, given how these features evolve between releases?
Why does Astro.request.url not include search parameters on prerendered pages but includes them when rendered on demand?

On prerendered pages, `Astro.request.url` lacks search parameters because they cannot be determined during static builds. For on-demand rendered routes, the URL includes search parameters since they are resolved from the actual server request at runtime.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/api-reference/#request
What is the difference between 'limited' and 'unsupported' support levels in Astro adapters, and when should I use each?
My component under test renders only static markup and uses no client:* directives — do I still need to register a client renderer with the container?

No. If your component uses no `client:*` directives, it renders as static HTML only — no hydration occurs. The docs state: "By default, a UI Framework component is not hydrated in the client. If no `client:*` directive is provided, its HTML is rendered onto the page without JavaScript." Client renderers are only "additionally needed to hydrate client-side components using `client:*` directives." A server renderer alone is sufficient.
My Astro config file lives at `config/astro.config.mjs` instead of the project root. Which CLI flag do I pass to `astro dev` to point at it, and how is that path resolved?

Pass `--config config/astro.config.mjs` to `astro dev`. The path is resolved relative to the project root (the current working directory by default, or the directory specified via `--root`). Example: `astro --config config/astro.config.mjs dev`.
What are the requirements for configuring the `variants` property in a custom font provider that uses local font files?

If I set `prefetch.defaultStrategy` to `'viewport'` but write `data-astro-prefetch="tap"` on one specific link, which strategy applies to that link, and what happens on links where the attribute has no value?

The link with `data-astro-prefetch="tap"` uses the `tap` strategy (explicit attribute value overrides the default). Links with `data-astro-prefetch` and no value use the configured `prefetch.defaultStrategy` (`viewport` in this case).
How do I show a loading placeholder while a `client:only` component is still booting on the client, and where does that placeholder markup go?

Put a child element marked `slot="fallback"` inside the component tag — Astro shows that markup only until the client component is available: ```astro
Loading

You must also pass the framework hint (e.g. `client:only="vue"`), or Astro fails with NoClientOnlyHint since it never runs the component and cannot guess the renderer.
How can you use local font files in your Astro project without using the built-in `local` provider?

Write your own font provider that reads the files itself: in `init()` use `context.root` (the project root, useful for resolving local file paths) to locate the files and `context.storage` for caching, then return the faces from `resolveFont()`, which has the signature `(options: ResolveFontOptions) => Awaitable<{ fonts: FontFaceData[] } | undefined>`. This keeps full control over the `FontFaceData` entries instead of configuring `fontProviders.local()`'s `variants`.

When should I use `container.renderToResponse(Component)` instead of `container.renderToString(Component)` in a test with Astro 7's Container API?

Use `renderToResponse()` when you need the full `Response` object (e.g., to inspect status, headers, or pass the response along); use `renderToString()` when you only want the rendered HTML as a string. Under the hood, `renderToString()` is a convenience that calls `renderToResponse()` and then `Response.text()`, so for plain HTML assertions in tests `renderToString()` is the simpler choice. Both accept the same `ContainerRenderOptions` object (`slots`, `props`, `request`, `params`, `locals`, `routeType`, `partial`) as a second argument.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/container-reference/

I have three Astro sites in `apps/` of a monorepo, each with its own `tsconfig.json`, and I want one CI job to type-check all of them. How should I invoke `astro check` per site, what do `--root` and `--tsconfig` change about what gets checked, and when would I reach for `--noSync`?

Run `astro check` once per site, either from each site's directory in sequence (e.g. `cd apps/site-a && astro check`) or from the monorepo root with `--root apps/site-a`; `--root <path>` sets a different root directory to check instead of the current working directory. `--tsconfig <path>` manually selects which `tsconfig.json` to use — without it, Astro finds or infers the project's config — so pass it when a site's tsconfig isn't where Astro would look. Reach for `--noSync` to skip running `astro sync` before checking (useful if sync already ran, or to avoid regenerating types in CI). Exits 1 on errors, making it CI-friendly.

I'm writing an integration that needs to branch its behavior on the project's `i18n.strategy` (e.g. `domains-prefix-always`) after the SSR build. Where in the integration hooks do I read that value, and what form does it arrive in?

I need my custom CDN cache provider to set ETag and Last-Modified headers on responses based on the CacheOptions passed to setHeaders(). Which utility from astro/cache/provider-utils should I use, and what parameters does it accept?

Use `setConditionalHeaders()` from `astro/cache/provider-utils` — the same helper used by the first-party Netlify, Vercel, and Cloudflare providers:

```ts
import { setConditionalHeaders } from 'astro/cache/provider-utils';

setConditionalHeaders(headers, options);
```

Its type is `(headers: Headers, options: CacheOptions) => void`: it sets `Last-Modified` and `ETag` on the `Headers` object from the corresponding `CacheOptions` values, so call it inside `setHeaders(options)` with the `Headers` you're building.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/cache-provider-reference/
How does the `renderToStaticMarkup` function contribute to the rendering process in Astro?

`renderToStaticMarkup()` is a renderer's server-side rendering function: it renders a framework component to HTML during SSR or static builds and returns `{ html: string; attrs?: Record<string, string> }`, where `attrs` are optional attributes forwarded to the client entrypoint for hydration. Astro calls it with the component, props, slots, and optional `AstroComponentMetadata` after the renderer's `check()` has claimed the component, so it is the step that turns framework components into static markup in the page output.
What's the practical difference between calling pathTag(path) and collectInvalidationTags({ path }) when implementing invalidate() in a custom provider?

`pathTag(path)` generates a single tag string `astro-path:{path}` for a given path. `collectInvalidationTags({ path })` returns an array of all tags needed for invalidation, including the path tag when `options.path` is set. Use `collectInvalidationTags()` in `invalidate()` to handle both tag and path invalidation uniformly on tag-only platforms.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/cache-provider-reference/

In my toolbar app's `init(canvas, app, server)` I call `server.send('my-app:my-message', { message: 'Hello!' })`. How do I receive a reply from the server inside the same app, and why should I bother prefixing the event name with my app ID?

Inside `init(canvas, app, server)`, use `server.on('my-app:my-reply', (data) => { ... })` to receive a reply from the server. Prefix the event name with your app ID (e.g., `my-app:my-message`) to avoid collisions with other toolbar apps or integrations listening on the same channel. The server-side integration should listen with `toolbar.on('my-app:my-message', ...)` and reply via `toolbar.send('my-app:my-reply', payload)`.

My CI job runs `astro check` and I need the build to fail if there are any type errors in `.astro` files. What exit code does `astro check` return when errors are found, and is this the default behavior or does it require a flag?

`astro check` exits with code **1** when errors are found. This is the default behavior — no flag is required. The `--minimumFailingSeverity` flag (defaulting to `error`) controls what severity triggers that exit code, but the exit code itself is always 1.
I want to test a full Astro page with its layout and all nested components. Is the Container API the right tool for this, or should I use a different approach?

The Container API renders components in isolation—it does not automatically compose full pages with layouts and nested components. For testing complete pages with layouts, use Astro's built-in testing utilities or integration tests that exercise the full routing and rendering pipeline. The Container API is designed for unit-testing individual components.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/container-reference/
How do you list all available fonts using the `registryFontProvider`?

Via the provider's `listFonts` callback, which returns `Object.keys(data)` — the font names fetched by `retrieveFonts(token)` in `init()`:

```ts
listFonts: () => { return Object.keys(data); },
```

Because `init()` populates `data` before listing, `listFonts()` yields every family in the registry. It is optional and must return `Awaitable<string[] | undefined>`.

My CI job runs `astro sync` as its own step and then `astro check`, but every `astro check` run kicks off another sync, wasting time on each build. What flag skips that pre-check sync, and when is it safe to use it?

Use `astro check --noSync`, which specifies that `astro sync` should not run before checking the project. It is safe when generated types are already current for your sources — e.g., your CI's preceding `astro sync` step has just run and nothing changed afterward. Keep in mind that `sync` generates `.astro/types.d.ts` plus the `astro:content`, `astro:env`, and `astro:actions` modules; if those types are missing or stale, `astro check` will report diagnostics against outdated type definitions, so re-run `astro sync` whenever type-relevant files change.
My `<Image>` source URL 302-redirects to a storage bucket host that isn't listed in `image.remotePatterns`, and the image fails to load. Which URL does Astro's pattern check apply to?

Both, in sequence: Astro follows HTTP redirects only when the image URL matches a `remotePatterns` entry, and then the final destination URL must also be among the allowed patterns. Your source URL passes the first check but the redirect target (the storage-bucket host) fails the second, so the image is rejected with `Remote image is not allowed`. Add the bucket host to `image.remotePatterns` (e.g. `{ protocol: 'https', hostname: '**.amazonaws.com' }`) or to `image.domains`, then the optimized image will load.
Why is it recommended to update Astro frequently while using experimental flags?

Because experimental features are not guaranteed to be stable and may include breaking changes even in small `patch` releases while under active development. Updating Astro frequently, and keeping up with release notes in the Astro changelog, informs you of any changes your project code needs; experimental feature docs are only updated for the current released version, so an outdated install can drift from what is documented. Frequent updates also let you remove flags that are deleted when features stabilize (as happened in v2, v5, and v6) and adopt new defaults.
If I'm using `client:only` on a component that renders only on the client, how can I show a loading message while it's booting up?

Use `slot="fallback"` on a child element of the `client:only` component; it displays until the client component is available: ```

How do you specify a range of weights for a variable font in the `weight` property of a local variant?

For a local variable font, set the `weight` property of the variant to a string range (e.g. `"100 900"`) instead of a single number. In the local provider’s `variants` array, each variant specifies that range along with `style` and `src`. For example:
```js
variants: [{
  weight: "100 900",
  style: "normal",
  src: ["./src/assets/fonts/InterVariable.woff2"]
}]
```
If the weight/style cannot be inferred from the file, set them manually; this is the local provider configuration for variable fonts in Astro 7.
How do I disable session support entirely in my Astro config, and what happens to the SSR bundle when I do?
Exactly when does the `init(canvas, app, server)` function of a `defineToolbarApp()` app run, and what happens if the user never clicks my app in the toolbar UI?

`init(canvas, app, server)` runs **once** when the app is loaded — either when the browser becomes idle **or** when the user clicks the app in the toolbar, whichever happens first. If the user never clicks the app, `init` still executes during the browser's idle period.

I need one route under `src/pages/` to serve a bare HTML fragment (no `<!DOCTYPE html>`, no Astro-injected head) to a server-side rendering library, while every other route stays a full page in default static mode. How should that route be set up, and what constraints apply to the value it exports?

In a custom local Astro image service, how do you determine the transformed image URL from the provided transformation options?

Through `getURL()`. In dev mode and on-demand rendering, `<Image />` and `getImage()` pass their options to `getURL()`, which serializes them into an endpoint URL (e.g. `/_image?href=...&w=...`), and the endpoint then calls `parseURL()` to recover the properties and hands them to `transform()`. At build time for static sites and prerendered routes, `getURL()` is unused: `transform()` is called directly with the options, and output files land in `dist/_astro` named by a hash of `propertiesToHash` (defaults to `['src', 'width', 'height', 'format', 'quality']`).

I'm unit-testing an isolated `Card.astro` component with `container.renderToString(Card, { partial: false })` and my snapshot now includes a full `<!DOCTYPE html>` page shell. Should I keep `partial: false` for this kind of component test?

No — drop `partial: false` and rely on the default. The `partial` option defaults to `true`, which renders the component in isolation without a full page shell; `partial: false` opts into full-page rendering including `<!DOCTYPE html>`, which is meant for pages rather than isolated unit tests of components. Note that page partials strip scoped styles/scripts from the output, so use default (`true`) partial rendering for component snapshots and reserve `partial: false` for testing full-page output.
How do I render `src/pages/[locale]/[slug].astro` in a test with `container.renderToString()` so that `Astro.params` inside the component resolves to `locale: "en"` and `slug: "getting-started"`?
What is the difference between using `fontProviders.google()` and `fontProviders.googleicons()` in terms of their intended use cases and available options?

`fontProviders.google()` retrieves fonts from Google Fonts for general typography, supporting `experimental.glyphs` and `experimental.variableAxis` options. `fontProviders.googleicons()` retrieves icons from Google Material Symbols, supporting only `experimental.glyphs` to reduce icon font size. Both use the same `fontProviders` import from `astro/config`.

What is the difference between `astro check --minimumFailingSeverity warning` and `astro check --minimumSeverity warning`? I keep seeing both flags and I'm not sure which one controls the exit code versus which one controls what gets printed to the console.

`--minimumFailingSeverity` controls the **exit code**: it sets the minimum severity that causes `astro check` to exit with an error code (defaults to `error`). `--minimumSeverity` controls **output**: it sets the minimum severity of diagnostics printed to the console (defaults to `hint`). So `--minimumFailingSeverity warning` makes warnings fail the build; `--minimumSeverity warning` hides hints from output without affecting the exit code.

A stylesheet targets the injected content with `.slot > :first-child`. When I switch from `<div set:html={content} />` to `<Fragment set:html={content} />`, why does that selector begin matching the first element of my HTML string?

Because `<Fragment />` emits no wrapper element, whereas the `<div>` did. With `<div set:html={content} />`, the `<div>` sat as the first child of `.slot`, so `.slot > :first-child` matched that wrapper, and the first element of your HTML string was nested one level deeper (`div > :first-child`), unreachable by that selector. With `<Fragment set:html={content} />` the wrapper disappears: the HTML string's first element becomes a direct child of `.slot` and, being the first one, is matched by `.slot > :first-child`. That wrapper-avoidance is exactly what `<Fragment />` is useful for with `set:*` directives.

How do you ensure type-safe access to your `params` and `props` when using TypeScript?

`--force` shows up in two unrelated situations in Astro 7: one about the content layer cache and one about an already-running background server. What does `astro build --force` do, and what does `astro dev --background --force` do?

`astro build --force` forces a full rebuild without clearing the content layer cache. `astro dev --background --force` stops any existing background dev server for the project and starts a new one, bypassing the normal check for running servers.
